Elegy On The Death Of Robert Ruisseaux1

Now Robin lies in his last lair, Heâll gabble rhyme, nor sing nae mair; Cauld poverty, wiâ hungry stare, Nae mair shall fear him; Nor anxious fear, nor cankert care, Eâer mair come near him. To tell the truth, they seldom fashâd him, Except the moment that they crushâd him; For sune as chance or fate had hushâd âem Thoâ eâer sae short. Then wiâ a rhyme or sang he lashâd âem, And thought it sport. [Footnote 1: Ruisseaux is French for rivulets or âburns,â a translation of his name.] Thoâhe was bred to kintra-wark, And counted was baith wight and stark, Yet that was never Robinâs mark To mak a man; But tell him, he was learnâd and clark, Ye roosâd him then!





Epistle To John Goldie, In Kilmarnock

Author Of The Gospel Recovered.âAugust, 1785 O Gowdie, terror oâ the whigs, Dread oâ blackcoats and revârend wigs! Sour Bigotry, on her last legs, Girns anâ looks back, Wishing the ten Egyptian plagues May seize you quick. Poor gapinâ, glowrinâ Superstition! Waeâs me, sheâs in a sad condition: Fye: bring Black Jock,1 her state physician, To see her water; Alas, thereâs ground for great suspicion Sheâll neâer get better. Enthusiasmâs past redemption, Gane in a gallopinâ consumption: Not aâ her quacks, wiâ aâ their gumption, Can ever mend her; Her feeble pulse gies strong presumption, Sheâll soon surrender. Auld Orthodoxy lang did grapple, For every hole to get a stapple; But now she fetches at the thrapple, Anâ fights for breath; Haste, gie her name up in the chapel,2 Near unto death. Itâs you anâ Taylor3 are the chief To blame for aâ this black mischief; [Footnote 1: The Rev. J. Russell, Kilmarnock.âR. B.] [Footnote 2: Mr. Russellâs Kirk.âR. B.] [Footnote 3: Dr. Taylor of Norwich.âR. B.] But, could the Lordâs ain folk get leave, A toom tar barrel Anâ twa red peats wad bring relief, And end the quarrel. For me, my skillâs but very smaâ, Anâ skill in prose Iâve nane avaâ; But quietlins-wise, between us twa, Weel may you speed! And thoâ they sud your sair miscaâ, Neâer fash your head. Eâen swinge the dogs, and thresh them sicker! The mair they squeel aye chap the thicker; And still âmang hands a hearty bicker Oâ something stout; It gars an owthorâs pulse beat quicker, And helps his wit. Thereâs naething like the honest nappy; Whareâll ye eâer see men sae happy, Or women sonsie, saft anâ sappy, âTween morn and morn, As them wha like to taste the drappie, In glass or horn? Iâve seen me dazed upon a time, I scarce could wink or see a styme; Just ae half-mutchkin does me prime,â Ought less is littleâ Then back I rattle on the rhyme, As glegâs a whittle.





The Holy Fair1

A robe of seeming truth and trust Hid crafty Observation; And secret hung, with poisonâd crust, The dirk of Defamation: [Footnote 1: âHoly Fairâ is a common phrase in the west of Scotland for a sacramental occasion.âR. B.] A mask that like the gorget showâd, Dye-varying on the pigeon; And for a mantle large and broad, He wrapt him in Religion. Hypocrisy A-La-Mode Upon a simmer Sunday morn When Natureâs face is fair, I walked forth to view the corn, Anâ snuff the caller air. The rising sun owre Galston muirs Wiâ glorious light was glintin; The hares were hirplin down the furrs, The lavârocks they were chantin Fuâ sweet that day. As lightsomely I glowrâd abroad, To see a scene sae gay, Three hizzies, early at the road, Cam skelpin up the way. Twa had manteeles oâ dolefuâ black, But ane wiâ lyart lining; The third, that gaed a wee a-back, Was in the fashion shining Fuâ gay that day. The twa appearâd like sisters twin, In feature, form, anâ claes; Their visage witherâd, lang anâ thin, Anâ sour as only slaes: The third cam up, hap-stap-anâ-lowp, As light as ony lambie, Anâ wiâa curchie low did stoop, As soon as eâer she saw me, Fuâ kind that day. Wiâ bonnet aff, quoth I, âSweet lass, I think ye seem to ken me; Iâm sure Iâve seen that bonie face But yet I canna name ye.â Quoâ she, anâ laughin as she spak, Anâ taks me by the hanâs, âYe, for my sake, hae gien the feck Of aâ the ten commanâs A screed some day.â âMy name is Funâyour cronie dear, The nearest friend ye hae; Anâ this is Superstitution here, Anâ thatâs Hypocrisy. Iâm gaun to Mauchline Holy Fair, To spend an hour in daffin: Gin yeâll go there, yon runklâd pair, We will get famous laughin At them this day.â Quoth I, âWiâ aâ my heart, Iâll doât; Iâll get my Sundayâs sark on, Anâ meet you on the holy spot; Faith, weâse hae fine remarkin!â Then I gaed hame at crowdie-time, Anâ soon I made me ready; For roads were clad, frae side to side, Wiâ mony a weary body In droves that day. Here farmers gash, in ridin graith, Gaed hoddin by their cotters; There swankies young, in braw braid-claith, Are springing owre the gutters. The lasses, skelpin barefit, thrang, In silks anâ scarlets glitter; Wiâ sweet-milk cheese, in mony a whang, Anâ farls, bakâd wiâ butter, Fuâ crump that day. When by the plate we set our nose, Weel heaped up wiâ haâpence, A greedy glowr black-bonnet throws, Anâ we maun draw our tippence. Then in we go to see the show: On evâry side theyâre gathârin; Some carrying dails, some chairs anâ stools, Anâ some are busy blethârin Right loud that day. Here stands a shed to fend the showârs, Anâ screen our countra gentry; There Racer Jess,2 anâ twa-three whores, Are blinkin at the entry. Here sits a raw oâ tittlin jads, Wiâ heaving breast anâ bare neck; Anâ there a batch oâ wabster lads, Blackguarding frae Kilmarnock, For fun this day. Here, some are thinkin on their sins, Anâ some upoâ their claes; Ane curses feet that fylâd his shins, Anither sighs anâ prays: On this hand sits a chosen swatch, Wiâ screwed-up, grace-proud faces; On that a set oâ chaps, at watch, Thrang winkin on the lasses To chairs that day. O happy is that man, anâ blest! Nae wonder that it pride him! Whase ain dear lass, that he likes best, Comes clinkin down beside him! Wiâ arms reposâd on the chair back, He sweetly does compose him; Which, by degrees, slips round her neck, Anâs loof upon her bosom, Unkend that day. Now aâ the congregation oâer Is silent expectation; For Moodie3 speels the holy door, Wiâ tidings oâ damnation: [Footnote 2: Racer Jess (d. 1813) was a half-witted daughter of Possie Nansie. She was a great pedestrian.] [Footnote 3: Rev. Alexander Moodie of Riccarton.] Should Hornie, as in ancient days, âMang sons oâ God present him, The vera sight oâ Moodieâs face, To âs ain het hame had sent him Wiâ fright that day. Hear how he clears the point oâ faith Wiâ rattlin and wiâ thumpin! Now meekly calm, now wild in wrath, Heâs stampin, anâ heâs jumpin! His lengthenâd chin, his turned-up snout, His eldritch squeel anâ gestures, O how they fire the heart devout, Like cantharidian plaisters On sic a day! But hark! the tent has changâd its voice, Thereâs peace anâ rest nae langer; For aâ the real judges rise, They canna sit for anger, Smith4 opens out his cauld harangues, On practice and on morals; Anâ aff the godly pour in thrangs, To gie the jars anâ barrels A lift that day. What signifies his barren shine, Of moral powers anâ reason? His English style, anâ gesture fine Are aâ clean out oâ season. Like Socrates or Antonine, Or some auld pagan heathen, The moral man he does define, But neâer a word oâ faith in Thatâs right that day. In guid time comes an antidote Against sic poisonâd nostrum; For Peebles,5 frae the water-fit, Ascends the holy rostrum: [Footnote 4: Rev. George Smith of Galston.] [Footnote 5: Rev. Wm. Peebles of Newton-upon-Ayr.] See, up heâs got, the word oâ God, Anâ meek anâ mim has viewâd it, While Common-sense has taen the road, Anâ aff, anâ up the Cowgate6 Fast, fast that day. Wee Miller7 neist the guard relieves, Anâ Orthodoxy raibles, Thoâ in his heart he weel believes, Anâ thinks it auld wivesâ fables: But faith! the birkie wants a manse, So, cannilie he hums them; Althoâ his carnal wit anâ sense Like hafflins-wise oâercomes him At times that day. Now, butt anâ ben, the change-house fills, Wiâ yill-caup commentators; Here âs cryin out for bakes and gills, Anâ there the pint-stowp clatters; While thick anâ thrang, anâ loud anâ lang, Wiâ logic anâ wiâ scripture, They raise a din, that in the end Is like to breed a rupture Oâ wrath that day. Leeze me on drink! it gies us mair Than either school or college; It kindles wit, it waukens lear, It pangs us fou oâ knowledge: Beât whisky-gill or penny wheep, Or ony stronger potion, It never fails, or drinkin deep, To kittle up our notion, By night or day. The lads anâ lasses, blythely bent To mind baith saul anâ body, Sit round the table, weel content, Anâ steer about the toddy: [Footnote 6: A street so called which faces the tent in Mauchline.âR. B.] [Footnote 7: Rev. Alex. Miller, afterward of Kilmaurs.] On this aneâs dress, anâ that aneâs leuk, Theyâre makin observations; While some are cozie iâ the neuk, Anâ forming assignations To meet some day. But now the Lordâs ain trumpet touts, Till aâ the hills are rairin, And echoes back return the shouts; Black Russell is na sparin: His piercin words, like Highlanâ swords, Divide the joints anâ marrow; His talk oâ Hell, whare devils dwell, Our vera âsauls does harrowâ Wiâ fright that day! A vast, unbottomâd, boundless pit, Fillâd fou oâ lowin brunstane, Whase raging flame, anâ scorching heat, Wad melt the hardest whun-stane! The half-asleep start up wiâ fear, Anâ think they hear it roarin; When presently it does appear, âTwas but some neibor snorin Asleep that day. âTwad be owre lang a tale to tell, How mony stories past; Anâ how they crouded to the yill, When they were aâ dismist; How drink gaed round, in cogs anâ caups, Amang the furms anâ benches; Anâ cheese anâ bread, frae womenâs laps, Was dealt about in lunches Anâ dawds that day. In comes a gawsie, gash guidwife, Anâ sits down by the fire, Syne draws her kebbuck anâ her knife; The lasses they are shyer: The auld guidmen, about the grace Frae side to side they bother; Till some ane by his bonnet lays, Anâ gies themât like a tether, Fuâ lang that day. Waesucks! for him that gets nae lass, Or lasses that hae naething! Smaâ need has he to say a grace, Or melvie his braw claithing! O wives, be mindfuâ ance yourselâ How bonie lads ye wanted; Anâ dinna for a kebbuck-heel Let lasses be affronted On sic a day! Now Clinkumbell, wiâ rattlin tow, Begins to jow anâ croon; Some swagger hame the best they dow, Some wait the afternoon. At slaps the billies halt a blink, Till lasses strip their shoon: Wiâ faith anâ hope, anâ love anâ drink, Theyâre aâ in famous tune For crack that day. How mony hearts this day converts Oâ sinners and oâ lasses! Their hearts oâ stane, gin night, are gane As saft as ony flesh is: Thereâs some are fou oâ love divine; Thereâs some are fou oâ brandy; Anâ mony jobs that day begin, May end in houghmagandie Some ither day.





Third Epistle To J. Lapraik

Guid speed and furder to you, Johnie, Guid health, hale hanâs, anâ weather bonie; Now, when yeâre nickin down fuâ cannie The staff oâ bread, May ye neâer want a stoup oâ branây To clear your head. May Boreas never thresh your rigs, Nor kick your rickles aff their legs, Sendin the stuff oâer muirs anâ haggs Like drivin wrack; But may the tapmost grain that wags Come to the sack. Iâm bizzie, too, anâ skelpin at it, But bitter, daudin showers hae wat it; Sae my auld stumpie pen I gat it Wiâ muckle wark, Anâ took my jocteleg an whatt it, Like ony clark. Itâs now twa month that Iâm your debtor, For your braw, nameless, dateless letter, Abusin me for harsh ill-nature On holy men, While deil a hair yourselâ yeâre better, But mair profane. But let the kirk-folk ring their bells, Letâs sing about our noble selâs: Weâll cry nae jads frae heathen hills To help, or roose us; But browster wives anâ whisky stills, They are the muses. Your friendship, Sir, I winna quat it, Anâ if ye makâ objections at it, Then hand in neive some day weâll knot it, Anâ witness take, Anâ when wiâ usquabae weâve wat it It winna break. But if the beast anâ branks be sparâd Till kye be gaun without the herd, And aâ the vittel in the yard, Anâ theekit right, I mean your ingle-side to guard Ae winter night. Then muse-inspirinâ aqua-vitae Shall make us baith sae blythe and witty, Till ye forget yeâre auld anâ gatty, Anâ be as canty As ye were nine years less than threttyâ Sweet ane anâ twenty! But stooks are cowpit wiâ the blast, And now the sinn keeks in the west, Then I maun rin amang the rest, Anâ quat my chanter; Sae I subscribe myselfâ in haste, Yours, Rab the Ranter.





Epistle To The Rev. John Mâmath

Sept. 13, 1785. Inclosing A Copy Of âHoly Willieâs Prayer,â Which He Had Requested, Sept. 17, 1785 While at the stook the shearers cowâr To shun the bitter blaudinâ showâr, Or in gulravage rinnin scowr To pass the time, To you I dedicate the hour In idle rhyme. My musie, tirâd wiâ mony a sonnet On gown, anâ banâ, anâ douse black bonnet, Is grown right eerie now sheâs done it, Lest they should blame her, Anâ rouse their holy thunder on it An anathem her. I own âtwas rash, anâ rather hardy, That I, a simple, country bardie, Should meddle wiâ a pack sae sturdy, Wha, if they ken me, Can easy, wiâ a single wordie, Lowse hell upon me. But I gae mad at their grimaces, Their sighin, cantin, grace-proud faces, Their three-mile prayers, anâ half-mile graces, Their raxin conscience, Whase greed, revenge, anâ pride disgraces Waur nor their nonsense. Thereâs Gawân, miscaâd waur than a beast, Wha has mair honour in his breast Than mony scores as guidâs the priest Wha sae abusâd him: And may a bard no crack his jest What way theyâve usâd him? See him, the poor manâs friend in need, The gentleman in word anâ deedâ Anâ shall his fame anâ honour bleed By worthless, skellums, Anâ not a muse erect her head To cowe the blellums? O Pope, had I thy satireâs darts To gie the rascals their deserts, Iâd rip their rotten, hollow hearts, Anâ tell aloud Their jugglin hocus-pocus arts To cheat the crowd. God knows, Iâm no the thing I should be, Nor am I even the thing I could be, But twenty times I rather would be An atheist clean, Than under gospel colours hid be Just for a screen. An honest man may like a glass, An honest man may like a lass, But mean revenge, anâ malice fause Heâll still disdain, Anâ then cry zeal for gospel laws, Like some we ken. They take religion in their mouth; They talk oâ mercy, grace, anâ truth, For what?âto gie their malice skouth On some puir wight, Anâ hunt him down, owre right and ruth, To ruin straight. All hail, Religion! maid divine! Pardon a muse sae mean as mine, Who in her rough imperfect line Thus daurs to name thee; To stigmatise false friends of thine Can neâer defame thee. Thoâ blotchât and foul wiâ mony a stain, Anâ far unworthy of thy train, With trembling voice I tune my strain, To join with those Who boldly dare thy cause maintain In spite of foes: In spite oâ crowds, in spite oâ mobs, In spite oâ undermining jobs, In spite oâ dark banditti stabs At worth anâ merit, By scoundrels, even wiâ holy robes, But hellish spirit. O Ayr! my dear, my native ground, Within thy presbyterial bound A candid liberal band is found Of public teachers, As men, as Christians too, renownâd, Anâ manly preachers. Sir, in that circle you are namâd; Sir, in that circle you are famâd; Anâ some, by whom your doctrineâs blamâd (Which gies you honour) Even, sir, by them your heartâs esteemâd, Anâ winning manner. Pardon this freedom I have taâen, Anâ if impertinent Iâve been, Impute it not, good Sir, in ane Whase heart neâer wrangâd ye, But to his utmost would befriend Ought that belangâd ye.





Second Epistle to Davie

A Brother Poet Auld Neibour, Iâm three times doubly oâer your debtor, For your auld-farrant, frienâly letter; Thoâ I maun sayât I doubt ye flatter, Ye speak sae fair; For my puir, silly, rhymin clatter Some less maun sair. Hale be your heart, hale be your fiddle, Lang may your elbuck jink diddle, To cheer you throâ the weary widdle Oâ warâly cares; Till barinsâ barins kindly cuddle Your auld grey hairs. But Davie, lad, Iâm red yeâre glaikit; Iâm tauld the muse ye hae negleckit; An, gif itâs sae, ye sud by lickit Until ye fyke; Sic haunâs as you sud neâer be faikit, Be hainât wha like. For me, Iâm on Parnassusâ brink, Rivin the words to gar them clink; Whiles dazed wiâ love, whiles dazed wiâ drink, Wiâ jads or masons; Anâ whiles, but aye owre late, I think Braw sober lessons. Of aâ the thoughtless sons oâ man, Commenâ to me the bardie clan; Except it be some idle plan Oâ rhymin clink, The devil haet,âthat I sud banâ They ever think. Nae thought, nae view, nae scheme oâ livin, Nae cares to gie us joy or grievin, But just the pouchie put the neive in, Anâ while oughtâs there, Then, hiltie, skiltie, we gae scrievinâ, Anâ fash nae mair. Leeze me on rhyme! itâs aye a treasure, My chief, amaist my only pleasure; At hame, a-fielâ, at wark, or leisure, The Muse, poor hizzie! Thoâ rough anâ raploch be her measure, Sheâs seldom lazy. Haud to the Muse, my daintie Davie: The warlâ may play you mony a shavie; But for the Muse, sheâll never leave ye, Thoâ eâer sae puir, Na, even thoâ limpin wiâ the spavie Frae door tae door.





SongâYoung Peggy Blooms

TuneââLoch Eroch-side.â
Young Peggy blooms our boniest lass, Her blush is like the morning, The rosy dawn, the springing grass, With early gems adorning. Her eyes outshine the radiant beams That gild the passing shower, And glitter oâer the crystal streams, And cheer each freshâning flower. Her lips, more than the cherries bright, A richer dye has graced them; They charm thâ admiring gazerâs sight, And sweetly tempt to taste them; Her smile is as the evening mild, When featherâd pairs are courting, And little lambkins wanton wild, In playful bands disporting. Were Fortune lovely Peggyâs foe, Such sweetness would relent her; As blooming spring unbends the brow Of surly, savage Winter. Detractionâs eye no aim can gain, Her winning powârs to lessen; And fretful Envy grins in vain The poisonâd tooth to fasten. Ye Powârs of Honour, Love, and Truth, From evâry ill defend her! Inspire the highly-favourâd youth The destinies intend her: Still fan the sweet connubial flame Responsive in each bosom; And bless the dear parental name With many a filial blossom.





SongâFarewell To Ballochmyle

TuneââMiss Forbeâs farewell to Banff.â
The Catrine woods were yellow seen, The flowers decayâd on Catrine lee, Nae lavârock sang on hillock green, But nature sickenâd on the eâe. Throâ faded groves Maria sang, Herselâ in beautyâs bloom the while; And aye the wild-wood ehoes rang, Fareweel the braes oâ Ballochmyle! Low in your wintry beds, ye flowers, Again yeâll flourish fresh and fair; Ye birdies dumb, in withâring bowers, Again yeâll charm the vocal air. But here, alas! for me nae mair Shall birdie charm, or floweret smile; Fareweel the bonie banks of Ayr, Fareweel, fareweel! sweet Ballochmyle!





FragmentâHer Flowing Locks

Her flowing locks, the ravenâs wing, Adown her neck and bosom hing; How sweet unto that breast to cling, And round that neck entwine her! Her lips are roses wat wiâ dew, Oâ what a feast her bonie mouâ! Her cheeks a mair celestial hue, A crimson still diviner!





Halloween1

[Footnote 1: Is thought to be a night when witches, devils, and other mischief-making beings are abroad on their baneful midnight errands; particularly those aerial people, the fairies, are said on that night to hold a grand anniversary,.âR.B.]

The following poem will, by many readers, be well enough understood; but for the sake of those who are unacquainted with the manners and traditions of the country where the scene is cast, notes are added to give some account of the principal charms and spells of that night, so big with prophecy to the peasantry in the west of Scotland. The passion of prying into futurity makes a striking part of the history of human nature in its rude state, in all ages and nations; and it may be some entertainment to a philosophic mind, if any such honour the author with a perusal, to see the remains of it among the more unenlightened in our own.âR.B.

Yes! let the rich deride, the proud disdain, The simple pleasure of the lowly train; To me more dear, congenial to my heart, One native charm, than all the gloss of art.âGoldsmith. Upon that night, when fairies light On Cassilis Downans2 dance, Or owre the lays, in splendid blaze, On sprightly coursers prance; Or for Colean the rout is taâen, Beneath the moonâs pale beams; There, up the Cove,3 to stray anâ rove, Amang the rocks and streams To sport that night; [Footnote 2: Certain little, romantic, rocky, green hills, in the neighbourhood of the ancient seat of the Earls of Cassilis.âR.B.] [Footnote 3: A noted cavern near Colean house, called the Cove of Colean; which, as well as Cassilis Downans, is famed, in country story, for being a favorite haunt of fairies.âR.B.] Amang the bonie winding banks, Where Doon rins, wimplin, clear; Where Bruce4 ance rulâd the martial ranks, Anâ shook his Carrick spear; Some merry, friendly, countra-folks Together did convene, To burn their nits, anâ pou their stocks, Anâ haud their Halloween Fuâ blythe that night. [Footnote 4: The famous family of that name, the ancestors of Robert, the great deliverer of his country, were Earls of Carrick.âR.B.] The lasses feat, anâ cleanly neat, Mair braw than when theyâre fine; Their faces blythe, fuâ sweetly kythe, Hearts leal, anâ warm, anâ kinâ: The lads sae trig, wiâ wooer-babs Weel-knotted on their garten; Some unco blate, anâ some wiâ gabs Gar lassesâ hearts gang startin Whiles fast at night. Then, first anâ foremost, throâ the kail, Their stocks5 maun aâ be sought ance; [Footnote 5: The first ceremony of Halloween is pulling each a âstock,â or plant of kail. They must go out, hand in hand, with eyes shut, and pull the first they meet with: its being big or little, straight or crooked, is prophetic of the size and shape of the grand object of all their spellsâthe husband or wife. If any âyird,â or earth, stick to the root, that is âtocher,â or fortune; and the taste of the âcustock,â that is, the heart of the stem, is indicative of the natural temper and disposition. Lastly, the stems, or, to give them their ordinary appellation, the ârunts,â are placed somewhere above the head of the door; and the Christian names of the people whom chance brings into the house are, according to the priority of placing the ârunts,â the names in question.âR. B.] They steek their een, and grape anâ wale For muckle anes, anâ straught anes. Poor havârel Will fell aff the drift, Anâ wandered throâ the bow-kail, Anâ pouât for want oâ better shift A runt was like a sow-tail Sae bowât that night. Then, straught or crooked, yird or nane, They roar anâ cry aâ throuâther; The vera wee-things, toddlin, rin, Wiâ stocks out owre their shouther: Anâ gif the custockâs sweet or sour, Wiâ joctelegs they taste them; Syne coziely, aboon the door, Wiâ cannie care, theyâve placâd them To lie that night. The lassies staw frae âmang them aâ, To pou their stalks oâ corn;6 But Rab slips out, anâ jinks about, Behint the muckle thorn: He grippit Nelly hard and fast: Loud skirlâd aâ the lasses; But her tap-pickle maist was lost, Whan kiutlin in the fause-house7 Wiâ him that night. [Footnote 6: They go to the barnyard, and pull each, at three different times, a stalk of oats. If the third stalk wants the âtop-pickle,â that is, the grain at the top of the stalk, the party in question will come to the marriage-bed anything but a maid.âR.B.] [Footnote 7: When the corn is in a doubtful state, by being too green or wet, the stack-builder, by means of old timber, etc., makes a large apartment in his stack, with an opening in the side which is fairest exposed to the wind: this he calls a âfause-house.ââR.B.] The auld guid-wifeâs weel-hoordit nits8 Are round anâ round dividend, Anâ mony lads anâ lassesâ fates Are there that night decided: Some kindle couthie side by side, And burn thegither trimly; Some start awa wiâ saucy pride, Anâ jump out owre the chimlie Fuâ high that night. [Footnote 8: Burning the nuts is a favorite charm. They name the lad and lass to each particular nut, as they lay them in the fire; and according as they burn quietly together, or start from beside one another, the course and issue of the courtship will be.âR.B.] Jean slips in twa, wiâ tentie eâe; Wha âtwas, she wadna tell; But this is Jock, anâ this is me, She says in to herselâ: He bleezâd owre her, anâ she owre him, As they wad never mair part: Till fuff! he started up the lum, Anâ Jean had eâen a sair heart To seeât that night. Poor Willie, wiâ his bow-kail runt, Was brunt wiâ primsie Mallie; Anâ Mary, nae doubt, took the drunt, To be comparâd to Willie: Mallâs nit lap out, wiâ pridefuâ fling, Anâ her ain fit, it brunt it; While Willie lap, and swore by jing, âTwas just the way he wanted To be that night. Nell had the fause-house in her minâ, She pits hersel anâ Rob in; In loving bleeze they sweetly join, Till white in ase theyâre sobbin: Nellâs heart was dancin at the view; She whisperâd Rob to leuk forât: Rob, stownlins, prieâd her bonie mouâ, Fuâ cozie in the neuk forât, Unseen that night. But Merran sat behint their backs, Her thoughts on Andrew Bell: She leaâes them gashin at their cracks, Anâ slips outâby herselâ; She throâ the yard the nearest taks, Anâ for the kiln she goes then, Anâ darklins grapit for the bauks, And in the blue-clue9 throws then, Right fearât that night. [Footnote 9: Whoever would, with success, try this spell, must strictly observe these directions: Steal out, all alone, to the kiln, and darkling, throw into the âpotâ a clue of blue yarn; wind it in a new clue off the old one; and, toward the latter end, something will hold the thread: demand, âWha hauds?â i.e., who holds? and answer will be returned from the kiln-pot, by naming the Christian and surname of your future spouse.âR.B.] Anâ ay she winât, anâ ay she swatâ I wat she made nae jaukin; Till something held within the pat, Good Lord! but she was quaukin! But whether âtwas the deil himsel, Or whether âtwas a bauk-enâ, Or whether it was Andrew Bell, She did na wait on talkin To spier that night. Wee Jenny to her graunie says, âWill ye go wiâ me, graunie? Iâll eat the apple at the glass,10 I gat frae uncle Johnie:â She fuffât her pipe wiâ sic a lunt, In wrath she was sae vapârin, She noticât na an aizle brunt Her braw, new, worset apron Out throâ that night. [Footnote 10: Take a candle and go alone to a looking-glass; eat an apple before it, and some traditions say you should comb your hair all the time; the face of your conjungal companion, to be, will be seen in the glass, as if peeping over your shoulder.âR.B.] âYe little skelpie-limmerâs face! I daur you try sic sportin, As seek the foul thief ony place, For him to spae your fortune: Nae doubt but ye may get a sight! Great cause ye hae to fear it; For mony a ane has gotten a fright, Anâ livâd anâ died deleerit, On sic a night. âAe hairst afore the Sherra-moor, I mindât as weelâs yestreenâ I was a gilpey then, Iâm sure I was na past fyfteen: The simmer had been cauld anâ wat, Anâ stuff was unco green; Anâ eye a rantin kirn we gat, Anâ just on Halloween It fell that night. âOur stibble-rig was Rab MâGraen, A clever, sturdy fallow; His sin gat Eppie Sim wiâ wean, That lived in Achmacalla: He gat hemp-seed,11 I mind it weel, Anâhe made unco light oât; But mony a day was by himselâ, He was sae sairly frighted That vera night.â [Footnote 11: Steal out, unperceived, and sow a handful of hemp-seed, harrowing it with anything you can conveniently draw after you. Repeat now and then: âHemp-seed, I saw thee, hemp-seed, I saw thee; and him (or her) that is to be my true love, come after me and pou thee.â Look over your left shoulder, and you will see the appearance of the person invoked, in the attitude of pulling hemp. Some traditions say, âCome after me and shaw thee,â that is, show thyself; in which case, it simply appears. Others omit the harrowing, and say: âCome after me and harrow thee.ââR.B.] Then up gat fechtin Jamie Fleck, Anâ he swoor by his conscience, That he could saw hemp-seed a peck; For it was aâ but nonsense: The auld guidman raught down the pock, Anâ out a handfuâ gied him; Syne bad him slip fraeâ mang the folk, Sometime when nae ane seeâd him, Anâ tryât that night. He marches throâ amang the stacks, Thoâ he was something sturtin; The graip he for a harrow taks, Anâ haurls at his curpin: And evâry now anâ then, he says, âHemp-seed I saw thee, Anâ her that is to be my lass Come after me, anâ draw thee As fast this night.â He wistlâd up Lord Lennoxâ March To keep his courage cherry; Althoâ his hair began to arch, He was sae fleyâd anâ eerie: Till presently he hears a squeak, Anâ then a grane anâ gruntle; He by his shouther gae a keek, Anâ tumbled wiâ a wintle Out-owre that night. He roarâd a horrid murder-shout, In dreadfuâ desperation! Anâ young anâ auld come rinnin out, Anâ hear the sad narration: He swoor âtwas hilchin Jean MâCraw, Or crouchie Merran Humphieâ Till stop! she trotted throâ them aâ; And wha was it but grumphie Asteer that night! Meg fain wad to the barn gaen, To winn three wechts oâ naething;12 But for to meet the deil her lane, She pat but little faith in: [Footnote 12: This charm must likewise be performed unperceived and alone. You go to the barn, and open both doors, taking them off the hinges, if possible; for there is danger that the being about to appear may shut the doors, and do you some mischief. Then take that instrument used in winnowing the corn, which in our country dialect we call a âwecht,â and go through all the attitudes of letting down corn against the wind. Repeat it three times, and the third time an apparition will pass through the barn, in at the windy door and out at the other, having both the figure in question, and the appearance or retinue, marking the employment or station in life.âR.B.] She gies the herd a pickle nits, Anâ twa red cheekit apples, To watch, while for the barn she sets, In hopes to see Tam Kipples That vera night. She turns the key wiâ cannie thraw, Anâowre the threshold ventures; But first on Sawnie gies a caâ, Syne baudly in she enters: A ratton rattlâd up the waâ, Anâ she cryâd Lord preserve her! Anâ ran throâ midden-hole anâ aâ, Anâ prayâd wiâ zeal and fervour, Fuâ fast that night. They hoyât out Will, wiâ sair advice; They hecht him some fine braw ane; It chancâd the stack he faddomât thrice13 Was timmer-propt for thrawin: He taks a swirlie auld moss-oak For some black, grousome carlin; Anâ loot a winze, anâ drew a stroke, Till skin in blypes cam haurlin Affâs nieves that night. [Footnote 13: Take an opportunity of going unnoticed to a âbear-stack,â and fathom it three times round. The last fathom of the last time you will catch in your arms the appearance of your future conjugal yoke-fellow.âR.B.] A wanton widow Leezie was, As cantie as a kittlen; But och! that night, amang the shaws, She gat a fearfuâ settlin! She throâ the whins, anâ by the cairn, Anâ owre the hill gaed scrievin; Whare three lairdsâ lanâs met at a burn,14 To dip her left sark-sleeve in, Was bent that night. [Footnote 14: You go out, one or more (for this is a social spell), to a south running spring, or rivulet, where âthree lairdsâ lands meet,â and dip your left shirt sleeve. Go to bed in sight of a fire, and hang your wet sleeve before it to dry. Lie awake, and, some time near midnight, an apparition, having the exact figure of the grand object in question, will come and turn the sleeve, as if to dry the other side of it.âR.B.] Whiles owre a linn the burnie plays, As throâ the glen it wimplât; Whiles round a rocky scar it strays, Whiles in a wiel it dimplât; Whiles glitterâd to the nightly rays, Wiâ bickerinâ, dancinâ dazzle; Whiles cookit undeneath the braes, Below the spreading hazel Unseen that night. Amang the brachens, on the brae, Between her anâ the moon, The deil, or else an outler quey, Gat up anâ gaâe a croon: Poor Leezieâs heart maist lap the hool; Near lavârock-height she jumpit, But mist a fit, anâ in the pool Out-owre the lugs she plumpit, Wiâ a plunge that night. In order, on the clean hearth-stane, The luggies15 three are ranged; Anâ evâry time great care is taâen To see them duly changed: Auld uncle John, wha wedlockâs joys Sinâ Marâs-year did desire, Because he gat the toom dish thrice, He heavâd them on the fire In wrath that night. [Footnote 15: Take three dishes, put clean water in one, foul water in another, and leave the third empty; blindfold a person and lead him to the hearth where the dishes are ranged; he (or she) dips the left hand; if by chance in the clean water, the future (husband or) wife will come to the bar of matrimony a maid; if in the foul, a widow; if in the empty dish, it foretells, with equal certainty, no marriage at all. It is repeated three times, and every time the arrangement of the dishes is altered.âR.B.] Wiâ merry sangs, anâ friendly cracks, I wat they did na weary; And unco tales, anâ funnie jokesâ Their sports were cheap anâ cheery: Till butterâd sowens,16 wiâ fragrant lunt, [Footnote 16: Sowens, with butter instead of milk to them, is always the Halloween Supper.âR.B.] Set aâ their gabs a-steerin; Syne, wiâ a social glass oâ strunt, They parted aff careerin Fuâ blythe that night.





To A Mouse, On Turning Her Up In Her Nest With The Plough, November, 1785

Wee, sleekit, cowârin, timârous beastie, O, what a panicâs in thy breastie! Thou need na start awa sae hasty, Wiâ bickering brattle! I wad be laith to rin anâ chase thee, Wiâ murdâring pattle! Iâm truly sorry manâs dominion, Has broken natureâs social union, Anâ justifies that ill opinion, Which makes thee startle At me, thy poor, earth-born companion, Anâ fellow-mortal! I doubt na, whiles, but thou may thieve; What then? poor beastie, thou maun live! A daimen icker in a thrave âS a smaâ request; Iâll get a blessin wiâ the lave, Anâ never missât! Thy wee bit housie, too, in ruin! Itâs silly waâs the winâs are strewin! Anâ naething, now, to big a new ane, Oâ foggage green! Anâ bleak Decemberâs winds ensuin, Baith snell anâ keen! Thou saw the fields laid bare anâ waste, Anâ weary winter comin fast, Anâ cozie here, beneath the blast, Thou thought to dwellâ Till crash! the cruel coulter past Out throâ thy cell. That wee bit heap oâ leaves anâ stibble, Has cost thee mony a weary nibble! Now thouâs turnâd out, for aâ thy trouble, But house or hald, To thole the winterâs sleety dribble, Anâ cranreuch cauld! But, Mousie, thou art no thy lane, In proving foresight may be vain; The best-laid schemes oâ mice an âmen Gang aft agley, Anâleaâe us nought but grief anâ pain, For promisâd joy! Still thou art blest, comparâd wiâ me The present only toucheth thee: But, Och! I backward cast my eâe. On prospects drear! Anâ forward, thoâ I canna see, I guess anâ fear!





Epitaph On John Dove, Innkeeper

Here lies Johnie Pigeon; What was his religion? Whaeâer desires to ken, To some other warlâ Maun follow the carl, For here Johnie Pigeon had nane! Strong ale was ablution, Small beer persecution, A dram was memento mori; But a full-flowing bowl Was the saving his soul, And port was celestial glory.





Epitaph For James Smith

Lament him, Mauchline husbands aâ, He aften did assist ye; For had ye staid hale weeks awa, Your wives they neâer had missâd ye. Ye Mauchline bairns, as on ye press To school in bands thegither, O tread ye lightly on his grass,â Perhaps he was your father!





Adam Armourâs Prayer

Gude pity me, because Iâm little! For though I am an elf oâ mettle, Anâ can, like ony wabsterâs shuttle, Jink there or here, Yet, scarce as langâs a gude kail-whittle, Iâm unco queer. Anâ now Thou kens our waefuâ case; For Geordieâs jurr weâre in disgrace, Because we stangâd her through the place, Anâ hurt her spleuchan; For whilk we daurna show our face Within the clachan. Anâ now weâre dernâd in dens and hollows, And hunted, as was William Wallace, Wiâ constables-thae blackguard fallows, Anâ sodgers baith; But Gude preserve us frae the gallows, That shamefuâ death! Auld grim black-bearded Geordieâs selââ O shake him owre the mouth oâ hell! There let him hing, anâ roar, anâ yell Wiâ hideous din, And if he offers to rebel, Then heave him in. When Death comes in wiâ glimmerin blink, Anâ tips auld drucken Nanse the wink, May Sautan gie her doup a clink Within his yett, Anâ fill her up wiâ brimstone drink, Red-reekin het. Though Jock anâ havârel Jean are merryâ Some devil seize them in a hurry, Anâ waft them in thâ infernal wherry Straught through the lake, Anâ gie their hides a noble curry Wiâ oil of aik! As for the jurr-puir worthless body! Sheâs got mischief enough already; Wiâ stanged hips, and buttocks bluidy Sheâs sufferâd sair; But, may she wintle in a woody, If she wh-e mair!





The Jolly Beggars: A Cantata1

[Footnote 1: Not published by Burns.] Recitativo When lyart leaves bestrow the yird, Or wavering like the bauckie-bird, Bedim cauld Boreasâ blast; When hailstanes drive wiâ bitter skyte, And infant frosts begin to bite, In hoary cranreuch drest; Ae night at eâen a merry core Oâ randie, gangrel bodies, In Poosie-Nansieâs held the splore, To drink their orra duddies; Wiâ quaffing anâ laughing, They ranted anâ they sang, Wiâ jumping anâ thumping, The vera girdle rang, First, neist the fire, in auld red rags, Ane sat, weel bracâd wiâ mealy bags, And knapsack aâ in order; His doxy lay within his arm; Wiâ usquebae anâ blankets warm She blinkit on her sodger; Anâ aye he gies the tozie drab The tither skelpinâ kiss, While she held up her greedy gab, Just like an aumous dish; Ilk smack still, did crack still, Just like a cadgerâs whip; Then staggering anâ swaggering He roarâd this ditty upâ
Air TuneââSoldierâs Joy.â
I am a son of Mars who have been in many wars, And show my cuts and scars wherever I come; This here was for a wench, and that other in a trench, When welcoming the French at the sound of the drum. Lal de daudle, &c. My âprenticeship I past where my leader breathâd his last, When the bloody die was cast on the heights of Abram: and I served out my trade when the gallant game was playâd, And the Morro low was laid at the sound of the drum. I lastly was with Curtis among the floating battâries, And there I left for witness an arm and a limb; Yet let my country need me, with Elliot to head me, Iâd clatter on my stumps at the sound of a drum. And now thoâ I must beg, with a wooden arm and leg, And many a tatterâd rag hanging over my bum, Iâm as happy with my wallet, my bottle, and my callet, As when I used in scarlet to follow a drum. What thoâ with hoary locks, I must stand the winter shocks, Beneath the woods and rocks oftentimes for a home, When the tâother bag I sell, and the tâother bottle tell, I could meet a troop of hell, at the sound of a drum.
Recitativo He ended; and the kebars sheuk, Aboon the chorus roar; While frighted rattons backward leuk, Anâ seek the benmost bore: A fairy fiddler frae the neuk, He skirlâd out, encore! But up arose the martial chuck, Anâ laid the loud uproar.
Air TuneââSodger Laddie.â
I once was a maid, thoâ I cannot tell when, And still my delight is in proper young men; Some one of a troop of dragoons was my daddie, No wonder Iâm fond of a sodger laddie, Sing, lal de lal, &c. The first of my loves was a swaggering blade, To rattle the thundering drum was his trade; His leg was so tight, and his cheek was so ruddy, Transported I was with my sodger laddie. But the godly old chaplain left him in the lurch; The sword I forsook for the sake of the church: He venturâd the soul, and I risked the body, âTwas then I proved false to my sodger laddie. Full soon I grew sick of my sanctified sot, The regiment at large for a husband I got; From the gilded spontoon to the fife I was ready, I asked no more but a sodger laddie. But the peace it reducâd me to beg in despair, Till I met old boy in a Cunningham fair, His rags regimental, they flutterâd so gaudy, My heart it rejoicâd at a sodger laddie. And now I have livâdâI know not how long, And still I can join in a cup and a song; But whilst with both hands I can hold the glass steady, Hereâs to thee, my hero, my sodger laddie.
Recitativo Poor Merry-Andrew, in the neuk, Sat guzzling wiâ a tinkler-hizzie; They mindât na wha the chorus teuk, Between themselves they were sae busy: At length, wiâ drink anâ courting dizzy, He stoiterâd up anâ made a face; Then turnâd anâ laid a smack on Grizzie, Syne tunâd his pipes wiâ grave grimace.
Air TuneââAuld Sir Symon.â
Sir Wisdomâs a fool when heâs fou; Sir Knave is a fool in a session; Heâs there but a âprentice I trow, But I am a fool by profession. My grannie she bought me a beuk, Anâ I held awa to the school; I fear I my talent misteuk, But what will ye hae of a fool? For drink I would venture my neck; A hizzieâs the half of my craft; But what could ye other expect Of ane thatâs avowedly daft? I ance was tied up like a stirk, For civilly swearing and quaffin; I ance was abusâd iâ the kirk, For towsing a lass iâ my daffin. Poor Andrew that tumbles for sport, Let naebody name wiâ a jeer; Thereâs even, Iâm tauld, iâ the Court A tumbler caâd the Premier. Observâd ye yon reverend lad Mak faces to tickle the mob; He rails at our mountebank squad,â Itâs rivalship just iâ the job. And now my conclusion Iâll tell, For faith Iâm confoundedly dry; The chiel thatâs a fool for himselâ, Guid Lord! heâs far dafter than I.
Recitativo Then niest outspak a raucle carlin, Wha kent fuâ weel to cleek the sterlin; For mony a pursie she had hooked, Anâ had in mony a well been douked; Her love had been a Highland laddie, But weary faâ the waefuâ woodie! Wiâ sighs anâ sobs she thus began To wail her braw John Highlandman.
Air TuneââO, an ye were dead, Guidman.â
A Highland lad my love was born, The Lalland laws he held in scorn; But he still was faithfuâ to his clan, My gallant, braw John Highlandman.
Chorus Sing hey my braw John Highlandman! Sing ho my braw John Highlandman! Thereâs not a lad in aâ the lanâ Was match for my John Highlandman. With his philibeg anâ tartan plaid, Anâ guid claymore down by his side, The ladiesâ hearts he did trepan, My gallant, braw John Highlandman. Sing hey, &c. We ranged aâ from Tweed to Spey, Anâ livâd like lords anâ ladies gay; For a Lalland face he feared none,â My gallant, braw John Highlandman. Sing hey, &c. They banishâd him beyond the sea. But ere the bud was on the tree, Adown my cheeks the pearls ran, Embracing my John Highlandman. Sing hey, &c. But, och! they catchâd him at the last, And bound him in a dungeon fast: My curse upon them every one, Theyâve hangâd my braw John Highlandman! Sing hey, &c. And now a widow, I must mourn The pleasures that will neâer return: The comfort but a hearty can, When I think on John Highlandman. Sing hey, &c.
Recitativo A pigmy scraper wiâ his fiddle, Wha usâd at trystes anâ fairs to driddle. Her strappin limb and gausy middle (He reachâd nae higher) Had holâd his heartie like a riddle, Anâ blawnât on fire. Wiâ hand on hainch, and upward eâe, He croonâd his gamut, one, two, three, Then in an arioso key, The wee Apoll Set off wiâ allegretto glee His giga solo.
Air TuneââWhistle owre the lave oât.â
Let me ryke up to dight that tear, Anâ go wiâ me anâ be my dear; Anâ then your every care anâ fear May whistle owre the lave oât.
Chorus I am a fiddler to my trade, Anâ aâ the tunes that eâer I played, The sweetest still to wife or maid, Was whistle owre the lave oât. At kirns anâ weddins weâse be there, Anâ O sae nicelyâs we will fare! Weâll bowse about till Daddie Care Sing whistle owre the lave oât. I am, &c. Sae merrilyâs the banes weâll pyke, Anâ sun ourselâs about the dyke; Anâ at our leisure, when ye like, Weâll whistle owre the lave oât. I am, &c. But bless me wiâ your heavân oâ charms, Anâ while I kittle hair on thairms, Hunger, cauld, anâ aâ sic harms, May whistle owre the lave oât. I am, &c.
Recitativo Her charms had struck a sturdy caird, As weel as poor gut-scraper; He taks the fiddler by the beard, Anâ draws a roosty rapierâ He swoor, by aâ was swearing worth, To speet him like a pliver, Unless he would from that time forth Relinquish her for ever. Wiâ ghastly eâe poor tweedle-dee Upon his hunkers bended, Anâ prayâd for grace wiâ ruefuâ face, Anâ so the quarrel ended. But thoâ his little heart did grieve When round the tinkler prest her, He feignâd to snirtle in his sleeve, When thus the caird addressâd her:
