The Cotterâs Saturday Night

Inscribed to R. Aiken, Esq., of Ayr. Let not Ambition mock their useful toil, Their homely joys, and destiny obscure; Nor Grandeur hear, with a disdainful smile, The short and simple annals of the Poor. Gray. My lovâd, my honourâd, much respected friend! No mercenary bard his homage pays; With honest pride, I scorn each selfish end, My dearest meed, a friendâs esteem and praise: To you I sing, in simple Scottish lays, The lowly train in lifeâs sequesterâd scene, The native feelings strong, the guileless ways, What Aiken in a cottage would have been; Ah! thoâ his worth unknown, far happier there I ween! November chill blaws loud wiâ angry sugh; The shortâning winter-day is near a close; The miry beasts retreating frae the pleugh; The blackâning trains oâ craws to their repose: The toil-worn Cotter frae his labour goes,â This night his weekly moil is at an end, Collects his spades, his mattocks, and his hoes, Hoping the morn in ease and rest to spend, And weary, oâer the moor, his course does hameward bend. At length his lonely cot appears in view, Beneath the shelter of an aged tree; Thâ expectant wee-things, toddlin, stacher through To meet their dead, wiâ flichterin noise and glee. His wee bit ingle, blinkin bonilie, His clean hearth-stane, his thrifty wifieâs smile, The lisping infant, prattling on his knee, Does aâ his weary kiaugh and care beguile, And makes him quite forget his labour and his toil. Belyve, the elder bairns come drapping in, At service out, amang the farmers rounâ; Some caâ the pleugh, some herd, some tentie rin A cannie errand to a neibor town: Their eldest hope, their Jenny, woman-grown, In youthfuâ bloom-love sparkling in her eâeâ Comes hame, perhaps to shew a braw new gown, Or deposite her sair-won penny-fee, To help her parents dear, if they in hardship be. With joy unfeignâd, brothers and sisters meet, And each for otherâs weelfare kindly speirs: The social hours, swift-wingâd, unnoticâd fleet: Each tells the uncos that he sees or hears. The parents, partial, eye their hopeful years; Anticipation forward points the view; The mother, wiâ her needle and her shears, Gars auld claes look amaist as weelâs the new; The father mixes aâ wiâ admonition due. Their masterâs and their mistressâ command, The younkers aâ are warned to obey; And mind their labours wiâ an eydent hand, And neâer, thoâ out oâ sight, to jauk or play; âAnd O! be sure to fear the Lord alway, And mind your duty, duly, morn and night; Lest in temptationâs path ye gang astray, Implore His counsel and assisting might: They never sought in vain that sought the Lord aright.â But hark! a rap comes gently to the door; Jenny, wha kens the meaning oâ the same, Tells how a neibor lad came oâer the moor, To do some errands, and convoy her hame. The wily mother sees the conscious flame Sparkle in Jennyâs eâe, and flush her cheek; With heart-struck anxious care, enquires his name, While Jenny hafflins is afraid to speak; Weel-pleased the mother hears, itâs nae wild, worthless rake. Wiâ kindly welcome, Jenny brings him ben; A strappin youth, he takes the motherâs eye; Blythe Jenny sees the visitâs no ill taâen; The father cracks of horses, pleughs, and kye. The youngsterâs artless heart oâerflows wiâ joy, But blate anâ laithfuâ, scarce can weel behave; The mother, wiâ a womanâs wiles, can spy What makes the youth sae bashfuâ and sae grave, Weel-pleasâd to think her bairnâs respected like the lave. O happy love! where love like this is found: O heart-felt raptures! bliss beyond compare! Iâve paced much this weary, mortal round, And sage experience bids me this declare,â âIf Heaven a draught of heavenly pleasure spareâ One cordial in this melancholy vale, âTis when a youthful, loving, modest pair In otherâsarms, breathe out the tender tale, Beneath the milk-white thorn that scents the evening gale.â Is there, in human form, that bears a heart, A wretch! a villain! lost to love and truth! That can, with studied, sly, ensnaring art, Betray sweet Jennyâs unsuspecting youth? Curse on his perjurâd arts! dissembling smooth! Are honour, virtue, conscience, all exilâd? Is there no pity, no relenting ruth, Points to the parents fondling oâer their child? Then paints the ruinâd maid, and their distraction wild? But now the supper crowns their simple board, The halesome parritch, chief of Scotiaâs food; The sowp their only hawkie does afford, That, âyont the hallan snugly chows her cood: The dame brings forth, in complimental mood, To grace the lad, her weel-hainâd kebbuck, fell; And aft heâs prest, and aft he caâs it guid: The frugal wifie, garrulous, will tell How tâwas a towmond auld, sinâ lint was iâ the bell. The cheerfuâ supper done, wiâ serious face, They, round the ingle, form a circle wide; The sire turns oâer, with patriarchal grace, The big haâbible, ance his fatherâs pride: His bonnet revârently is laid aside, His lyart haffets wearing thin and bare; Those strains that once did sweet in Zion glide, He wales a portion with judicious care; And âLet us worship God!â he says with solemn air. They chant their artless notes in simple guise, They tune their hearts, by far the noblest aim; Perhaps Dundeeâs wild-warbling measures rise; Or plaintive Martyrs, worthy of the name; Or noble Elgin beets the heaven-ward flame; The sweetest far of Scotiaâs holy lays: Comparâd with these, Italian trills are tame; The ticklâd ears no heart-felt raptures raise; Nae unison hae they with our Creatorâs praise. The priest-like father reads the sacred page, How Abram was the friend of God on high; Or Moses bade eternal warfare wage With Amalekâs ungracious progeny; Or how the royal bard did groaning lie Beneath the stroke of Heavenâs avenging ire; Or Jobâs pathetic plaint, and wailing cry; Or rapt Isaiahâs wild, seraphic fire; Or other holy seers that tune the sacred lyre. Perhaps the Christian volume is the theme, How guiltless blood for guilty man was shed; How He, who bore in Heaven the second name, Had not on earth whereon to lay His head: How His first followers and servants sped; The precepts sage they wrote to many a land: How he, who lone in Patmos banished, Saw in the sun a mighty angel stand, And heard great Babâlonâs doom pronouncâd by Heavenâs command. Then, kneeling down to Heavenâs Eternal King, The saint, the father, and the husband prays: Hope âsprings exulting on triumphant wing,â1 That thus they all shall meet in future days, There, ever bask in uncreated rays, No more to sigh, or shed the bitter tear, Together hymning their Creatorâs praise, In such society, yet still more dear; While circling Time moves round in an eternal sphere Comparâd with this, how poor Religionâs pride, In all the pomp of method, and of art; When men display to congregations wide [Footnote 1: Popeâs âWindsor Forest.ââR.B.] Devotionâs evâry grace, except the heart! The Power, incensâd, the pageant will desert, The pompous strain, the sacerdotal stole; But haply, in some cottage far apart, May hear, well-pleasâd, the language of the soul; And in His Book of Life the inmates poor enroll. Then homeward all take off their sevâral way; The youngling cottagers retire to rest: The parent-pair their secret homage pay, And proffer up to Heaven the warm request, That he who stills the ravenâs clamârous nest, And decks the lily fair in flowâry pride, Would, in the way His wisdom sees the best, For them and for their little ones provide; But chiefly, in their hearts with grace divine preside. From scenes like these, old Scotiaâs grandeur springs, That makes her lovâd at home, reverâd abroad: Princes and lords are but the breath of kings, âAn honest manâs the noblest work of God;â And certes, in fair virtueâs heavenly road, The cottage leaves the palace far behind; What is a lordlingâs pomp? a cumbrous load, Disguising oft the wretch of human kind, Studied in arts of hell, in wickedness refinâd! O Scotia! my dear, my native soil! For whom my warmest wish to Heaven is sent, Long may thy hardy sons of rustic toil Be blest with health, and peace, and sweet content! And O! may Heaven their simple lives prevent From luxuryâs contagion, weak and vile! Then howeâer crowns and coronets be rent, A virtuous populace may rise the while, And stand a wall of fire around their much-lovâd isle. O Thou! who pourâd the patriotic tide, That streamâd throâ Wallaceâs undaunted heart, Who darâd to nobly stem tyrannic pride, Or nobly die, the second glorious part: (The patriotâs God peculiarly thou art, His friend, inspirer, guardian, and reward!) O never, never Scotiaâs realm desert; But still the patriot, and the patriot-bard In bright succession raise, her ornament and guard!





Address To The Deil

O Prince! O chief of many throned Powârs That led thâ embattlâd Seraphim to warâ Milton. O Thou! whatever title suit theeâ Auld Hornie, Satan, Nick, or Clootie, Wha in yon cavern grim anâ sootie, Closâd under hatches, Spairges about the brunstane cootie, To scaud poor wretches! Hear me, auld Hangie, for a wee, Anâ let poor damned bodies be; Iâm sure smaâ pleasure it can gie, Evân to a deil, To skelp anâ scaud poor dogs like me, Anâ hear us squeel! Great is thy powâr anâ great thy fame; Far kenâd anâ noted is thy name; Anâ thoâ yon lowinâ heuchâs thy hame, Thou travels far; Anâ faith! thouâs neither lag nor lame, Nor blate, nor scaur. Whiles, ranging like a roarin lion, For prey, aâ holes and corners tryin; Whiles, on the strong-windâd tempest flyin, Tirlin the kirks; Whiles, in the human bosom pryin, Unseen thou lurks. Iâve heard my revârend graunie say, In lanely glens ye like to stray; Or where auld ruinâd castles grey Nod to the moon, Ye fright the nightly wandârerâs way, Wiâ eldritch croon. When twilight did my graunie summon, To say her prayârs, douse, honest woman! Aftâyont the dyke sheâs heard you bummin, Wiâ eerie drone; Or, rustlin, throâ the boortrees comin, Wiâ heavy groan. Ae dreary, windy, winter night, The stars shot down wiâ sklentin light, Wiâ you, myselâ I gat a fright, Ayont the lough; Ye, like a rash-buss, stood in sight, Wiâ wavinâ sough. The cudgel in my nieve did shake, Each bristâld hair stood like a stake, When wiâ an eldritch, stoor âquaick, quaick,â Amang the springs, Awa ye squatterâd like a drake, On whistlinâ wings. Let warlocks grim, anâ witherâd hags, Tell how wiâ you, on ragweed nags, They skim the muirs anâ dizzy crags, Wiâ wicked speed; And in kirk-yards renew their leagues, Owre howkit dead. Thence countra wives, wiâ toil and pain, May plunge anâ plunge the kirn in vain; For oh! the yellow treasureâs taâen By witchinâ skill; Anâ dawtit, twal-pint hawkieâs gane As yellâs the bill. Thence mystic knots mak great abuse On young guidmen, fond, keen anâ crouse, When the best wark-lume iâ the house, By cantrip wit, Is instant made no worth a louse, Just at the bit. When thowes dissolve the snawy hoord, Anâ float the jinglinâ icy boord, Then water-kelpies haunt the foord, By your direction, And ânighted travâllers are allurâd To their destruction. And aft your moss-traversin Spunkies Decoy the wight that late anâ drunk is: The bleezin, curst, mischievous monkies Delude his eyes, Till in some miry slough he sunk is, Neâer mair to rise. When masonsâ mystic word anâ grip In storms anâ tempests raise you up, Some cock or cat your rage maun stop, Or, strange to tell! The youngest brither ye wad whip Aff straught to hell. Lang syne in Edenâs bonie yard, When youthfuâ lovers first were pairâd, Anâ all the soul of love they sharâd, The rapturâd hour, Sweet on the fragrant flowâry swaird, In shady bower;1 Then you, ye auld, snick-drawing dog! Ye cam to Paradise incog, [Footnote 1: The verse originally ran: âLang syne, in Edenâs happy scene When strappin Adamâs days were green, And Eve was like my bonie Jean, My dearest part, A dancin, sweet, young handsome quean, Oâ guileless heart.â] Anâ playâd on man a cursed brogue, (Black be your faâ!) Anâ gied the infant warld a shog, âMaist ruiâd aâ. Dâye mind that day when in a bizz Wiâ reekit duds, anâ reestit gizz, Ye did present your smoutie phiz âMang better folk, Anâ sklented on the man of Uzz Your spitefuâ joke? Anâ how ye gat him iâ your thrall, Anâ brak him out oâ house an halâ, While scabs and botches did him gall, Wiâ bitter claw; Anâ lowsâd his ill-tonguâd wicked scaulâ, Was warst ava? But aâ your doings to rehearse, Your wily snares anâ fechtin fierce, Sinâ that day Michael2 did you pierce, Down to this time, Wad ding a Lallan tounge, or Erse, In prose or rhyme. Anâ now, auld Cloots, I ken yeâre thinkin, A certain bardieâs rantin, drinkin, Some luckless hour will send him linkin To your black pit; But faith! heâll turn a corner jinkin, Anâ cheat you yet. But fare-you-weel, auld Nickie-ben! O wad ye tak a thought anâ menâ! Ye aiblins mightâI dinna kenâ Stil hae a stake: Iâm wae to think upâ yon den, Evân for your sake! [Footnote 2: Vide Milton, Book vi.âR. B.]





Scotch Drink

Gie him strong drink until he wink, Thatâs sinking in despair; Anâ liquor guid to fire his bluid, Thatâs prest wiâ grief and care: There let him bouse, anâ deep carouse, Wiâ bumpers flowing oâer, Till he forgets his loves or debts, Anâ minds his griefs no more. (Solomonâs Proverbs, xxxi. 6, 7.) Let other poets raise a fracas âBout vines, anâ wines, anâ drucken Bacchus, Anâ crabbit names anâstories wrack us, Anâ grate our lug: I sing the juice Scotch bear can mak us, In glass or jug. O thou, my muse! guid auld Scotch drink! Whether throâ wimplin worms thou jink, Or, richly brown, ream owre the brink, In glorious faem, Inspire me, till I lisp anâ wink, To sing thy name! Let husky wheat the haughs adorn, Anâ aits set up their awnie horn, Anâ pease and beans, at eâen or morn, Perfume the plain: Leeze me on thee, John Barleycorn, Thou king oâ grain! On thee aft Scotland chows her cood, In souple scones, the wale oâfood! Or tumblin in the boiling flood Wiâ kail anâ beef; But when thou pours thy strong heartâs blood, There thou shines chief. Food fills the wame, anâ keeps us leevin; Thoâ lifeâs a gift no worth receivin, When heavy-draggâd wiâ pine anâ grievin; But, oilâd by thee, The wheels oâ life gae down-hill, scrievin, Wiâ rattlin glee. Thou clears the head oâdoited Lear; Thou cheers ahe heart oâ drooping Care; Thou strings the nerves oâ Labour sair, Atâs weary toil; Though even brightens dark Despair Wiâ gloomy smile. Aft, clad in massy siller weed, Wiâ gentles thou erects thy head; Yet, humbly kind in time oâ need, The poor manâs wine; His weep drap parritch, or his bread, Thou kitchens fine. Thou art the life oâ public haunts; But thee, what were our fairs and rants? Evân godly meetings oâ the saunts, By thee inspired, When gaping they besiege the tents, Are doubly firâd. That merry night we get the corn in, O sweetly, then, thou reams the horn in! Or reekin on a New-year mornin In cog or bicker, Anâ just a wee drap spâritual burn in, Anâ gusty sucker! When Vulcan gies his bellows breath, Anâ ploughmen gather wiâ their graith, O rare! to see thee fizz an freath Iâ thâ luggit caup! Then Burnewin comes on like death At every chap. Nae mercy then, for airn or steel; The brawnie, banie, ploughman chiel, Brings hard owrehip, wiâ sturdy wheel, The strong forehammer, Till block anâ studdie ring an reel, Wiâ dinsome clamour. When skirling weanies see the light, Though maks the gossips clatter bright, How fumblinâ cuiffs their dearies slight; Wae worth the name! Nae howdie gets a social night, Or plack frae them. When neibors anger at a plea, Anâ just as wud as wud can be, How easy can the barley brie Cement the quarrel! Itâs aye the cheapest lawyerâs fee, To taste the barrel. Alake! that eâer my muse has reason, To wyte her countrymen wiâ treason! But mony daily weet their weason Wiâ liquors nice, Anâ hardly, in a winter season, Eâer Spier her price. Wae worth that brandy, burnin trash! Fell source oâ mony a pain anâ brash! Twins mony a poor, doylt, drucken hash, Oâ half his days; Anâ sends, beside, auld Scotlandâs cash To her warst faes. Ye Scots, wha wish auld Scotland well! Ye chief, to you my tale I tell, Poor, plackless devils like myselâ! It sets you ill, Wiâ bitter, dearthfuâ wines to mell, Or foreign gill. May gravels round his blather wrench, Anâ gouts torment him, inch by inch, What twists his gruntle wiâ a glunch Oâ sour disdain, Out owre a glass oâ whisky-punch Wiâ honest men! O Whisky! soul oâ plays and pranks! Accept a bardieâs gratfuâ thanks! When wanting thee, what tuneless cranks Are my poor verses! Thou comesâthey rattle in their ranks, At itherâs a-s! Thee, Ferintosh! O sadly lost! Scotland lament frae coast to coast! Now colic grips, anâ barkin hoast May kill us aâ; For loyal Forbesâ charterâd boast Is taâen awa? Thae curst horse-leeches oâ theâ Excise, Wha mak the whisky stells their prize! Haud up thy hanâ, Deil! ance, twice, thrice! There, seize the blinkers! Anâ bake them up in brunstane pies For poor damnâd drinkers. Fortune! if thouâll but gie me still Hale breeks, a scone, anâ whisky gill, Anâ rowth oâ rhyme to rave at will, Tak aâ the rest, Anâ dealât about as thy blind skill Directs thee best.





1786





The Auld Farmerâs New-Year-Morning Salutation To His Auld Mare, Maggie

On giving her the accustomed ripp of corn to hansel in the New Year. A Guid New-year I wish thee, Maggie! Hae, thereâs a ripp to thy auld baggie: Thoâ thouâs howe-backit now, anâ knaggie, Iâve seen the day Thou could hae gaen like ony staggie, Out-owre the lay. Thoâ now thouâs dowie, stiff, anâ crazy, Anâ thy auld hide as whiteâs a daisie, Iâve seen thee dapplât, sleek anâ glaizie, A bonie gray: He should been tight that daurât to raize thee, Ance in a day. Thou ance was iâ the foremost rank, A filly buirdly, steeve, anâ swank; Anâ set weel down a shapely shank, As eâer tread yird; Anâ could hae flown out-owre a stank, Like ony bird. Itâs now some nine-anâ-twenty year, Sinâ thou was my guid-fatherâs mear; He gied me thee, oâ tocher clear, Anâ fifty mark; Thoâ it was smaâ, âtwas weel-won gear, Anâ thou was stark. When first I gaed to woo my Jenny, Ye then was trotting wiâ your minnie: Thoâ ye was trickie, slee, anâ funnie, Ye neâer was donsie; But hamely, tawie, quiet, anâ cannie, Anâ unco sonsie. That day, ye prancâd wiâ muckle pride, When ye bure hame my bonie bride: Anâ sweet anâ gracefuâ she did ride, Wiâ maiden air! Kyle-Stewart I could bragged wide For sic a pair. Thoâ now ye dow but hoyte and hobble, Anâ wintle like a saumont coble, That day, ye was a jinker noble, For heels anâ winâ! Anâ ran them till they aâ did wauble, Far, far, behinâ! When thou anâ I were young anâ skeigh, Anâ stable-meals at fairs were dreigh, How thou wad prance, and snore, anâ skreigh Anâ tak the road! Townâs-bodies ran, anâ stood abeigh, Anâ caât thee mad. When thou was cornât, anâ I was mellow, We took the road aye like a swallow: At brooses thou had neâer a fellow, For pith anâ speed; But evâry tail thou payât them hollowm Whareâer thou gaed. The smaâ, droop-rumplât, hunter cattle Might aiblins waurât thee for a brattle; But sax Scotch mile, thou tryât their mettle, Anâ garât them whaizle: Nae whip nor spur, but just a wattle Oâ saugh or hazel. Thou was a noble fittie-lanâ, As eâer in tug or tow was drawn! Aft thee anâ I, in aught hoursâ gaun, In guid March-weather, Hae turnâd sax rood beside our hanâ, For days thegither. Thou never braingât, anâ fetchât, anâ fliskit; But thy auld tail thou wad hae whiskit, Anâ spread abreed thy weel-fillâd brisket, Wiâ pith anâ power; Till sprittie knowes wad rairât anâ riskit Anâ slypet owre. When frosts lay lang, anâ snaws were deep, Anâ threatenâd labour back to keep, I gied thy cog a wee bit heap Aboon the timmer: I kenâd my Maggie wad na sleep, For that, or simmer. In cart or car thou never reestit; The steyest brae thou wad hae facât it; Thou never lap, anâ stenât, and breastit, Then stood to blaw; But just thy step a wee thing hastit, Thou snoovât awa. My pleugh is now thy bairn-time aâ, Four gallant brutes as eâer did draw; Forbye sax mae Iâve sellât awa, That thou hast nurst: They drew me thretteen pund anâ twa, The vera warst. Mony a sair daurk we twa hae wrought, Anâ wiâ the weary warlâ fought! Anâ mony an anxious day, I thought We wad be beat! Yet here to crazy age weâre brought, Wiâ something yet. Anâ think naâ, my auld trusty servanâ, That now perhaps thouâs less deservin, Anâ thy auld days may end in starvin; For my last fow, A heapit stimpart, Iâll reserve ane Laid by for you. Weâve worn to crazy years thegither; Weâll toyte about wiâ ane anither; Wiâ tentie care Iâll flit thy tether To some hainâd rig, Whare ye may nobly rax your leather, Wiâ smaâ fatigue.





The Twa Dogs1

A Tale âTwas in that place oâ Scotlandâs isle, That bears the name oâ auld King Coil, Upon a bonie day in June, When wearinâ throâ the afternoon, Twa dogs, that were na thrang at hame, Forgatherâd ance upon a time. The first Iâll name, they caâd him Caesar, Was keepit for His Honorâs pleasure: His hair, his size, his mouth, his lugs, Shewâd he was nane oâ Scotlandâs dogs; But whalpit some place far abroad, Whare sailors gang to fish for cod. His locked, letterâd, braw brass collar Shewâd him the gentleman anâ scholar; But though he was oâ high degree, The fient a pride, nae pride had he; But wad hae spent an hour caressin, Evân wiâ al tinkler-gipsyâs messin: At kirk or market, mill or smiddie, Nae tawted tyke, thoâ eâer sae duddie, But he wad stanât, as glad to see him, Anâ stroanât on stanes anâ hillocks wiâ him. The tither was a ploughmanâs collieâ A rhyming, ranting, raving billie, Wha for his friend anâ comrade had him, And in freak had Luath caâd him, After some dog in Highland Sang,2 Was made lang syne,âLord knows how lang. He was a gash anâ faithfuâ tyke, As ever lap a sheugh or dyke. His honest, sonsie, bawsânt face Aye gat him friends in ilka place; His breast was white, his touzie back Weel clad wiâ coat oâ glossy black; His gawsie tail, wiâ upward curl, Hung owre his hurdieâs wiâ a swirl. [Footnote 1: Luath was Burnsâ own dog.] [Footnote 2: Luath, Cuchullinâs dog in Ossianâs âFingal.ââR. B.] Nae doubt but they were fain oâ ither, And unco pack anâ thick thegither; Wiâ social nose whiles snuffâd anâ snowkit; Whiles mice anâ moudieworts they howkit; Whiles scourâd awaâ in lang excursion, Anâ worryâd ither in diversion; Until wiâ daffinâ weary grown Upon a knowe they set them down. Anâ there began a lang digression. About the âlords oâ the creation.â
Caesar Iâve aften wonderâd, honest Luath, What sort oâ life poor dogs like you have; Anâ when the gentryâs life I saw, What way poor bodies livâd ava. Our laird gets in his racked rents, His coals, his kane, anâ aâ his stents: He rises when he likes himselâ; His flunkies answer at the bell; He caâs his coach; he caâs his horse; He draws a bonie silken purse, As langâs my tail, where, throâ the steeks, The yellow letterâd Geordie keeks. Frae morn to eâen, itâs nought but toiling At baking, roasting, frying, boiling; Anâ thoâ the gentry first are stechin, Yet evân the haâ folk fill their pechan Wiâ sauce, ragouts, anâ sic like trashtrie, Thatâs little short oâ downright wastrie. Our whipper-in, wee, blasted wonner, Poor, worthless elf, it eats a dinner, Better than ony tenant-man His Honour has in aâ the lanâ: Anâ what poor cot-folk pit their painch in, I own itâs past my comprehension.
Luath Trowth, Caesar, whiles theyâre fashât eneugh: A cottar howkin in a sheugh, Wiâ dirty stanes biggin a dyke, Baring a quarry, anâ sic like; Himselâ, a wife, he thus sustains, A smytrie oâ wee duddie weans, Anâ nought but his hanâ-daurk, to keep Them right anâ tight in thack anâ rape. Anâ when they meet wiâ sair disasters, Like loss oâ health or want oâ masters, Ye maist wad think, a wee touch langer, Anâ they maun starve oâ cauld anâ hunger: But how it comes, I never kent yet, Theyâre maistly wonderfuâ contented; Anâ buirdly chiels, anâ clever hizzies, Are bred in sic a way as this is.
Caesar But then to see how yeâre negleckit, How huffâd, anâ cuffâd, anâ disrespeckit! Lord man, our gentry care as little For delvers, ditchers, anâ sic cattle; They gang as saucy by poor folk, As I wad by a stinkin brock. Iâve noticâd, on our lairdâs court-day,â Anâ mony a time my heartâs been wae,â Poor tenant bodies, scant oâcash, How they maun thole a factorâs snash; Heâll stamp anâ threaten, curse anâ swear Heâll apprehend them, poind their gear; While they maun stanâ, wiâ aspect humble, Anâ hear it aâ, anâ fear anâ tremble! I see how folk live that hae riches; But surely poor-folk maun be wretches!
Luath Theyâre no sae wretchedâs ane wad think. Thoâ constantly on poortithâs brink, Theyâre sae accustomâd wiâ the sight, The view oât gives them little fright. Then chance and fortune are sae guided, Theyâre aye in less or mair provided: Anâ thoâ fatigued wiâ close employment, A blink oâ restâs a sweet enjoyment. The dearest comfort oâ their lives, Their grushie weans anâ faithfuâ wives; The prattling things are just their pride, That sweetens aâ their fire-side. Anâ whiles twalpennie worth oâ nappy Can mak the bodies unco happy: They lay aside their private cares, To mind the Kirk and State affairs; Theyâll talk oâ patronage anâ priests, Wiâ kindling fury iâ their breasts, Or tell what new taxationâs comin, Anâ ferlie at the folk in Lonâon. As bleak-facâd Hallowmass returns, They get the jovial, rantin kirns, When rural life, of evâry station, Unite in common recreation; Love blinks, Wit slaps, anâ social Mirth Forgets thereâs Care upoâ the earth. That merry day the year begins, They bar the door on frosty winâs; The nappy reeks wiâ mantling ream, Anâ sheds a heart-inspiring steam; The luntin pipe, anâ sneeshin mill, Are handed round wiâ right guid will; The cantie auld folks crackin crouse, The young anes rantin throâ the houseâ My heart has been sae fain to see them, That I for joy hae barkit wiâ them. Still itâs owre true that ye hae said, Sic game is now owre aften playâd; Thereâs mony a creditable stock Oâ decent, honest, fawsont folk, Are riven out baith root anâ branch, Some rascalâs pridefuâ greed to quench, Wha thinks to knit himsel the faster In favour wiâ some gentle master, Wha, aiblins, thrang a parliamentin, For Britainâs guid his saul indentinâ
Caesar Haith, lad, ye little ken about it: For Britainâs guid! guid faith! I doubt it. Say rather, gaun as Premiers lead him: Anâ saying ay or noâs they bid him: At operas anâ plays parading, Mortgaging, gambling, masquerading: Or maybe, in a frolic daft, To Hague or Calais takes a waft, To mak a tour anâ tak a whirl, To learn bon ton, anâ see the worlâ. There, at Vienna, or Versailles, He rives his fatherâs auld entails; Or by Madrid he takes the rout, To thrum guitars anâ fecht wiâ nowt; Or down Italian vista startles, Whore-hunting amang groves oâ myrtles: Then bowses drumlie German-water, To mak himsel look fair anâ fatter, Anâ clear the consequential sorrows, Love-gifts of Carnival signoras. For Britainâs guid! for her destruction! Wiâ dissipation, feud, anâ faction.
Luath Hech, man! dear sirs! is that the gate They waste sae mony a braw estate! Are we sae foughten anâ harassâd For gear to gang that gate at last? O would they stay aback frae courts, Anâ please themsels wiâ country sports, It wad for evâry ane be better, The laird, the tenant, anâ the cotter! For thae frank, rantin, ramblin billies, Feint haet oâ themâs ill-hearted fellows; Except for breakin oâ their timmer, Or speakin lightly oâ their limmer, Or shootin of a hare or moor-cock, The neâer-a-bit theyâre ill to poor folk, But will ye tell me, Master Caesar, Sure great folkâs lifeâs a life oâ pleasure? Nae cauld nor hunger eâer can steer them, The very thought oât need na fear them.
Caesar Lord, man, were ye but whiles whare I am, The gentles, ye wad neâer envy them! Itâs true, they need na starve or sweat, Throâ winterâs cauld, or simmerâs heat: Theyâve nae sair wark to craze their banes, Anâ fill auld age wiâ grips anâ granes: But human bodies are sic fools, For aâ their colleges anâ schools, That when nae real ills perplex them, They mak enow themselâs to vex them; Anâ aye the less they hae to sturt them, In like proportion, less will hurt them. A country fellow at the pleugh, His acreâs tillâd, heâs right eneugh; A country girl at her wheel, Her dizzenâs dune, sheâs unco weel; But gentlemen, anâ ladies warst, Wiâ evân-down want oâ wark are curst. They loiter, lounging, lank anâ lazy; Thoâ deil-haet ails them, yet uneasy; Their days insipid, dull, anâ tasteless; Their nights unquiet, lang, anâ restless. Anâevân their sports, their balls anâ races, Their galloping through public places, Thereâs sic parade, sic pomp, anâ art, The joy can scarcely reach the heart. The men cast out in party-matches, Then sowther aâ in deep debauches. Ae night theyâre mad wiâ drink anâ whoring, Niest day their life is past enduring. The ladies arm-in-arm in clusters, As great anâ gracious aâ as sisters; But hear their absent thoughts oâ ither, Theyâre aâ run-deils anâ jads thegither. Whiles, owre the wee bit cup anâ platie, They sip the scandal-potion pretty; Or lee-lang nights, wiâ crabbit leuks Pore owre the devilâs picturâd beuks; Stake on a chance a farmerâs stackyard, Anâ cheat like ony unhanged blackguard. Thereâs some exceptions, man anâ woman; But this is gentryâs life in common. By this, the sun was out of sight, Anâ darker gloamin brought the night; The bum-clock hummâd wiâ lazy drone; The kye stood rowtin iâ the loan; When up they gat anâ shook their lugs, Rejoicâd they werena men but dogs; Anâ each took aff his several way, Resolvâd to meet some ither day.





The Authorâs Earnest Cry And Prayer

To the Right Honourable and Honourable Scotch Representatives in the House of Commons.1 Dearest of distillation! last and bestâ âHow art thou lost!â
Parody on Milton. Ye Irish lords, ye knights anâ squires, Wha represent our brughs anâ shires, Anâ doucely manage our affairs In parliament, To you a simple poetâs prayârs Are humbly sent. Alas! my roupit Muse is hearse! Your Honoursâ hearts wiâ grief âtwad pierce, To see her sittin on her arse Low iâ the dust, And scriechinhout prosaic verse, An like to brust! [Footnote 1: This was written before the Act anent the Scotch distilleries, of session 1786, for which Scotland and the author return their most grateful thanks.âR.B.] Tell them wha hae the chief direction, Scotland anâ meâs in great affliction, Eâer sinâ they laid that curst restriction On aqua-vitae; Anâ rouse them up to strong conviction, Anâ move their pity. Stand forth anâ tell yon Premier youth The honest, open, naked truth: Tell him oâ mine anâ Scotlandâs drouth, His servants humble: The muckle deevil blaw you south If ye dissemble! Does ony great man glunch anâ gloom? Speak out, anâ never fash your thumb! Let posts anâ pensions sink or soom Wiâ them wha grant them; If honestly they canna come, Far better want them. In gathârin votes you were na slack; Now stand as tightly by your tack: Neâer claw your lug, anâ fidge your back, Anâ hum anâ haw; But raise your arm, anâ tell your crack Before them aâ. Paint Scotland greetin owre her thrissle; Her mutchkin stowp as toomâs a whissle; Anâ damnâd excisemen in a bussle, Seizin a stell, Triumphant crushinât like a mussel, Or limpet shell! Then, on the tither hand present herâ A blackguard smuggler right behint her, Anâ cheek-for-chow, a chuffie vintner Colleaguing join, Picking her pouch as bare as winter Of aâ kind coin. Is there, that bears the name oâ Scot, But feels his heartâs bluid rising hot, To see his poor auld mitherâs pot Thus dung in staves, Anâ plunderâd oâ her hindmost groat By gallows knaves? Alas! Iâm but a nameless wight, Trode iâ the mire out oâ sight? But could I like Montgomeries fight, Or gab like Boswell,2 Thereâs some sark-necks I wad draw tight, Anâ tie some hose well. God bless your Honours! can ye seeâtâ The kind, auld cantie carlin greet, Anâ no get warmly to your feet, Anâ gar them hear it, Anâ tell them wiâa patriot-heat Ye winna bear it? Some oâ you nicely ken the laws, To round the period anâ pause, Anâ with rhetoric clause on clause To mak harangues; Then echo throâ Saint Stephenâs waâs Auld Scotlandâs wrangs. Dempster,3 a true blue Scot Iâse warranâ; Thee, aith-detesting, chaste Kilkerran;4 Anâ that glib-gabbit Highland baron, The Laird oâ Graham;5 Anâ ane, a chap thatâs damnâd aulfarranâ, Dundas his name:6 Erskine, a spunkie Norland billie;7 True Campbells, Frederick and Ilay;8 [Footnote 2: James Boswell of Auchinleck, the biographer of Johnson.] [Footnote 3: George Dempster of Dunnichen.] [Footnote 4: Sir Adam Ferguson of Kilkerran, Bart.] [Footnote 5: The Marquis of Graham, eldest son of the Duke of Montrose.] [Footnote 6: Right Hon. Henry Dundas, M. P.] [Footnote 7: Probably Thomas, afterward Lord Erskine.] [Footnote 8: Lord Frederick Campbell, second brother of the Duke of Argyll, and Ilay Campbell, Lord Advocate for Scotland, afterward President of the Court of Session.] Anâ Livistone, the bauld Sir Willie;9 Anâ mony ithers, Whom auld Demosthenes or Tully Might own for brithers. See sodger Hugh,10 my watchman stented, If poets eâer are represented; I ken if that your sword were wanted, Yeâd lend a hand; But when thereâs ought to say anent it, Yeâre at a stand. Arouse, my boys! exert your mettle, To get auld Scotland back her kettle; Or faith! Iâll wad my new pleugh-pettle, Yeâll seeât or lang, Sheâll teach you, wiâ a reekin whittle, Anither sang. This while sheâs been in crankous mood, Her lost Militia firâd her bluid; (Deil na they never mair do guid, Playâd her that pliskie!) Anâ now sheâs like to rin red-wud About her whisky. Anâ Lord! if ance they pit her tillât, Her tartan petticoat sheâll kilt, Anâdurk anâ pistol at her belt, Sheâll tak the streets, Anâ rin her whittle to the hilt, Iâ the first she meets! For God sake, sirs! then speak her fair, Anâ straik her cannie wiâ the hair, Anâ to the muckle house repair, Wiâ instant speed, Anâ strive, wiâ aâ your wit anâ lear, To get remead. [Footnote 9: Sir Wm. Augustus Cunningham, Baronet, of Livingstone.] [Footnote 10: Col. Hugh Montgomery, afterward Earl of Eglinton.] Yon ill-tonguâd tinkler, Charlie Fox, May taunt you wiâ his jeers and mocks; But gie himât het, my hearty cocks! Eâen cowe the cadie! Anâ send him to his dicing box Anâ sportinâ lady. Tell you guid bluid oâ auld Boconnockâs, 11 Iâll be his debt twa mashlum bonnocks, Anâ drink his health in auld Nance Tinnockâs 12 Nine times a-week, If he some scheme, like tea anâ winnocks, Was kindly seek. Could he some commutation broach, Iâll pledge my aith in guid braid Scotch, He needna fear their foul reproach Nor erudition, Yon mixtie-maxtie, queer hotch-potch, The Coalition. Auld Scotland has a raucle tongue; Sheâs just a devil wiâ a rung; Anâ if she promise auld or young To tak their part, Thoâ by the neck she should be strung, Sheâll no desert. And now, ye chosen Five-and-Forty, May still you mitherâs heart support ye; Then, thoâa minister grow dorty, Anâ kick your place, Yeâll snap your gingers, poor anâ hearty, Before his face. God bless your Honours, aâ your days, Wiâ sowps oâ kail and brats oâ claise, [Footnote 11: Pitt, whose grandfather was of Boconnock in Cornwall.] [Footnote 12: A worthy old hostess of the authorâs in Mauchline, where he sometimes studies politics over a glass of gude auld Scotch Drink.âR.B.] In spite oâ aâ the thievish kaes, That haunt St. Jamieâs! Your humble poet sings anâ prays, While Rab his name is.
Postscript Let half-starvâd slaves in warmer skies See future wines, rich-clustâring, rise; Their lot auld Scotland neâre envies, But, blythe and frisky, She eyes her freeborn, martial boys Tak aff their whisky. What thoâ their Phoebus kinder warms, While fragrance blooms and beauty charms, When wretches range, in famishâd swarms, The scented groves; Or, hounded forth, dishonour arms In hungry droves! Their gunâs a burden on their shouther; They downa bide the stink oâ powther; Their bauldest thoughtâs a hankâring swither To stanâ or rin, Till skelpâa shotâtheyâre aff, aâthrowâther, To save their skin. But bring a Scotchman frae his hill, Clap in his cheek a Highland gill, Say, such is royal Georgeâs will, Anâ thereâs the foe! He has nae thought but how to kill Twa at a blow. Nae cauld, faint-hearted doubtings tease him; Death comes, wiâ fearless eye he sees him; Wiâbluidy hand a welcome gies him; Anâ when he faâs, His latest draught oâ breathin leaâes him In faint huzzas. Sages their solemn een may steek, Anâ raise a philosophic reek, Anâ physically causes seek, In clime anâ season; But tell me whiskyâs name in Greek Iâll tell the reason. Scotland, my auld, respected mither! Thoâ whiles ye moistify your leather, Till, whare ye sit on craps oâ heather, Ye tine your dam; Freedom anâ whisky gang thegither! Take aff your dram!





The Ordination

For sense they little owe to frugal Heavânâ To please the mob, they hide the little givân. Kilmarnock wabsters, fidge anâ claw, Anâ pour your creeshie nations; Anâ ye wha leather rax anâ draw, Of aâ denominations; Swith to the Ligh Kirk, ane anâ aâ Anâ there tak up your stations; Then aff to Begbieâs in a raw, Anâ pour divine libations For joy this day. Curst Common-sense, that imp oâ hell, Cam in wiâ Maggie Lauder;1 But Oliphant2 aft made her yell, Anâ Russell3 sair miscaâd her: This day Mackinlay4 taks the flail, Anâ heâs the boy will blaud her! Heâll clap a shangan on her tail, Anâ set the bairns to daud her Wiâ dirt this day. [Footnote 1: Alluding to a scoffing ballad which was made on the admission of the late reverend and worthy Mr. Lihdsay to the âLaigh Kirk.ââR.B.] [Footnote 2: Rev. James Oliphant, minister of Chapel of Ease, Kilmarnock.] [Footnote 3: Rev. John Russell of Kilmarnock.] [Footnote 4: Rev. James Mackinlay.] Mak haste anâ turn King David owre, And lilt wiâ holy clangor; Oâ double verse come gie us four, Anâ skirl up the Bangor: This day the kirk kicks up a stoure; Nae mair the knaves shall wrang her, For Heresy is in her powâr, And gloriously sheâll whang her Wiâ pith this day. Come, let a proper text be read, Anâ touch it aff wiâ vigour, How graceless Ham5 leugh at his dad, Which made Canaan a nigger; Or Phineas6 drove the murdering blade, Wiâ whore-abhorring rigour; Or Zipporah,7 the scauldin jad, Was like a bluidy tiger Iâ thâ inn that day. There, try his mettle on the creed, Anâ bind him down wiâ caution, That stipend is a carnal weed He taks by for the fashion; And gie him oâer the flock, to feed, And punish each transgression; Especial, rams that cross the breed, Gie them sufficient threshin; Spare them nae day. Now, auld Kilmarnock, cock thy tail, Anâ toss thy horns fuâ canty; Nae mair thouâlt rowt out-owre the dale, Because thy pastureâs scanty; For lapfuâs large oâ gospel kail Shall fill thy crib in plenty, Anâ runts oâ grace the pick anâ wale, No giâen by way oâ dainty, But ilka day. [Footnote 5: Genesis ix. 22.âR. B.] [Footnote : Numbers xxv. 8.âR. B.] [Footnote 7: Exodus iv. 52.âR. B] Nae mair by Babelâs streams weâll weep, To think upon our Zion; And hing our fiddles up to sleep, Like baby-clouts a-dryin! Come, screw the pegs wiâ tunefuâ cheep, And oâer the thairms be tryin; Oh, rare to see our elbucks wheep, And aâ like lamb-tails flyin Fuâ fast this day. Lang, Patronage, with rod oâ airn, Has shorâd the Kirkâs undoin; As lately Fenwick, sair forfairn, Has proven to its ruin:8 Our patron, honest man! Glencairn, He saw mischief was brewin; Anâ like a godly, elect bairn, Heâs waled us out a true ane, And sound, this day. Now Robertson9 harangue nae mair, But steek your gab for ever; Or try the wicked town of Ayr, For there theyâll think you clever; Or, nae reflection on your lear, Ye may commence a shaver; Or to the Netherton10 repair, Anâ turn a carpet weaver Aff-hand this day. Muâtrie11 and you were just a match, We never had sic twa drones; Auld Hornie did the Laigh Kirk watch, Just like a winkin baudrons, And aye he catchâd the tither wretch, To fry them in his caudrons; But now his Honour maun detach, Wiâ aâ his brimstone squadrons, Fast, fast this day. [Footnote 8: Rev. Wm. Boyd, pastor of Fenwick.] [Footnote 9: Rev. John Robertson.] [Footnote 10: A district of Kilmarnock.] [Footnote 11: The Rev. John Multrie, a âModerate,â whom Mackinlay succeeded.] See, see auld Orthodoxyâs faes Sheâs swingein throâ the city! Hark, how the nine-tailâd cat she plays! I vow itâs unco pretty: There, Learning, with his Greekish face, Grunts out some Latin ditty; And Common-sense is gaun, she says, To mak to Jamie Beattie Her plaint this day. But thereâs Morality himselâ, Embracing all opinions; Hear, how he gies the tither yell, Between his twa companions! See, how she peels the skin anâ fell, As ane were peelin onions! Now there, theyâre packed aff to hell, Anâ banishâd our dominions, Henceforth this day. O happy day! rejoice, rejoice! Come bouse about the porter! Moralityâs demure decoys Shall here nae mair find quarter: Mackinlay, Russell, are the boys That heresy can torture; Theyâll gie her on a rape a hoyse, And cowe her measure shorter By thâ head some day. Come, bring the tither mutchkin in, And hereâsâfor a conclusionâ To evâry New Light12 motherâs son, From this time forth, Confusion! If mair they deave us wiâ their din, Or Patronage intrusion, Weâll light a spunk, and evâry skin, Weâll rin them aff in fusion Like oil, some day. [Footnote 12: âNew Lightâ is a cant phrase in the west of Scotland for those religious opinions which Dr. Taylor of Norwich has so strenuously defended.âR. B.]





Epistle To James Smith

Friendship, mysterious cement of the soul! Sweetâner of Life, and solder of Society! I owe thee muchâBlair. Dear Smith, the sleeâst, pawkie thief, That eâer attempted stealth or rief! Ye surely hae some warlock-brief Owre human hearts; For neâer a bosom yet was prief Against your arts. For me, I swear by sun anâ moon, Anâ evâry star that blinks aboon, Yeâve cost me twenty pair oâ shoon, Just gaun to see you; Anâ evâry ither pair thatâs done, Mair taen Iâm wiâ you. That auld, capricious carlin, Nature, To mak amends for scrimpit stature, Sheâs turnâd you off, a human creature On her first plan, And in her freaks, on evâry feature Sheâs wrote the Man. Just now Iâve taâen the fit oâ rhyme, My barmie noddleâs working prime. My fancy yerkit up sublime, Wiâ hasty summon; Hae ye a leisure-momentâs time To hear whatâs comin? Some rhyme a neiborâs name to lash; Some rhyme (vain thought!) for needfuâ cash; Some rhyme to court the countra clash, Anâ raise a din; For me, an aim I never fash; I rhyme for fun. The star that rules my luckless lot, Has fated me the russet coat, Anâ damnâd my fortune to the groat; But, in requit, Has blest me with a random-shot Oâcountra wit. This while my notionâs taen a sklent, To try my fate in guid, black prent; But still the mair Iâm that way bent, Something cries âHooklie!â I red you, honest man, tak tent? Yeâll shaw your folly; âThereâs ither poets, much your betters, Far seen in Greek, deep men oâ letters, Hae thought they had ensurâd their debtors, Aâ future ages; Now moths deform, in shapeless tatters, Their unknown pages.â Then farewell hopes of laurel-boughs, To garland my poetic brows! Henceforth Iâll rove where busy ploughs Are whistlinâ thrang, Anâ teach the lanely heights anâ howes My rustic sang. Iâll wander on, wiâ tentless heed How never-halting moments speed, Till fate shall snap the brittle thread; Then, all unknown, Iâll lay me with thâ inglorious dead Forgot and gone! But why oâ death being a tale? Just now weâre living sound and hale; Then top and maintop crowd the sail, Heave Care oâer-side! And large, before Enjoymentâs gale, Letâs tak the tide. This life, sae farâs I understand, Is aâ enchanted fairy-land, Where Pleasure is the magic-wand, That, wielded right, Maks hours like minutes, hand in hand, Dance by fuâ light. The magic-wand then let us wield; For ance that five-anâ-fortyâs speelâd, See, crazy, weary, joyless eild, Wiâ wrinklâd face, Comes hostin, hirplin owre the field, Weâ creepin pace. When ance lifeâs day draws near the gloamin, Then fareweel vacant, careless roamin; Anâ fareweel cheerfuâ tankards foamin, Anâ social noise: Anâ fareweel dear, deluding woman, The Joy of joys! O Life! how pleasant, in thy morning, Young Fancyâs rays the hills adorning! Cold-pausing Cautionâs lesson scorning, We frisk away, Like school-boys, at thâ expected warning, To joy anâ play. We wander there, we wander here, We eye the rose upon the brier, Unmindful that the thorn is near, Among the leaves; And thoâ the puny wound appear, Short while it grieves. Some, lucky, find a flowâry spot, For which they never toilâd nor swat; They drink the sweet and eat the fat, But care or pain; And haply eye the barren hut With high disdain. With steady aim, some Fortune chase; Keen hope does evâry sinew brace; Throâ fair, throâ foul, they urge the race, Anâ seize the prey: Then cannie, in some cozie place, They close the day. And others, like your humble servanâ, Poor wights! nae rules nor roads observin, To right or left eternal swervin, They zig-zag on; Till, curst with age, obscure anâ starvin, They aften groan. Alas! what bitter toil anâ strainingâ But truce with peevish, poor complaining! Is fortuneâs fickle Luna waning? Eân let her gang! Beneath what light she has remaining, Letâs sing our sang. My pen I here fling to the door, And kneel, ye Powârs! and warm implore, âThoâ I should wander Terra oâer, In all her climes, Grant me but this, I ask no more, Aye rowth oâ rhymes. âGie dreepin roasts to countra lairds, Till icicles hing frae their beards; Gie fine braw claes to fine life-guards, And maids of honour; Anâ yill anâ whisky gie to cairds, Until they sconner. âA title, Dempster1 merits it; A garter gie to Willie Pitt; Gie wealth to some be-ledgerâd cit, In cent. per cent.; But give me real, sterling wit, And Iâm content. [Footnote 1: George Dempster of Dunnichen, M.P.] âWhile ye are pleasâd to keep me hale, Iâll sit down oâer my scanty meal, Beât water-brose or muslin-kail, Wiâ cheerfuâ face, As langâs the Muses dinna fail To say the grace.â An anxious eâe I never throws Behint my lug, or by my nose; I jouk beneath Misfortuneâs blows As weelâs I may; Sworn foe to sorrow, care, and prose, I rhyme away. O ye douce folk that live by rule, Grave, tideless-blooded, calm anâcool, Comparâd wiâ youâO fool! fool! fool! How much unlike! Your hearts are just a standing pool, Your lives, a dyke! Nae hair-brainâd, sentimental traces In your unletterâd, nameless faces! In arioso trills and graces Ye never stray; But gravissimo, solemn basses Ye hum away. Ye are sae grave, nae doubt yeâre wise; Nae ferly thoâ ye do despise The hairum-scairum, ram-stam boys, The rattling squad: I see ye upward cast your eyesâ Ye ken the road! Whilst Iâbut I shall haud me there, Wiâ you Iâll scarce gang ony whereâ Then, Jamie, I shall say nae mair, But quat my sang, Content wiâ you to mak a pair. Whareâer I gang.





The Vision

Duan First1 The sun had closâd the winter day, The curless quat their roarin play, And hungerâd maukin taen her way, To kail-yards green, While faithless snaws ilk step betray Whare she has been. The thresherâs weary flingin-tree, The lee-lang day had tired me; And when the day had closâd his eâe, Far iâ the west, Ben iâ the spence, right pensivelie, I gaed to rest. There, lanely by the ingle-cheek, I sat and eyâd the spewing reek, That fillâd, wiâ hoast-provoking smeek, The auld clay biggin; Anâ heard the restless rattons squeak About the riggin. All in this mottie, misty clime, I backward musâd on wasted time, How I had spent my youthfuâ prime, Anâ done nae thing, But stringing blethers up in rhyme, For fools to sing. Had I to guid advice but harkit, I might, by this, hae led a market, Or strutted in a bank and clarkit My cash-account; While here, half-mad, half-fed, half-sarkit. Is aâ thâ amount. [Footnote 1: Duan, a term of Ossianâs for the different divisions of a digressive poem. See his Cath-Loda, vol. 2 of MâPhersonâs translation.âR. B.] I started, muttâring, âblockhead! coof!â And heavâd on high my waukit loof, To swear by aâ yon starry roof, Or some rash aith, That I henceforth wad be rhyme-proof Till my last breathâ When click! the string the snick did draw; Anâ jee! the door gaed to the waâ; Anâ by my ingle-lowe I saw, Now bleezin bright, A tight, outlandish hizzie, braw, Come full in sight. Ye need na doubt, I held my whisht; The infant aith, half-formâd, was crusht I glowrâd as eerieâs Iâd been dusht In some wild glen; When sweet, like honest Worth, she blusht, Anâ stepped ben. Green, slender, leaf-clad holly-boughs Were twisted, gracefuâ, round her brows; I took her for some Scottish Muse, By that same token; And come to stop those reckless vows, Would soon been broken. A âhair-brainâd, sentimental traceâ Was strongly marked in her face; A wildly-witty, rustic grace Shone full upon her; Her eye, evân turnâd on empty space, Beamâd keen with honour. Down flowâd her robe, a tartan sheen, Till half a leg was scrimply seen; Anâ such a leg! my bonie Jean Could only peer it; Sae straught, sae taper, tight anâ cleanâ Nane else came near it. Her mantle large, of greenish hue, My gazing wonder chiefly drew: Deep lights and shades, bold-mingling, threw A lustre grand; And seemâd, to my astonishâd view, A well-known land. Here, rivers in the sea were lost; There, mountains to the skies were tossât: Here, tumbling billows markâd the coast, With surging foam; There, distant shone Artâs lofty boast, The lordly dome. Here, Doon pourâd down his far-fetchâd floods; There, well-fed Irwine stately thuds: Auld hermit Ayr staw throâ his woods, On to the shore; And many a lesser torrent scuds, With seeming roar. Low, in a sandy valley spread, An ancient borough rearâd her head; Still, as in Scottish story read, She boasts a race To evâry nobler virtue bred, And polishâd grace.2 By stately towâr, or palace fair, Or ruins pendent in the air, Bold stems of heroes, here and there, I could discern; Some seemâd to muse, some seemâd to dare, With feature stern. My heart did glowing transport feel, To see a race heroic3 wheel, [Footnote 2: The seven stanzas following this were first printed in the Edinburgh edition, 1787. Other stanzas, never published by Burns himself, are given on p. 180.] [Footnote 3: The Wallaces.âR. B.] And brandish round the deep-dyed steel, In sturdy blows; While, back-recoiling, seemâd to reel Their Suthron foes. His Countryâs Saviour,4 mark him well! Bold Richardtonâs heroic swell;5 The chief, on Sark who glorious fell,6 In high command; And he whom ruthless fates expel His native land. There, where a sceptrâd Pictish shade Stalkâd round his ashes lowly laid,7 I markâd a martial race, pourtrayâd In colours strong: Bold, soldier-featurâd, undismayâd, They strode along. Throâ many a wild, romantic grove,8 Near many a hermit-fancied cove (Fit haunts for friendship or for love, In musing mood), An aged Judge, I saw him rove, Dispensing good. With deep-struck, reverential awe, The learned Sire and Son I saw:9 To Natureâs God, and Natureâs law, They gave their lore; This, all its source and end to draw, That, to adore. [Footnote 4: William Wallace.âR.B.] [Footnote 5: Adam Wallace of Richardton, cousin to the immortal preserver of Scottish independence.âR.B.] [Footnote 6: Wallace, laird of Craigie, who was second in command under Douglas, Earl of Ormond, at the famous battle on the banks of Sark, fought anno 1448. That glorious victory was principally owing to the judicious conduct and intrepid valour of the gallant laird of Craigie, who died of his wounds after the action.âR.B.] [Footnote 7: Coilus, King of the Picts, from whom the district of Kyle is said to take its name, lies buried, as tradition says, near the family seat of the Montgomeries of Coilsfield, where his burialâplace is still shown.âR.B.] [Footnote 8: Barskimming, the seat of the Lord Justiceâ Clerk.âR.B.] [Footnote 9: Catrine, the seat of the late Doctor and present Professor Stewart.âR.B.] Brydonâs brave ward10 I well could spy, Beneath old Scotiaâs smiling eye: Who callâd on Fame, low standing by, To hand him on, Where many a patriot-name on high, And hero shone.
Duan Second With musing-deep, astonishâd stare, I viewâd the heavenly-seeming Fair; A whispering throb did witness bear Of kindred sweet, When with an elder sisterâs air She did me greet. âAll hail! my own inspired bard! In me thy native Muse regard; Nor longer mourn thy fate is hard, Thus poorly low; I come to give thee such reward, As we bestow! âKnow, the great genius of this land Has many a light aerial band, Who, all beneath his high command, Harmoniously, As arts or arms they understand, Their labours ply. âThey Scotiaâs race among them share: Some fire the soldier on to dare; Some rouse the patriot up to bare Corruptionâs heart: Some teach the bardâa darling careâ The tuneful art. ââMong swelling floods of reeking gore, They, ardent, kindling spirits pour; [Footnote 10: Colonel Fullarton.âR.B. This gentleman had travelled under the care of Patrick Brydone, author of a well-known âTour Through Sicily and Malta.â] Or, âmid the venal senateâs roar, They, sightless, stand, To mend the honest patriot-lore, And grace the hand. âAnd when the bard, or hoary sage, Charm or instruct the future age, They bind the wild poetric rage In energy, Or point the inconclusive page Full on the eye. âHence, Fullarton, the brave and young; Hence, Dempsterâs zeal-inspired tongue; Hence, sweet, harmonious Beattie sung His âMinstrel laysâ; Or tore, with noble ardour stung, The scepticâs bays. âTo lower orders are assignâd The humbler ranks of human-kind, The rustic bard, the labâring hind, The artisan; All choose, as various theyâre inclinâd, The various man. âWhen yellow waves the heavy grain, The threatâning storm some strongly rein; Some teach to meliorate the plain With tillage-skill; And some instruct the shepherd-train, Blythe oâer the hill. âSome hint the loverâs harmless wile; Some grace the maidenâs artless smile; Some soothe the labârerâs weary toil For humble gains, And make his cottage-scenes beguile His cares and pains. âSome, bounded to a district-space Explore at large manâs infant race, To mark the embryotic trace Of rustic bard; And careful note each opening grace, A guide and guard. âOf these am IâCoila my name: And this district as mine I claim, Where once the Campbells, chiefs of fame, Held ruling power: I markâd thy embryo-tuneful flame, Thy natal hour. âWith future hope I oft would gaze Fond, on thy little early ways, Thy rudely, carollâd, chiming phrase, In uncouth rhymes; Firâd at the simple, artless lays Of other times. âI saw thee seek the sounding shore, Delighted with the dashing roar; Or when the North his fleecy store Drove throâ the sky, I saw grim Natureâs visage hoar Struck thy young eye. âOr when the deep green-mantled earth Warm cherishâd evâry floweretâs birth, And joy and music pouring forth In evâry grove; I saw thee eye the general mirth With boundless love. âWhen ripenâd fields and azure skies Callâd forth the reapersâ rustling noise, I saw thee leave their evâning joys, And lonely stalk, To vent thy bosomâs swelling rise, In pensive walk. âWhen youthful love, warm-blushing, strong, Keen-shivering, shot thy nerves along, Those accents grateful to thy tongue, Thâ adored Name, I taught thee how to pour in song, To soothe thy flame. âI saw thy pulseâs maddening play, Wild send thee Pleasureâs devious way, Misled by Fancyâs meteor-ray, By passion driven; But yet the light that led astray Was light from Heaven. âI taught thy manners-painting strains, The loves, the ways of simple swains, Till now, oâer all my wide domains Thy fame extends; And some, the pride of Coilaâs plains, Become thy friends. âThou canst not learn, nor I can show, To paint with Thomsonâs landscape glow; Or wake the bosom-melting throe, With Shenstoneâs art; Or pour, with Gray, the moving flow Warm on the heart. âYet, all beneath thâ unrivallâd rose, T e lowly daisy sweetly blows; Thoâ large the forestâs monarch throws His army shade, Yet green the juicy hawthorn grows, Adown the glade. âThen never murmur nor repine; Strive in thy humble sphere to shine; And trust me, not Potosiâs mine, Nor kingâs regard, Can give a bliss oâermatching thine, A rustic bard. âTo give my counsels all in one, Thy tuneful flame still careful fan: Preserve the dignity of Man, With soul erect; And trust the Universal Plan Will all protect. âAnd wear thou thisââshe solemn said, And bound the holly round my head: The polishâd leaves and berries red Did rustling play; And, like a passing thought, she fled In light away. [To Mrs. Stewart of Stair, Burns presented a manuscript copy of the Vision. That copy embraces about twenty stanzas at the end of Duan First, which he cancelled when he came to print the price in his Kilmarnock volume. Seven of these he restored in printing his second edition, as noted on p. 174. The following are the verses which he left unpublished.]





Suppressed Stanzaâs Of âThe Visionâ

After 18th stanza of the text (at âHis native landâ):â With secret throes I marked that earth, That cottage, witness of my birth; And near I saw, bold issuing forth In youthful pride, A Lindsay race of noble worth, Famed far and wide. Where, hid behind a spreading wood, An ancient Pict-built mansion stood, I spied, among an angel brood, A female pair; Sweet shone their high maternal blood, And fatherâs air.1 An ancient tower2 to memory brought How Dettingenâs bold hero fought; Still, far from sinking into nought, It owns a lord Who far in western climates fought, With trusty sword. [Footnote 1: Sundrum.âR.B.] [Footnote 2: Stair.âR.B.] Among the rest I well could spy One gallant, graceful, martial boy, The soldier sparkled in his eye, A diamond water. I blest that noble badge with joy, That owned me frater.3
After 20th stanza of the text (at âDispensing goodâ):â Near by arose a mansion fine4 The seat of many a muse divine; Not rustic muses such as mine, With holly crownâd, But thâ ancient, tuneful, laurellâd Nine, From classic ground. I mournâd the card that Fortune dealt, To see where bonie Whitefoords dwelt;5 But other prospects made me melt, That village near;6 There Nature, Friendship, Love, I felt, Fond-mingling, dear! Hail! Natureâs pang, more strong than death! Warm Friendshipâs glow, like kindling wrath! Love, dearer than the parting breath Of dying friend! Not evân with lifeâs wild devious path, Your force shall end! The Power that gave the soft alarms In blooming Whitefoordâs rosy charms, Still threats the tiny, featherâd arms, The barbed dart, While lovely Wilhelmina warms The coldest heart.7
After 21st stanza of the text (at âThat, to adoreâ):â Where Lugar leaves his moorland plaid,8 Where lately Want was idly laid, [Footnote 3: Captain James Montgomerie, Master of St. Jamesâ Lodge, Tarbolton, to which the author has the honour to belong.âR.B.] [Footnote 4: Auchinleck.âR.B.] [Footnote 5: Ballochmyle.] [Footnote 6: Mauchline.] [Footnote 7: Miss Wilhelmina Alexander.] [Footnote 8: Cumnock.âR.B.] I marked busy, bustling Trade, In fervid flame, Beneath a Patronessâ aid, of noble name. Wild, countless hills I could survey, And countless flocks as wild as they; But other scenes did charms display, That better please, Where polishâd manners dwell with Gray, In rural ease.9 Where Cessnock pours with gurgling sound;10 And Irwine, marking out the bound, Enamourâd of the scenes around, Slow runs his race, A name I doubly honourâd found,11 With knightly grace. Brydonâs brave ward,12 I saw him stand, Fame humbly offering her hand, And near, his kinsmanâs rustic band,13 With one accord, Lamenting their late blessed land Must change its lord. The owner of a pleasant spot, Near and sandy wilds, I last did note;14 A heart too warm, a pulse too hot At times, oâerran: But large in evâry feature wrote, Appearâd the Man.
The Rantinâ Dog, The Daddie Oât TuneââWhareâll our guidman lie.â
O wha my babie-clouts will buy? O wha will tent me when I cry? Wha will kiss me where I lie? The rantinâ dog, the daddie oât. [Footnote 9: Mr. Farquhar Gray.âR.B.] [Footnote 10: Auchinskieth.âR.B.] [Footnote 11: Caprington.âR.B.] [Footnote 12: Colonel Fullerton.âR.B.] [Footnote 13: Dr. Fullerton.âR.B.] [Footnote 14: Orangefield.âR.B.] O wha will own he did the faut? The rantinâ dog, the daddie oât.
Hereâs His Health In Water TuneââThe Job of Journey-work.â
Althoâ my back be at the waâ, And thoâ he be the fautor; Althoâ my back be at the waâ, Yet, hereâs his health in water. O wae gae by his wanton sides, Sae brawlieâs he could flatter; Till for his sake Iâm slighted sair, And dree the kintra clatter: But thoâ my back be at the waâ, And thoâ he be the fautor; But thoâ my back be at the waâ, Yet hereâs his health in water!





Address To The Unco Guid, Or The Rigidly Righteous

My Son, these maxims make a rule, Anâ lump them aye thegither; The Rigid Righteous is a fool, The Rigid Wise anither: The cleanest corn that ere was dight May hae some pyles oâ caff in; So neâer a fellow-creature slight For random fits oâ daffin. (Solomon.âEccles. ch. vii. verse 16.) O ye wha are sae guid yourselâ, Sae pious and sae holy, Yeâve nought to do but mark and tell Your neiboursâ fauts and folly! Whase life is like a weel-gaun mill, Supplied wiâ store oâ water; The heaped happerâs ebbing still, Anâ still the clap plays clatter. Hear me, ye venerable core, As counsel for poor mortals That frequent pass douce Wisdomâs door For glaikit Follyâs portals: I, for their thoughtless, careless sakes, Would here propone defencesâ Their donsie tricks, their black mistakes, Their failings and mischances. Ye see your state wiâ theirs compared, And shudder at the niffer; But cast a momentâs fair regard, What maks the mighty differ; Discount what scant occasion gave, That purity ye pride in; And (whatâs aft mair than aâ the lave), Your better art oâ hidin. Think, when your castigated pulse Gies now and then a wallop! What ragings must his veins convulse, That still eternal gallop! Wiâ wind and tide fair iâ your tail, Right on ye scud your sea-way; But in the teeth oâ baith to sail, It maks a unco lee-way. See Social Life and Glee sit down, All joyous and unthinking, Till, quite transmugrified, theyâre grown Debauchery and Drinking: O would they stay to calculate Thâ eternal consequences; Or your more dreaded hell to state, Damnation of expenses! Ye high, exalted, virtuous dames, Tied up in godly laces, Before ye gie poor Frailty names, Suppose a change oâ cases; A dear-lovâd lad, convenience snug, A treachârous inclinationâ But let me whisper iâ your lug, Yeâre aiblins nae temptation. Then gently scan your brother man, Still gentler sister woman; Thoâ they may gang a kennin wrang, To step aside is human: One point must still be greatly dark,â The moving Why they do it; And just as lamely can ye mark, How far perhaps they rue it. Who made the heart, âtis He alone Decidedly can try us; He knows each chord, its various tone, Each spring, its various bias: Then at the balance letâs be mute, We never can adjust it; Whatâs done we partly may compute, But know not whatâs resisted.





The Inventory1

In answer to a mandate by the Surveyor of the Taxes Sir, as your mandate did request, I send you here a faithfuâ list, Oâ gudes anâ gear, anâ aâ my graith, To which Iâm clear to giâe my aith. Imprimis, then, for carriage cattle, I hae four brutes oâ gallant mettle, As ever drew afore a pettle. My hand-afore âs a guid auld has-been, Anâ wight anâ wilfuâ aâ his days been: My hand-ahin âs a weel gaun fillie, That aft has borne me hame frae Killie.2 Anâ your auld borough mony a time In days when riding was nae crime. But ance, when in my wooing pride I, like a blockhead, boost to ride, The wilfuâ creature sae I pat to, (Lord pardon aâ my sins, anâ that too!) I playâd my fillie sic a shavie, Sheâs aâ bedevilâd wiâ the spavie. My furr-ahin âs a wordy beast, As eâer in tug or tow was traced. The fourthâs a Highland Donald hastle, A damnâd red-wud Kilburnie blastie! Foreby a cowt, oâ cowts the wale, As ever ran afore a tail: Gin he be sparâd to be a beast, Heâll draw me fifteen pund at least. Wheel-carriages I haâe but few, Three carts, anâ twa are feckly new; An auld wheelbarrow, mair for token, Ae leg anâ baith the trams are broken; I made a poker oâ the spinâle, Anâ my auld mither brunt the trinâle. [Footnote 1: The âInventoryâ was addressed to Mr. Aitken of Ayr, surveyor of taxes for the district.] [Footnote 2: Kilmarnock.âR. B.] For men, Iâve three mischievous boys, Run-deils for ranting anâ for noise; A gaudsman ane, a thrasher tâ other: Wee Davock hauds the nowt in fother. I rule them as I ought, discreetly, Anâ aften labour them completely; Anâ aye on Sundays duly, nightly, I on the Questions targe them tightly; Till, faith! wee Davockâs grown sae gleg, Thoâ scarcely langer than your leg, Heâll screed you aff Effectual Calling, As fast as ony in the dwalling. Iâve nane in female servant station, (Lord keep me aye frae aâ temptation!) I hae nae wifeâand thay my bliss is, Anâ ye have laid nae tax on misses; Anâ then, if kirk folks dinna clutch me, I ken the deevils darena touch me. Wiâ weans Iâm mair than weel contented, Heavân sent me ane mae than I wanted! My sonsie, smirking, dear-bought Bess, She stares the daddy in her face, Enough of ought ye like but grace; But her, my bonie, sweet wee lady, Iâve paid enough for her already; Anâ gin ye tax her or her mither, By the Lord, yeâse get them aâ thegither! And now, remember, Mr. Aiken, Nae kind of licence out Iâm takin: Frae this time forth, I do declare Iâse neâer ride horse nor hizzie mair; Throâ dirt and dub for life Iâll paidle, Ere I sae dear pay for a saddle; My travel aâ on foot Iâll shank it, Iâve sturdy bearers, Gude the thankit! The kirk and you may tak you that, It puts but little in your pat; Sae dinna put me in your beuk, Nor for my ten white shillings leuk. This list, wiâ my ain hand I wrote it, The day and date as under noted; Then know all ye whom it concerns, Subscripsi huic, Robert Burns. Mossgiel, February 22, 1786.





To John Kennedy, Dumfries House

Now, Kennedy, if foot or horse Eâer bring you in by Mauchlin corse, (Lord, man, thereâs lasses there wad force A hermitâs fancy; Anâ down the gate in faith theyâre worse, Anâ mair unchancy). But as Iâm sayin, please step to Dowâs, Anâ taste sic gear as Johnie brews, Till some bit callan bring me news That ye are there; Anâ if we dinna hae a bouze, Iâse neâer drink mair. Itâs no I like to sit anâ swallow, Then like a swine to puke anâ wallow; But gie me just a true good fallow, Wiâ right ingine, And spunkie ance to mak us mellow, Anâ then weâll shine. Now if yeâre ane oâ warlâs folk, Wha rate the wearer by the cloak, Anâ sklent on poverty their joke, Wiâ bitter sneer, Wiâ you nae friendship I will troke, Nor cheap nor dear. But if, as Iâm informed weel, Ye hate as illâs the very deil The flinty heart that canna feelâ Come, sir, hereâs to you! Hae, thereâs my haunâ, I wiss you weel, Anâ gude be wiâ you.
