To Mr. MâAdam, Of Craigen-Gillan

In answer to an obliging Letter he sent in the commencement of my poetic career. Sir, oâer a gill I gat your card, I trow it made me proud; âSee wha taks notice oâ the bard!â I lap and cried fuâ loud. Now deil-ma-care about their jaw, The senseless, gawky million; Iâll cock my nose abune them aâ, Iâm roosâd by Craigen-Gillan! âTwas noble, sir; âtwas like yourselfâ, To grant your high protection: A great manâs smile ye ken fuâ well Is aye a blest infection. Thoâ, by his banes wha in a tub Matchâd Macedonian Sandy! On my ain legs throâ dirt and dub, I independent stand aye,â And when those legs to gude, warm kail, Wiâ welcome canna bear me, A lee dyke-side, a sybow-tail, Anâ barley-scone shall cheer me. Heaven spare you lang to kiss the breath Oâ mony flowâry simmers! Anâ bless your bonie lasses baith, Iâm tauld theyâre loosome kimmers! Anâ God bless young Dunaskinâs laird, The blossom of our gentry! Anâ may he wear and auld manâs beard, A credit to his country.





To A Louse, On Seeing One On A Ladyâs Bonnet, At Church

Ha! whaur ye gaun, ye crowlin ferlie? Your impudence protects you sairly; I canna say but ye strunt rarely, Owre gauze and lace; Thoâ, faith! I fear ye dine but sparely On sic a place. Ye ugly, creepin, blastit wonner, Detested, shunnâd by saunt anâ sinner, How daur ye set your fit upon herâ Sae fine a lady? Gae somewhere else and seek your dinner On some poor body. Swith! in some beggarâs haffet squattle; There ye may creep, and sprawl, and sprattle, Wiâ ither kindred, jumping cattle, In shoals and nations; Whaur horn nor bane neâer daur unsettle Your thick plantations. Now haud you there, yeâre out oâ sight, Below the fattârels, snug and tight; Na, faith ye yet! yeâll no be right, Till yeâve got on itâ The verra tapmost, towârin height Oâ Missâ bonnet. My sooth! right bauld ye set your nose out, As plump anâ grey as ony groset: O for some rank, mercurial rozet, Or fell, red smeddum, Iâd gie you sic a hearty dose oât, Wad dress your droddum. I wad na been surprisâd to spy You on an auld wifeâs flainen toy; Or aiblins some bit dubbie boy, Onâs wyliecoat; But Missâ fine Lunardi! fye! How daur ye doât? O Jeany, dinna toss your head, Anâ set your beauties aâ abread! Ye little ken what cursed speed The blastieâs makin: Thae winks anâ finger-ends, I dread, Are notice takin. O wad some Power the giftie gie us To see oursels as ithers see us! It wad frae mony a blunder free us, Anâ foolish notion: What airs in dress anâ gait wad leaâe us, Anâ evân devotion!





Inscribed On A Work Of Hannah Moreâs

Presented to the Author by a Lady. Thou flattâring mark of friendship kind, Still may thy pages call to mind The dear, the beauteous donor; Thoâ sweetly female evâry part, Yet such a head, and more the heart Does both the sexes honour: She showâd her taste refinâd and just, When she selected thee; Yet deviating, own I must, For sae approving me: But kind still Iâll mind still The giver in the gift; Iâll bless her, anâ wiss her A Friend aboon the lift.





Song, Composed In Spring

TuneââJockeyâs Grey Breeks.â
Again rejoicing Nature sees Her robe assume its vernal hues: Her leafy locks wave in the breeze, All freshly steepâd in morning dews. Chorus.âAnd maun I still on Menie doat, And bear the scorn thatâs in her eâe? For itâs jet, jet black, anâ itâs like a hawk, Anâ it winna let a body be. In vain to me the cowslips blaw, In vain to me the viâlets spring; In vain to me in glen or shaw, The mavis and the lintwhite sing. And maun I still, &c. The merry ploughboy cheers his team, Wiâ joy the tentie seedsman stalks; But life to meâs a weary dream, A dream of ane that never wauks. And maun I still, &c. The wanton coot the water skims, Amang the reeds the ducklings cry, The stately swan majestic swims, And evâry thing is blest but I. And maun I still, &c. The sheep-herd steeks his faulding slap, And oâer the moorlands whistles shill: Wiâ wild, unequal, wandâring step, I meet him on the dewy hill. And maun I still, &c. And when the lark, âtween light and dark, Blythe waukens by the daisyâs side, And mounts and sings on flittering wings, A woe-worn ghaist I hameward glide. And maun I still, &c. Come winter, with thine angry howl, And raging, bend the naked tree; Thy gloom will soothe my cheerless soul, When nature all is sad like me! And maun I still, &c.





To A Mountain Daisy,

On turning down with the Plough, in April, 1786. Wee, modest crimson-tipped flowâr, Thouâs met me in an evil hour; For I maun crush amang the stoure Thy slender stem: To spare thee now is past my powâr, Thou bonie gem. Alas! itâs no thy neibor sweet, The bonie lark, companion meet, Bending thee âmang the dewy weet, Wiâ sprecklâd breast! When upward-springing, blythe, to greet The purpling east. Cauld blew the bitter-biting north Upon thy early, humble birth; Yet cheerfully thou glinted forth Amid the storm, Scarce rearâd above the parent-earth Thy tender form. The flaunting flowârs our gardens yield, High sheltâring woods and waâs maun shield; But thou, beneath the random bield Oâ clod or stane, Adorns the histie stibble field, Unseen, alane. There, in thy scanty mantle clad, Thy snawie bosom sun-ward spread, Thou lifts thy unassuming head In humble guise; But now the share uptears thy bed, And low thou lies! Such is the fate of artless maid, Sweet flowâret of the rural shade! By loveâs simplicity betrayâd, And guileless trust; Till she, like thee, all soilâd, is laid Low iâ the dust. Such is the fate of simple bard, On lifeâs rough ocean luckless starrâd! Unskilful he to note the card Of prudent lore, Till billows rage, and gales blow hard, And whelm him oâer! Such fate to suffering worth is givân, Who long with wants and woes has strivân, By human pride or cunning drivân To misâryâs brink; Till wrenchâd of evâry stay but Heavân, He, ruinâd, sink! Evân thou who mournâst the Daisyâs fate, That fate is thineâno distant date; Stern Ruinâs plough-share drives elate, Full on thy bloom, Till crushâd beneath the furrowâs weight, Shall be thy doom!





To Ruin

All hail! inexorable lord! At whose destruction-breathing word, The mightiest empires fall! Thy cruel, woe-delighted train, The ministers of grief and pain, A sullen welcome, all! With stern-resolvâd, despairing eye, I see each aimed dart; For one has cut my dearest tie, And quivers in my heart. Then lowâring, and pouring, The storm no more I dread; Thoâ thickâning, and blackâning, Round my devoted head. And thou grim Powâr by life abhorrâd, While life a pleasure can afford, Oh! hear a wretchâs prayâr! Nor more I shrink appallâd, afraid; I court, I beg thy friendly aid, To close this scene of care! When shall my soul, in silent peace, Resign lifeâs joyless dayâ My weary heart its throbbing cease, Cold mouldâring in the clay? No fear more, no tear more, To stain my lifeless face, Enclasped, and grasped, Within thy cold embrace!





The Lament

Occasioned by the unfortunate issue of a Friendâs Amour. Alas! how oft does goodness would itself, And sweet affection prove the spring of woe! Home. O thou pale orb that silent shines While care-untroubled mortals sleep! Thou seest a wretch who inly pines. And wanders here to wail and weep! With woe I nightly vigils keep, Beneath thy wan, unwarming beam; And mourn, in lamentation deep, How life and love are all a dream! I joyless view thy rays adorn The faintly-marked, distant hill; I joyless view thy trembling horn, Reflected in the gurgling rill: My fondly-fluttering heart, be still! Thou busy powâr, remembrance, cease! Ah! must the agonizing thrill For ever bar returning peace! No idly-feignâd, poetic pains, My sad, love-lorn lamentings claim: No shepherdâs pipe-Arcadian strains; No fabled tortures, quaint and tame. The plighted faith, the mutual flame, The oft-attested powârs above, The promisâd fatherâs tender name; These were the pledges of my love! Encircled in her clasping arms, How have the rapturâd moments flown! How have I wishâd for fortuneâs charms, For her dear sake, and herâs alone! And, must I think it! is she gone, My secret heartâs exulting boast? And does she heedless hear my groan? And is she ever, ever lost? Oh! can she bear so base a heart, So lost to honour, lost to truth, As from the fondest lover part, The plighted husband of her youth? Alas! lifeâs path may be unsmooth! Her way may lie throâ rough distress! Then, who her pangs and pains will soothe Her sorrows share, and make them less? Ye winged hours that oâer us passâd, Enrapturâd more, the more enjoyâd, Your dear remembrance in my breast My fondly-treasurâd thoughts employâd: That breast, how dreary now, and void, For her too scanty once of room! Evân evâry ray of hope destroyâd, And not a wish to gild the gloom! The morn, that warns thâ approaching day, Awakes me up to toil and woe; I see the hours in long array, That I must suffer, lingering, slow: Full many a pang, and many a throe, Keen recollectionâs direful train, Must wring my soul, were Phoebus, low, Shall kiss the distant western main. And when my nightly couch I try, Sore harassâd out with care and grief, My toil-beat nerves, and tear-worn eye, Keep watchings with the nightly thief: Or if I slumber, fancy, chief, Reigns, haggardâwild, in sore affright: Evân day, all-bitter, brings relief From such a horror-breathing night. O thou bright queen, who oâer thâ expanse Now highest reignâst, with boundless sway Oft has thy silent-marking glance Observâd us, fondly-wandâring, stray! The time, unheeded, sped away, While loveâs luxurious pulse beat high, Beneath thy silver-gleaming ray, To mark the mutual-kindling eye. Oh! scenes in strong remembrance set! Scenes, never, never to return! Scenes, if in stupor I forget, Again I feel, again I burn! From evâry joy and pleasure torn, Lifeâs weary vale Iâll wander throâ; And hopeless, comfortless, Iâll mourn A faithless womanâs broken vow!





Despondency: An Ode

Oppressâd with grief, oppressâd with care, A burden more than I can bear, I set me down and sigh; O life! thou art a galling load, Along a rough, a weary road, To wretches such as I! Dim backward as I cast my view, What sickâning scenes appear! What sorrows yet may pierce me through, Too justly I may fear! Still caring, despairing, Must be my bitter doom; My woes here shall close neâer But with the closing tomb! Happy! ye sons of busy life, Who, equal to the bustling strife, No other view regard! Evân when the wished endâs denied, Yet while the busy means are plied, They bring their own reward: Whilst I, a hope-abandonâd wight, Unfitted with an aim, Meet evâry sad returning night, And joyless morn the same! You, bustling, and justling, Forget each grief and pain; I, listless, yet restless, Find evâry prospect vain. How blest the solitaryâs lot, Who, all-forgetting, all forgot, Within his humble cell, The cavern, wild with tangling roots, Sits oâer his newly gatherâd fruits, Beside his crystal well! Or haply, to his evâning thought, By unfrequented stream, The ways of men are distant brought, A faint, collected dream; While praising, and raising His thoughts to heavân on high, As wandâring, meandâring, He views the solemn sky. Than I, no lonely hermit placâd Where never human footstep tracâd, Less fit to play the part, The lucky moment to improve, And just to stop, and just to move, With self-respecting art: But ah! those pleasures, loves, and joys, Which I too keenly taste, The solitary can despise, Can want, and yet be blest! He needs not, he heeds not, Or human love or hate; Whilst I here must cry here At perfidy ingrate! O, enviable, early days, When dancing thoughtless pleasureâs maze, To care, to guilt unknown! How ill exchangâd for riper times, To feel the follies, or the crimes, Of others, or my own! Ye tiny elves that guiltless sport, Like linnets in the bush, Ye little know the ills ye court, When manhood is your wish! The losses, the crosses, That active man engage; The fears all, the tears all, Of dim declining age!





To Gavin Hamilton, Esq., Mauchline,

Recommending a Boy. Mossgaville, May 3, 1786. I hold it, sir, my bounden duty To warn you how that Master Tootie, Alias, Laird MâGaun, Was here to hire yon lad away âBout whom ye spak the tither day, Anâ wad hae donât aff hanâ; But lest he learn the callan tricksâ Anâ faith I muckle doubt himâ Like scrapin out auld Crummieâs nicks, Anâ tellin lies about them; As lieve then, Iâd have then Your clerkship he should sair, If sae be ye may be Not fitted otherwhere. Althoâ I sayât, heâs gleg enough, Anâ âbout a house thatâs rude anâ rough, The boy might learn to swear; But then, wiâ you, heâll be sae taught, Anâ get sic fair example straught, I hae na ony fear. Yeâll catechise him, every quirk, Anâ shore him weel wiâ hell; Anâ gar him follow to the kirkâ Aye when ye gang yoursel. If ye then maun be then Frae hame this cominâ Friday, Then please, sir, to leaâe, sir, The orders wiâ your lady. My word of honour I hae giâen, In Paisley Johnâs, that night at eâen, To meet the warldâs worm; To try to get the twa to gree, Anâ name the airles anâ the fee, In legal mode anâ form: I ken he weel a snick can draw, When simple bodies let him: Anâ if a Devil be at aâ, In faith heâs sure to get him. To phrase you and praise you, Ye ken your Laureat scorns: The prayâr still you share still Of grateful Minstrel Burns.

To tell the truth and shame the deil, I am as fou as Bartie: But Foorsday, sir, my promise leal, Expect me oâ your partie, If on a beastie I can speel, Or hurl in a cartie. Yours, Robert Burns. SongâWill Ye Go To The Indies, My Mary?

TuneââWill ye go to the Ewe-Bughts, Marion.â
Will ye go to the Indies, my Mary, And leave auld Scotiaâs shore? Will ye go to the Indies, my Mary, Across thâ Atlantic roar? O sweet grows the lime and the orange, And the apple on the pine; But aâ the charms oâ the Indies Can never equal thine. SongâMy Highland Lassie, O

TuneââThe deuks dang oâer my daddy.â

But while my crimson currents flow, Iâll love my Highland lassie, O. Althoâ throâ foreign climes I range, I know her heart will never change, For her bosom burns with honourâs glow, My faithful Highland lassie, O. For her Iâll dare the billowâs roar, For her Iâll trace a distant shore, That Indian wealth may lustre throw Around my Highland lassie, O. She has my heart, she has my hand, By secret troth and honourâs band! Till the mortal stroke shall lay me low, Iâm thine, my Highland lassie, O. Farewell the glen sae bushy, O! Farewell the plain sae rashy, O! To other lands I now must go, To sing my Highland lassie, O.





Epistle To A Young Friend

May __, 1786. I Lang hae thought, my youthfuâ friend, A something to have sent you, Thoâ it should serve nae ither end Than just a kind memento: But how the subject-theme may gang, Let time and chance determine; Perhaps it may turn out a sang: Perhaps turn out a sermon. Yeâll try the world soon, my lad; And, Andrew dear, believe me, Yeâll find mankind an unco squad, And muckle they may grieve ye: For care and trouble set your thought, Evân when your endâs attained; And aâ your views may come to nought, Where evâry nerve is strained. Iâll no say, men are villains aâ; The real, hardenâd wicked, Wha hae nae check but human law, Are to a few restricked; But, Och! mankind are unco weak, Anâ little to be trusted; If self the wavering balance shake, Itâs rarely right adjusted! Yet they wha faâ in fortuneâs strife, Their fate we shouldna censure; For still, thâ important end of life They equally may answer; A man may hae an honest heart, Thoâ poortith hourly stare him; A man may tak a neiborâs part, Yet hae nae cash to spare him. Aye free, aff-hanâ, your story tell, When wiâ a bosom crony; But still keep something to yourselâ, Ye scarcely tell to ony: Conceal yourselâ as weelâs ye can Frae critical dissection; But keek throâ evâry other man, Wiâ sharpenâd, sly inspection. The sacred lowe oâ weel-placâd love, Luxuriantly indulge it; But never tempt thâ illicit rove, Thoâ naething should divulge it: I waive the quantum oâ the sin, The hazard of concealing; But, Och! it hardens aâ within, And petrifies the feeling! To catch dame Fortuneâs golden smile, Assiduous wait upon her; And gather gear by evâry wile Thatâs justified by honour; Not for to hide it in a hedge, Nor for a train attendant; But for the glorious privilege Of being independent. The fear oâ hellâs a hangmanâs whip, To haud the wretch in order; But where ye feel your honour grip, Let that aye be your border; Its slightest touches, instant pauseâ Debar aâ side-pretences; And resolutely keep its laws, Uncaring consequences. The great Creator to revere, Must sure become the creature; But still the preaching cant forbear, And evân the rigid feature: Yet neâer with wits profane to range, Be complaisance extended; An atheist-laughâs a poor exchange For Deity offended! When ranting round in pleasureâs ring, Religion may be blinded; Or if she gie a random sting, It may be little minded; But when on life weâre tempest drivânâ A conscience but a cankerâ A correspondence fixâd wiâ Heavân, Is sure a noble anchor! Adieu, dear, amiable youth! Your heart can neâer be wanting! May prudence, fortitude, and truth, Erect your brow undaunting! In ploughman phrase, âGod send you speed,â Still daily to grow wiser; And may ye better reck the rede, Then ever did thâ adviser!





Address Of Beelzebub

To the Right Honourable the Earl of Breadalbane, President of the Right Honourable and Honourable the Highland Society, which met on the 23rd of May last at the Shakespeare, Covent Garden, to concert ways and means to frustrate the designs of five hundred Highlanders, who, as the Society were informed by Mr. MâKenzie of Applecross, were so audacious as to attempt an escape from their lawful lords and masters whose property they were, by emigrating from the lands of Mr. Macdonald of Glengary to the wilds of Canada, in search of that fantastic thingâLiberty.

Long life, my Lord, anâ health be yours, Unskaithed by hungerâd Highland boors; Lord grant me nae duddie, desperate beggar, Wiâ dirk, claymore, and rusty trigger, May twin auld Scotland oâ a life She likesâas butchers like a knife. Faith you and Applecross were right To keep the Highland hounds in sight: I doubt na! they wad bid nae better, Than let them ance out owre the water, Then up among thae lakes and seas, Theyâll mak what rules and laws they please: Some daring Hancocke, or a Franklin, May set their Highland bluid a-ranklin; Some Washington again may head them, Or some Montgomery, fearless, lead them, Till God knows what may be effected When by such heads and hearts directed, Poor dunghill sons of dirt and mire May to Patrician rights aspire! Nae sage North now, nor sager Sackville, To watch and premier oâer the pack vile,â Anâ whare will ye get Howes and Clintons To bring them to a right repentanceâ To cowe the rebel generation, Anâ save the honour oâ the nation? They, anâ be d-d! what right hae they To meat, or sleep, or light oâ day? Far lessâto riches, powâr, or freedom, But what your lordship likes to gie them? But hear, my lord! Glengarry, hear! Your handâs owre light to them, I fear; Your factors, grieves, trustees, and bailies, I canna say but they do gaylies; They lay aside aâ tender mercies, Anâ tirl the hallions to the birses; Yet while theyâre only poindât and herriet, Theyâll keep their stubborn Highland spirit: But smash them! crash them aâ to spails, Anâ rot the dyvors iâ the jails! The young dogs, swinge them to the labour; Let wark anâ hunger mak them sober! The hizzies, if theyâre aughtlins fawsont, Let them in Drury-lane be lessonâd! Anâ if the wives anâ dirty brats Come thiggin at your doors anâ yetts, Flaffin wiâ duds, anâ grey wiâ beasâ, Frightin away your ducks anâ geese; Get out a horsewhip or a jowler, The langest thong, the fiercest growler, Anâ gar the tatterâd gypsies pack Wiâ aâ their bastards on their back! Go on, my Lord! I lang to meet you, Anâ in my house at hame to greet you; Wiâ common lords ye shanna mingle, The benmost neuk beside the ingle, At my right hanâ assigned your seat, âTween Herodâs hip anâ Polycrate: Or if you on your station tarrow, Between Almagro and Pizarro, A seat, Iâm sure yeâre well deservinât; Anâ till ye comeâyour humble servant, Beelzebub. June 1st, Anno Mundi, 5790.





A Dream

Thoughts, words, and deeds, the Statute blames with reason; But surely Dreams were neâer indicted Treason.

On reading, in the public papers, the Laureateâs Ode, with the other parade of June 4th, 1786, the Author was no sooner dropt asleep, than he imagined himself transported to the Birth-day Levee: and, in his dreaming fancy, made the following Address:

Guid-Morninâ to our Majesty! May Heaven augment your blisses On evâry new birth-day ye see, A humble poet wishes. My bardship here, at your Levee On sic a day as this is, Is sure an uncouth sight to see, Amang thae birth-day dresses Sae fine this day. I see yeâre complimented thrang, By mony a lord anâ lady; âGod save the Kingâ âs a cuckoo sang Thatâs unco easy said aye: The poets, too, a venal gang, Wiâ rhymes weel-turnâd anâ ready, Wad gar you trow ye neâer do wrang, But aye unerring steady, On sic a day. For me! before a monarchâs face Evân there I winna flatter; For neither pension, post, nor place, Am I your humble debtor: So, nae reflection on your Grace, Your Kingship to bespatter; Thereâs mony waur been oâ the race, And aiblins ane been better Than you this day. âTis very true, my sovereign King, My skill may weel be doubted; But facts are chiels that winna ding, Anâ downa be disputed: Your royal nest, beneath your wing, Is eâen right reft and clouted, And now the third part oâ the string, Anâ less, will gang aboot it Than did ae day.1 Far beât frae me that I aspire To blame your legislation, Or say, ye wisdom want, or fire, To rule this mighty nation: But faith! I muckle doubt, my sire, Yeâve trusted ministration To chaps wha in barn or byre Wad better fillâd their station Than courts yon day. And now yeâve gien auld Britain peace, Her broken shins to plaister, Your sair taxation does her fleece, Till she has scarce a tester: For me, thank God, my lifeâs a lease, Nae bargain wearinâ faster, Or, faith! I fear, that, wiâ the geese, I shortly boost to pasture Iâ the craft some day. [Footnote 1: The American colonies had recently been lost.] Iâm no mistrusting Willie Pitt, When taxes he enlarges, (Anâ Willâs a true guid fallowâs get, A name not envy spairges), That he intends to pay your debt, Anâ lessen aâ your charges; But, God-sake! let nae saving fit Abridge your bonie barges Anâboats this day. Adieu, my Liege; may freedom geck Beneath your high protection; Anâ may ye rax Corruptionâs neck, And gie her for dissection! But since Iâm here, Iâll no neglect, In loyal, true affection, To pay your Queen, wiâ due respect, May fealty anâ subjection This great birth-day. Hail, Majesty most Excellent! While nobles strive to please ye, Will ye accept a compliment, A simple poet gies ye? Thae bonie bairntime, Heavân has lent, Still higher may they heeze ye In bliss, till fate some day is sent For ever to release ye Frae care that day. For you, young Potentate oâWales, I tell your highness fairly, Down Pleasureâs stream, wiâ swelling sails, Iâm tauld yeâre driving rarely; But some day ye may gnaw your nails, Anâ curse your folly sairly, That eâer ye brak Dianaâs pales, Or rattlâd dice wiâ Charlie By night or day. Yet aft a ragged cowtâs been known, To mak a noble aiver; So, ye may doucely fill the throne, For aâtheir clish-ma-claver: There, him2 at Agincourt wha shone, Few better were or braver: And yet, wiâ funny, queer Sir John,3 He was an unco shaver For mony a day. For you, right revârend Osnaburg, Nane sets the lawn-sleeve sweeter, Althoâ a ribbon at your lug Wad been a dress completer: As ye disown yon paughty dog, That bears the keys of Peter, Then swith! anâ get a wife to hug, Or trowth, yeâll stain the mitre Some luckless day! Young, royal Tarry-breeks, I learn, Yeâve lately come athwart herâ A glorious galley,4 stem and stern, Weel riggâd for Venusâ barter; But first hang out, that sheâll discern, Your hymeneal charter; Then heave aboard your grapple airn, Anâ large upon her quarter, Come full that day. Ye, lastly, bonie blossoms aâ, Ye royal lasses dainty, Heavân mak you guid as well as braw, Anâ gie you lads a-plenty! But sneer na British boys awa! For kings are unco scant aye, Anâ German gentles are but smaâ, Theyâre better just than want aye On ony day. [Footnote 2: King Henry V.âR.B.] [Footnote 3: Sir John Falstaff, vid. Shakespeare.âR. B.] [Footnote 4: Alluding to the newspaper account of a certain Royal sailorâs amour.âR. B. This was Prince William Henry, third son of George III, afterward King William IV.] Gad bless you aâ! consider now, Yeâre unco muckle dautit; But ere the course oâ life be through, It may be bitter sautit: Anâ I hae seen their coggie fou, That yet hae tarrowât at it. But or the day was done, I trow, The laggen they hae clautit Fuâ clean that day.





A Dedication

To Gavin Hamilton, Esq. Expect na, sir, in this narration, A fleechin, flethârin Dedication, To roose you up, anâ caâ you guid, Anâ sprung oâ great anâ noble bluid, Because yeâre surnamâd like His Graceâ Perhaps related to the race: Then, when Iâm tirâdâand sae are ye, Wiâ mony a fulsome, sinfuâ lie, Set up a face how I stop short, For fear your modesty be hurt. This may doâmaun do, sir, wiâ them wha Maun please the great folk for a wamefou; For me! sae laigh I need na bow, For, Lord be thankit, I can plough; And when I downa yoke a naig, Then, Lord be thankit, I can beg; Sae I shall sayâanâ thatâs nae flattârinâ Itâs just sic Poet anâ sic Patron. The Poet, some guid angel help him, Or else, I fear, some ill ane skelp him! He may do weel for aâ heâs done yet, But onlyâheâs no just begun yet. The Patron (sir, ye maun forgie me; I winna lie, come what will oâ me), On evâry hand it will allowâd be, Heâs justânae better than he should be. I readily and freely grant, He downa see a poor man want; Whatâs no his ain, he winna tak it; What ance he says, he winna break it; Ought he can lend heâll no refusât, Till aft his guidness is abusâd; And rascals whiles that do him wrang, Evân that, he does na mind it lang; As master, landlord, husband, father, He does na fail his part in either. But then, nae thanks to him for aâthat; Nae godly symptom ye can caâ that; Itâs naething but a milder feature Of our poor, sinfuâ corrupt nature: Yeâll get the best oâ moral works, âMang black Gentoos, and pagan Turks, Or hunters wild on Ponotaxi, Wha never heard of orthodoxy. That heâs the poor manâs friend in need, The gentleman in word and deed, Itâs no throâ terror of damnation; Itâs just a carnal inclination. Morality, thou deadly bane, Thy tens oâ thousands thou hast slain! Vain is his hope, whase stay anâ trust is In moral mercy, truth, and justice! Noâstretch a point to catch a plack: Abuse a brother to his back; Steal through the winnock frae a whore, But point the rake that taks the door; Be to the poor like ony whunstane, And haud their noses to the grunstane; Ply evâry art oâ legal thieving; No matterâstick to sound believing. Learn three-mile prayârs, anâ half-mile graces, Wiâ weel-spread looves, anâ lang, wry faces; Grunt up a solemn, lengthenâd groan, And damn aâ parties but your own; Iâll warrant they yeâre nae deceiver, A steady, sturdy, staunch believer. O ye wha leave the springs oâ Calvin, For gumlie dubs of your ain delvin! Ye sons of Heresy and Error, Yeâll some day squeel in quaking terror, When Vengeance draws the sword in wrath. And in the fire throws the sheath; When Ruin, with his sweeping besom, Just frets till Heavân commission gies him; While oâer the harp pale Misery moans, And strikes the ever-deepâning tones, Still louder shrieks, and heavier groans! Your pardon, sir, for this digression: I maist forgat my Dedication; But when divinity comes âcross me, My readers still are sure to lose me. So, sir, you see âtwas nae daft vapour; But I maturely thought it proper, When aâ my works I did review, To dedicate them, sir, to you: Because (ye need na tak it ill), I thought them something like yourselâ. Then patronize them wiâ your favor, And your petitioner shall everâ I had amaist said, ever pray, But thatâs a word I need na say; For prayin, I hae little skill oât, Iâm baith dead-sweer, anâ wretched ill oât; But Iâse repeat each poor manâs prayâr, That kens or hears about you, sirâ âMay neâer Misfortuneâs gowling bark, Howl throâ the dwelling oâ the clerk! May neâer his genrous, honest heart, For that same genârous spirit smart! May Kennedyâs far-honourâd name Lang beet his hymeneal flame, Till Hamiltons, at least a dizzen, Are frae their nuptial labours risen: Five bonie lasses round their table, And sevân braw fellows, stout anâ able, To serve their king anâ country weel, By word, or pen, or pointed steel! May health and peace, with mutual rays, Shine on the evâning oâ his days; Till his wee, curlie Johnâs ier-oe, When ebbing life nae mair shall flow, The last, sad, mournful rites bestow!â I will not wind a lang conclusion, With complimentary effusion; But, whilst your wishes and endeavours Are blest with Fortuneâs smiles and favours, I am, dear sir, with zeal most fervent, Your much indebted, humble servant. But if (which Powârs above prevent) That iron-hearted carl, Want, Attended, in his grim advances, By sad mistakes, and black mischances, While hopes, and joys, and pleasures fly him, Make you as poor a dog as I am, Your humble servant then no more; For who would humbly serve the poor? But, by a poor manâs hopes in Heavân! While recollectionâs powâr is givânâ If, in the vale of humble life, The victim sad of fortuneâs strife, I, throâ the tender-gushing tear, Should recognise my master dear; If friendless, low, we meet together, Then, sir, your handâmy Friend and Brother!





Versified Note To Dr. Mackenzie, Mauchline

Friday firstâs the day appointed By the Right Worshipful anointed, To hold our grand procession; To get a blad oâ Johnieâs morals, And taste a swatch oâ Mansonâs barrels Iâ the way of our profession. The Master and the Brotherhood Would aâ be glad to see you; For me I would be mair than proud To share the mercies wiâ you. If Death, then, wiâ skaith, then, Some mortal heart is hechtin, Inform him, and storm him, That Saturday youâll fecht him. Robert Burns. Mossgiel, An. M. 5790.





The Farewell To the Brethren of St. Jamesâ Lodge, Tarbolton.

TuneââGuidnight, and joy be wiâ you aâ.â
Adieu! a heart-warm fond adieu; Dear brothers of the mystic tie! Ye favoured, enlightenâd few, Companions of my social joy; Thoâ I to foreign lands must hie, Pursuing Fortuneâs sliddâry baâ; With melting heart, and brimful eye, Iâll mind you still, thoâ far awa. Oft have I met your social band, And spent the cheerful, festive night; Oft, honourâd with supreme command, Presided oâer the sons of light: And by that hieroglyphic bright, Which none but Craftsmen ever saw Strong Memâry on my heart shall write Those happy scenes, when far awa. May Freedom, Harmony, and Love, Unite you in the grand Design, Beneath thâ Omniscient Eye above, The glorious Architect Divine, That you may keep thâ unerring line, Still rising by the plummetâs law, Till Order bright completely shine, Shall be my prayâr when far awa. And you, farewell! whose merits claim Justly that highest badge to wear: Heavân bless your honourâd noble name, To Masonry and Scotia dear! A last request permit me here,â When yearly ye assemble aâ, One round, I ask it with a tear, To him, the Bard thatâs far awa.





On A Scotch Bard, Gone To The West Indies

Aâ ye wha live by sowps oâ drink, Aâ ye wha live by crambo-clink, Aâ ye wha live and never think, Come, mourn wiâ me! Our billie âs gien us aâ a jink, Anâ owre the sea! Lament him aâ ye rantin core, Wha dearly like a random splore; Nae mair heâll join the merry roar; In social key; For now heâs taen anither shore. Anâ owre the sea! The bonie lasses weel may wiss him, And in their dear petitions place him: The widows, wives, anâ aâ may bless him Wiâ tearfuâ eâe; For weel I wat theyâll sairly miss him Thatâs owre the sea! O Fortune, they hae room to grumble! Hadst thou taen aff some drowsy bummle, Wha can do nought but fyke anâ fumble, âTwad been nae plea; But he was gleg as ony wumble, Thatâs owre the sea! Auld, cantie Kyle may weepers wear, Anâ stain them wiâ the saut, saut tear; âTwill mak her poor auld heart, I fear, In flinders flee: He was her Laureat mony a year, Thatâs owre the sea! He saw Misfortuneâs cauld nor-west Lang mustering up a bitter blast; A jillet brak his heart at last, Ill may she be! So, took a berth afore the mast, Anâ owre the sea. To tremble under Fortuneâs cummock, On a scarce a bellyfuâ oâ drummock, Wiâ his proud, independent stomach, Could ill agree; So, rowât his hurdies in a hammock, Anâ owre the sea. He neâer was gien to great misguidin, Yet coin his pouches wad na bide in; Wiâ him it neâer was under hiding; He dealt it free: The Muse was aâ that he took pride in, Thatâs owre the sea. Jamaica bodies, use him weel, Anâ hap him in cozie biel: Yeâll find him aye a dainty chiel, Anâ fou oâ glee: He wad na wrangâd the vera deil, Thatâs owre the sea. Farewell, my rhyme-composing billie! Your native soil was right ill-willie; But may ye flourish like a lily, Now bonilie! Iâll toast you in my hindmost gillie, Thoâ owre the sea!





SongâFarewell To Eliza

TuneââGilderoy.â
From thee, Eliza, I must go, And from my native shore; The cruel fates between us throw A boundless oceanâs roar: But boundless oceans, roaring wide, Between my love and me, They never, never can divide My heart and soul from thee. Farewell, farewell, Eliza dear, The maid that I adore! A boding voice is in mine ear, We part to meet no more! But the latest throb that leaves my heart, While Death stands victor by,â That throb, Eliza, is thy part, And thine that latest sigh!





A Bardâs Epitaph

Is there a whim-inspired fool, Owre fast for thought, owre hot for rule, Owre blate to seek, owre proud to snool, Let him draw near; And owre this grassy heap sing dool, And drap a tear. Is there a bard of rustic song, Who, noteless, steals the crowds among, That weekly this area throng, O, pass not by! But, with a frater-feeling strong, Here, heave a sigh. Is there a man, whose judgment clear Can others teach the course to steer, Yet runs, himself, lifeâs mad career, Wild as the wave, Here pauseâand, throâ the starting tear, Survey this grave. The poor inhabitant below Was quick to learn the wise to know, And keenly felt the friendly glow, And softer flame; But thoughtless follies laid him low, And stainâd his name! Reader, attend! whether thy soul Soars fancyâs flights beyond the pole, Or darkling grubs this earthly hole, In low pursuit: Know, prudent, cautious, self-control Is wisdomâs root. Epitaph For Robert Aiken, Esq. Know thou, O stranger to the fame Of this much lovâd, much honoured name! (For none that knew him need be told) A warmer heart death neâer made cold. Epitaph For Gavin Hamilton, Esq. The poor man weepsâhere Gavin sleeps, Whom canting wretches blamâd; But with such as he, whereâer he be, May I be savâd or damnâd!

Hic Jacet wee Johnie. Whoeâer thou art, O reader, know That Death has murderâd Johnie; Anâ here his body lies fuâ low; For saul he neâer had ony.





The Lass Oâ Ballochmyle

TuneââEttrick Banks.â
âTwas evenâthe dewy fields were green, On every blade the pearls hang; The zephyr wantonâd round the bean, And bore its fragrant sweets alang: In evâry glen the mavis sang, All nature listâning seemâd the while, Except where greenwood echoes rang, Amang the braes oâ Ballochmyle. With careless step I onward strayâd, My heart rejoicâd in natureâs joy, When, musing in a lonely glade, A maiden fair I chancâd to spy: Her look was like the morningâs eye, Her air like natureâs vernal smile: Perfection whisperâd, passing by, âBehold the lass oâ Ballochmyle!â Fair is the morn in flowery May, And sweet is night in autumn mild; When roving throâ the garden gay, Or wandâring in the lonely wild: But woman, natureâs darling child! There all her charms she does compile; Even there her other works are foilâd By the bonie lass oâ Ballochmyle. O, had she been a country maid, And I the happy country swain, Thoâ shelterâd in the lowest shed That ever rose on Scotlandâs plain! Throâ weary winterâs wind and rain, With joy, with rapture, I would toil; And nightly to my bosom strain The bonie lass oâ Ballochmyle. Then pride might climb the slippâry steep, Where frame and honours lofty shine; And thirst of gold might tempt the deep, Or downward seek the Indian mine: Give me the cot below the pine, To tend the flocks or till the soil; And evâry day have joys divine With the bonie lass oâ Ballochmyle.





Lines To An Old Sweetheart

Once fondly lovâd, and still rememberâd dear, Sweet early object of my youthful vows, Accept this mark of friendship, warm, sincere, Friendship! âtis all cold duty now allows. And when you read the simple artless rhymes, One friendly sigh for himâhe asks no more, Who, distant, burns in flaming torrid climes, Or haply lies beneath thâ Atlantic roar.





Motto Prefixed To The Authorâs First Publication

The simple Bard, unbroke by rules of art, He pours the wild effusions of the heart; And if inspirâd âtis Natureâs powârs inspire; Herâs all the melting thrill, and herâs the kindling fire.





Lines To Mr. John Kennedy

Natureâs LawâA Poem

Humbly inscribed to Gavin Hamilton, Esq. Great Nature spoke: observant man obeyâdâPope.
Let other heroes boast their scars, The marks of sturt and strife: And other poets sing of wars, The plagues of human life: Shame faâ the fun, wiâ sword and gun To slap mankind like lumber! I sing his name, and nobler fame, Wha multiplies our number. Great Nature spoke, with air benign, âGo on, ye human race; This lower world I you resign; Be fruitful and increase. The liquid fire of strong desire Iâve pourâd it in each bosom; Here, on this hand, does Mankind stand, And there is Beautyâs blossom.â The Hero of these artless strains, A lowly bard was he, Who sung his rhymes in Coilaâs plains, With meikle mirth anâglee; Kind Natureâs care had given his share Large, of the flaming current; And, all devout, he never sought To stem the sacred torrent. He felt the powerful, high behest Thrill, vital, throâ and throâ; And sought a correspondent breast, To give obedience due: Propitious Powers screenâd the young flowârs, From mildews of abortion; And low! the bardâa great rewardâ Has got a double portion! Auld cantie Coil may count the day, As annual it returns, The third of Libraâs equal sway, That gave another Burns, With future rhymes, anâ other times, To emulate his sire: To sing auld Coil in nobler style With more poetic fire. Ye Powers of peace, and peaceful song, Look down with gracious eyes; And bless auld Coila, large and long, With multiplying joys; Lang may she stand to prop the land, The flowâr of ancient nations; And Burnses spring, her fame to sing, To endless generations!





SongâWillie Chalmers

Mr. Chalmers, a gentleman in Ayrshire, a particular friend of mine, asked me to write a poetic epistle to a young lady, his Dulcinea. I had seen her, but was scarcely acquainted with her, and wrote as follows:â

Wiâ braw new branks in mickle pride, And eke a braw new brechan, My Pegasus Iâm got astride, And up Parnassus pechin; Whiles owre a bush wiâ donwward crush, The doited beastie stammers; Then up he gets, and off he sets, For sake oâ Willie Chalmers. I doubt na, lass, that weel kenâd name May cost a pair oâ blushes; I am nae stranger to your fame, Nor his warm urged wishes. Your bonie face sae mild and sweet, His honest heart enamours, And faith yeâll no be lost a whit, Thoâ wairâd on Willie Chalmers. Auld Truth herselâ might swear yerâe fair, And Honour safely back her; And Modesty assume your air, And neâer a ane mistak her: And sic twa love-inspiring een Might fire even holy palmers; Nae wonder then theyâve fatal been To honest Willie Chalmers. I doubt na fortune may you shore Some mim-mouâd poutherâd priestie, Fuâ lifted up wiâ Hebrew lore, And band upon his breastie: But oh! what signifies to you His lexicons and grammars; The feeling heartâs the royal blue, And thatâs wiâ Willie Chalmers. Some gapinâ, glowrinâ countra laird May warsle for your favour; May claw his lug, and straik his beard, And hoast up some palaver: My bonie maid, before ye wed Sic clumsy-witted hammers, Seek Heaven for help, and barefit skelp Awa wiâ Willie Chalmers. Forgive the Bard! my fond regard For ane that shares my bosom, Inspires my Muse to gie âm his dues For deil a hair I roose him. May powers aboon unite you soon, And fructify your amours,â And every year come in mair dear To you and Willie Chalmers.

But, fegs! the session says I maun Gae faâ upoâ anither plan Than garrin lasses coup the cran, Clean heels ower body, Anâ sairly thole their motherâs ban Afore the howdy. Come hither lad, and answer forât, Yeâre blamâd for jobbin!â Wiâ pinch I put a Sundayâs face on, Anâ snoovâd awa before the Session: I made an open, fair confessionâ I scornât to lee, Anâ syne Mess John, beyond expression, Fell foul oâ me. (Quoâ I) I fear unless ye geld me, Iâll neâer be better!â âGeld you! (quoâ he) anâ what for no? If that your right hand, leg or toe Should ever prove your spâritual foe, You should remember To cut it affâanâ what for no Your dearest member?â âNa, na, (quoâ I,) Iâm no for that, Geldingâs nae better than âtis caât; Iâd rather suffer for my faut A hearty flewit, As sair owre hip as ye can drawât, Thoâ I should rue it. âOr, gin ye like to end the bother, To please us aââIâve just ae itherâ When next wiâ yon lass I forgather, Whateâer betide it, Iâll frankly gie her ât aâ thegither, Anâ let her guide it.â But, sir, this pleasâd them warst of aâ, Anâ therefore, Tam, when that I saw, I said âGude night,â anâ camâ awaâ, Anâ left the Session; I saw they were resolved aâ On my oppression.





The Brigs Of Ayr

A Poem Inscribed to John Ballantine, Esq., Ayr. The simple Bard, rough at the rustic plough, Learning his tuneful trade from evâry bough; The chanting linnet, or the mellow thrush, Hailing the setting sun, sweet, in the green thorn bush; The soaring lark, the perching red-breast shrill, Or deep-tonâd plovers grey, wild-whistling oâer the hill; Shall heânurst in the peasantâs lowly shed, To hardy independence bravely bred, By early poverty to hardship steelâd. And trainâd to arms in stern Misfortuneâs fieldâ Shall he be guilty of their hireling crimes, The servile, mercenary Swiss of rhymes? Or labour hard the panegyric close, With all the venal soul of dedicating prose? No! though his artless strains he rudely sings, And throws his hand uncouthly oâer the strings, He glows with all the spirit of the Bard, Fame, honest fame, his great, his dear reward. Still, if some patronâs genârous care he trace, Skillâd in the secret, to bestow with grace; When Ballantine befriends his humble name, And hands the rustic stranger up to fame, With heartfelt throes his grateful bosom swells, The godlike bliss, to give, alone excels. âTwas when the stacks get on their winter hap, And thack and rape secure the toil-won crap; Potatoe-bings are snugged up frae skaith Oâ coming Winterâs biting, frosty breath; The bees, rejoicing oâer their summer toils, Unnumberâd buds anâ flowârsâ delicious spoils, Sealâd up with frugal care in massive waxen piles, Are doomâd by Man, that tyrant oâer the weak, The death oâ devils, smoorâd wiâ brimstone reek: The thundering guns are heard on evâry side, The wounded coveys, reeling, scatter wide; The featherâd field-mates, bound by Natureâs tie, Sires, mothers, children, in one carnage lie: (What warm, poetic heart but inly bleeds, And execrates manâs savage, ruthless deeds!) Nae mair the flowâr in field or meadow springs, Nae mair the grove with airy concert rings, Except perhaps the Robinâs whistling glee, Proud oâ the height oâ some bit half-lang tree: The hoary morns precede the sunny days, Mild, calm, serene, wide spreads the noontide blaze, While thick the gosamour waves wanton in the rays. âTwas in that season, when a simple Bard, Unknown and poorâsimplicityâs reward!â Ae night, within the ancient brugh of Ayr, By whim inspirâd, or haply prest wiâ care, He left his bed, and took his wayward route, And down by Simpsonâs1 wheelâd the left about: (Whether impellâd by all-directing Fate, To witness what I after shall narrate; Or whether, rapt in meditation high, He wanderâd out, he knew not where or why:) The drowsy Dungeon-clock2 had numberâd two, and Wallace Tower2 had sworn the fact was true: The tide-swoln firth, with sullen-sounding roar, Through the still night dashâd hoarse along the shore. All else was hushâd as Natureâs closed eâe; The silent moon shone high oâer tower and tree; The chilly frost, beneath the silver beam, Crept, gently-crusting, oâer the glittering streamâ When, lo! on either hand the listâning Bard, The clanging sugh of whistling wings is heard; Two dusky forms dart through the midnight air; Swift as the gos3 drives on the wheeling hare; Ane on thâ Auld Brig his airy shape uprears, The other flutters oâer the rising piers: Our warlock Rhymer instantly dexcried The Sprites that owre the Brigs of Ayr preside. (That Bards are second-sighted is nae joke, And ken the lingo of the spâritual folk; Fays, Spunkies, Kelpies, aâ, they can explain them, And even the very deils they brawly ken them). Auld Brig appearâd of ancient Pictish race, The very wrinkles Gothic in his face; He seemâd as he wiâ Time had warstlâd lang, Yet, teughly doure, he bade an unco bang. [Footnote 1: A noted tavern at the Auld Brig end.âR. B.] [Footnote 2: The two steeples.âR. B.] [Footnote 3: The Gos-hawk, or Falcon.âR. B.] New Brig was buskit in a braw new coat, That he, at Lonâon, frae ane Adams got; In âs hand five taper staves as smooth âs a bead, Wiâ virls and whirlygigums at the head. The Goth was stalking round with anxious search, Spying the time-worn flaws in every arch; It chancâd his new-come neibor took his eâe, And eâen a vexed and angry heart had he! Wiâ thieveless sneer to see his modish mien, He, down the water, gies him this guid-eâen:â
Auld Brig âI doubt na, frienâ, yeâll think yeâre nae sheepshank, Ance ye were streekit owre frae bank to bank! But gin ye be a brig as auld as meâ Thoâ faith, that date, I doubt, yeâll never seeâ Thereâll be, if that day come, Iâll wad a boddle, Some fewer whigmaleeries in your noddle.â
New Brig âAuld Vandal! ye but show your little mense, Just much about it wiâ your scanty sense: Will your poor, narrow foot-path of a street, Where twa wheel-barrows tremble when they meet, Your ruinâd, formless bulk oâ stane and lime, Compare wiâ bonie brigs oâ modern time? Thereâs men of taste wouâd tak the Ducat stream,4 Thoâ they should cast the very sark and swim, Eâer they would grate their feelings wiâ the view Oâ sic an ugly, Gothic hulk as you.â
Auld Brig âConceited gowk! puffâd up wiâ windy pride! This mony a year Iâve stood the flood anâ tide; And thoâ wiâ crazy eild Iâm sair forfairn, Iâll be a brig when yeâre a shapeless cairn! As yet ye little ken about the matter, But twaâthree winters will inform ye better. When heavy, dark, continued, aâ-day rains, [Footnote 4: A noted ford, just above the Auld Brig.âR. B.] Wiâ deepening deluges oâerflow the plains; When from the hills where springs the brawling Coil, Or stately Lugarâs mossy fountains boil; Or where the Greenock winds his moorland course. Or haunted Garpal draws his feeble source, Aroused by blustering winds anâ spotting thowes, In mony a torrent down the snaw-broo rowes; While crashing ice, borne on the rolling spate, Sweeps dams, anâ mills, anâ brigs, aâ to the gate; And from Glenbuck,5 down to the Ratton-key,6 Auld Ayr is just one lengthenâd, tumbling seaâ Then down yeâll hurl, (deil nor ye never rise!) And dash the gumlie jaups up to the pouring skies! A lesson sadly teaching, to your cost, That Architectureâs noble art is lost!â
New Brig âFine architecture, trowth, I needs must sayât oât, The Lord be thankit that weâve tint the gate oât! Gaunt, ghastly, ghaist-alluring edifices, Hanging with threatâning jut, like precipices; Oâer-arching, mouldy, gloom-inspiring coves, Supporting roofs, fantastic, stony groves; Windows and doors in nameless sculptures drest With order, symmetry, or taste unblest; Forms like some bedlam Statuaryâs dream, The crazâd creations of misguided whim; Forms might be worshippâd on the bended knee, And still the second dread command be free; Their likeness is not found on earth, in air, or sea! Mansions that would disgrace the building taste Of any mason reptile, bird or beast: Fit only for a doited monkish race, Or frosty maids forsworn the dear embrace, Or cuifs of later times, wha held the notion, That sullen gloom was sterling, true devotion: Fancies that our guid Brugh denies protection, And soon may they expire, unblest wiâ resurrection!â [Footnote 5: The source of the River Ayr.âR. B.] [Footnote 6: A small landing place above the large quay.âR. B.]
Auld Brig âO ye, my dear-rememberâd, ancient yealings, Were ye but here to share my wounded feelings! Ye worthy Proveses, anâ mony a Bailie, Wha in the paths oâ righteousness did toil aye; Ye dainty Deacons, and ye douce Conveners, To whom our moderns are but causey-cleaners Ye godly Councils, wha hae blest this town; ye godly Brethren oâ the sacred gown, Wha meekly gie your hurdies to the smiters; And (what would now be strange), ye godly Writers; Aâ ye douce folk Iâve borne aboon the broo, Were ye but here, what would ye say or do? How would your spirits groan in deep vexation, To see each melancholy alteration; And, agonising, curse the time and place When ye begat the base degenârate race! Nae langer revârend men, their countryâs glory, In plain braid Scots hold forth a plain braid story; Nae langer thrifty citizens, anâ douce, Meet owre a pint, or in the Council-house; But staumrel, corky-headed, graceless Gentry, The herryment and ruin of the country; Men, three-parts made by tailors and by barbers, Wha waste your weel-hainâd gear on damnâd new brigs and harbours!â
New Brig âNow haud you there! for faith yeâve said enough, And muckle mair than ye can mak to through. As for your Priesthood, I shall say but little, Corbies and Clergy are a shot right kittle: But, under favour oâ your langer beard, Abuse oâ Magistrates might weel be sparâd; To liken them to your auld-warld squad, I must needs say, comparisons are odd. In Ayr, wag-wits nae mair can hae a handle To mouth âa Citizen,â a term oâ scandal; Nae mair the Council waddles down the street, In all the pomp of ignorant conceit; Men wha grew wise priggin owre hops and raisins, Or gatherâd libâral views in Bonds and Seisins: If haply Knowledge, on a random tramp, Had shorâd them with a glimmer of his lamp, And would to Common-sense for once betrayâd them, Plain, dull Stupidity stept kindly in to aid them.â What farther clish-ma-claver aight been said, What bloody wars, if Sprites had blood to shed, No man can tell; but, all before their sight, A fairy train appearâd in order bright; Adown the glittering stream they featly dancâd; Bright to the moon their various dresses glancâd: They footed oâer the watâry glass so neat, The infant ice scarce bent beneath their feet: While arts of Minstrelsy among them rung, And soul-ennobling Bards heroic ditties sung. O had MâLauchlan,7 thairm-inspiring sage, Been there to hear this heavenly band engage, When throâ his dear strathspeys they bore with Highland rage; Or when they struck old Scotiaâs melting airs, The loverâs raptured joys or bleeding cares; How would his Highland lug been nobler firâd, And evân his matchless hand with finer touch inspirâd! No guess could tell what instrument appearâd, But all the soul of Musicâs self was heard; Harmonious concert rung in every part, While simple melody pourâd moving on the heart. The Genius of the Stream in front appears, A venerable Chief advancâd in years; His hoary head with water-lilies crownâd, His manly leg with garter-tangle bound. Next came the loveliest pair in all the ring, Sweet female Beauty hand in hand with Spring; Then, crownâd with flowâry hay, came Rural Joy, And Summer, with his fervid-beaming eye; [Footnote 7: A well-known performer of Scottish music on the violin.âR. B.] All-cheering Plenty, with her flowing horn, Led yellow Autumn wreathâd with nodding corn; Then Winterâs time-bleachâd locks did hoary show, By Hospitality with cloudless brow: Next followed Courage with his martial stride, From where the Feal wild-woody coverts hide;8 Benevolence, with mild, benignant air, A female form, came from the towârs of Stair;9 Learning and Worth in equal measures trode, From simple Catrine, their long-lovâd abode:10 Last, white-robâd Peace, crownâd with a hazel wreath, To rustic Agriculture did bequeath The broken, iron instruments of death: At sight of whom our Sprites forgat their kindling wrath.

PrayerâO Thou Dread Power

Lying at a reverend friendâs house one night, the author left the following verses in the room where he slept:â

O Thou dread Power, who reignâst above, I know thou wilt me hear, When for this scene of peace and love, I make this prayer sincere. The hoary Sireâthe mortal stroke, Long, long be pleasâd to spare; To bless this little filial flock, And show what good men are. She, who her lovely offspring eyes With tender hopes and fears, O bless her with a motherâs joys, But spare a motherâs tears! Their hope, their stay, their darling youth. In manhoodâs dawning blush, Bless him, Thou God of love and truth, Up to a parentâs wish. The beauteous, seraph sister-bandâ With earnest tears I prayâ Thou knowâst the snares on evâry hand, Guide Thou their steps alway. When, soon or late, they reach that coast, Oâer Lifeâs rough ocean driven, May they rejoice, no wandârer lost, A family in Heaven!

TuneââRoslin Castle.â

âI composed this song as I conveyed my chest so far on my road to Greenock, where I was to embark in a few days for Jamaica. I meant it as my farewell dirge to my native land.ââR. B.

The gloomy night is gathâring fast, Loud roars the wild, inconstant blast, Yon murky cloud is foul with rain, I see it driving oâer the plain; The hunter now has left the moor. The scattâred coveys meet secure; While here I wander, prest with care, Along the lonely banks of Ayr. The Autumn mourns her ripâning corn By early Winterâs ravage torn; Across her placid, azure sky, She sees the scowling tempest fly: Chill runs my blood to hear it rave; I think upon the stormy wave, Where many a danger I must dare, Far from the bonie banks of Ayr. âTis not the surging billowâs roar, âTis not that fatal, deadly shore; Thoâ death in evâry shape appear, The wretched have no more to fear: But round my heart the ties are bound, That heart transpiercâd with many a wound; These bleed afresh, those ties I tear, To leave the bonie banks of Ayr. Farewell, old Coilaâs hills and dales, Her healthy moors and winding vales; The scenes where wretched Fancy roves, Pursuing past, unhappy loves! Farewell, my friends! farewell, my foes! My peace with these, my love with those: The bursting tears my heart declareâ Farewell, the bonie banks of Ayr!





Address To The Toothache

My curse upon your venomâd stang, That shoots my torturâd gums alang, Anâ throâ my lug gies mony a twang, Wiâ gnawing vengeance, Tearing my nerves wiâ bitter pang, Like racking engines! When fevers burn, or argues freezes, Rheumatics gnaw, or colics squeezes, Our neiborâs sympathy can ease us, Wiâ pitying moan; But theeâthou hell oâ aâ diseasesâ Aye mocks our groan. Adown my beard the slavers trickle I throw the wee stools oâer the mickle, While round the fire the giglets keckle, To see me loup, While, raving mad, I wish a heckle Were in their doup! In aâ the numerous human dools, Ill hairsts, daft bargains, cutty stools, Or worthy frienâs rakâd iâ the mools,â Sad sight to see! The tricks oâ knaves, or fash oâfools, Thou bearâst the gree! Whereâer that place be priests caâ hell, Where aâ the tones oâ misery yell, Anâ ranked plagues their numbers tell, In dreadfuâ raw, Thou, Toothache, surely bearâst the bell, Amang them aâ! O thou grim, mischief-making chiel, That gars the notes oâ discord squeel, Till daft mankind aft dance a reel In gore, a shoe-thick, Gie aâ the faes oâ Scotlandâs weal A townmondâs toothache!





Lines On Meeting With Lord Daer1

This wot ye all whom it concerns, I, Rhymer Robin, alias Burns, October twenty-third, [Footnote 1: At the house of Professor Dugald Stewart.] A neâer-to-be-forgotten day, Sae far I spracklâd up the brae, I dinnerâd wiâ a Lord. Iâve been at drucken writersâ feasts, Nay, been bitch-fou âmang godly priestsâ Wiâ revârence be it spoken!â Iâve even joinâd the honourâd jorum, When mighty Squireships of the quorum, Their hydra drouth did sloken. But wiâ a Lord!âstand out my shin, A Lordâa Peerâan Earlâs son! Up higher yet, my bonnet Anâ sic a Lord!âlang Scoth ells twa, Our Peerage he oâerlooks them aâ, As I look oâer my sonnet. But O for Hogarthâs magic powâr! To show Sir Bardieâs willyart glowâr, Anâ how he starâd and stammerâd, When, goavin, as if led wiâ branks, Anâ stumpin on his ploughman shanks, He in the parlour hammerâd. I sidying shelterâd in a nook, Anâ at his Lordship stealât a look, Like some portentous omen; Except good sense and social glee, Anâ (what surprisâd me) modesty, I marked nought uncommon. I watchâd the symptoms oâ the Great, The gentle pride, the lordly state, The arrogant assuming; The fient a pride, nae pride had he, Nor sauce, nor state, that I could see, Mair than an honest ploughman. Then from his Lordship I shall learn, Henceforth to meet with unconcern One rank as weelâs another; Nae honest, worthy man need care To meet with noble youthful Daer, For he but meets a brother.





Masonic Song

TuneââShawn-boy,â or âOver the water to Charlie.â
Ye sons of old Killie, assembled by Willie, To follow the noble vocation; Your thrifty old mother has scarce such another To sit in that honoured station. Iâve little to say, but only to pray, As prayingâs the ton of your fashion; A prayer from thee Muse you well may excuse âTis seldom her favourite passion. Ye powers who preside oâer the wind, and the tide, Who marked each elementâs border; Who formed this frame with beneficent aim, Whose sovereign statute is order:â Within this dear mansion, may wayward Contention Or withered Envy neâer enter; May secrecy round be the mystical bound, And brotherly Love be the centre!





Tam Samsonâs Elegy

An honest manâs the noblest work of GodâPope.

When this worthy old sportman went out, last muirfowl season, he supposed it was to be, in Ossianâs phrase, âthe last of his fields,â and expressed an ardent wish to die and be buried in the muirs. On this hint the author composed his elegy and epitaph.âR.B., 1787.

Has auld Kilmarnock seen the deil? Or great Mackinlay1 thrawn his heel? Or Robertson2 again grown weel, To preach anâ read? âNaâ waur than aâ!â cries ilka chiel, âTam Samsonâs dead!â [Footnote 1: A certain preacher, a great favourite with the million. Vide âThe Ordination.â stanza ii.âR. B.] [Footnote 2: Another preacher, an equal favourite with the few, who was at that time ailing. For him see also âThe Ordination,â stanza ix.âR.B.] Kilmarnock lang may grunt anâ grane, Anâ sigh, anâ sab, anâ greet her lane, Anâ cleed her bairns, man, wife, anâ wean, In mourning weed; To Death sheâs dearly payâd the kaneâ Tam Samsonâs dead! The Brethren, oâ the mystic level May hing their head in woefuâ bevel, While by their nose the tears will revel, Like ony bead; Deathâs gien the Lodge an unco devel; Tam Samsonâs dead! When Winter muffles up his cloak, And binds the mire like a rock; When to the loughs the curlers flock, Wiâ gleesome speed, Wha will they station at the cock? Tam Samsonâs dead! When Winter muffles up his cloak, He was the king oâ aâ the core, To guard, or draw, or wick a bore, Or up the rink like Jehu roar, In time oâ need; But now he lags on Deathâs hog-scoreâ Tam Samsonâs dead! Now safe the stately sawmont sail, And trouts bedroppâd wiâ crimson hail, And eels, weel-kenâd for souple tail, And geds for greed, Since, dark in Deathâs fish-creel, we wail Tam Samsonâs dead! Rejoice, ye birring paitricks aâ; Ye cootie muircocks, crousely craw; Ye maukins, cock your fud fuâ braw Withouten dread; Your mortal fae is now awa; Tam Samsonâs dead! That woefuâ morn be ever mournâd, Saw him in shooting graith adornâd, While pointers round impatient burnâd, Frae couples freeâd; But och! he gaed and neâer returnâd! Tam Samsonâs dead! In vain auld age his body batters, In vain the gout his ancles fetters, In vain the burns cam down like waters, An acre braid! Now evâry auld wife, greetin, clatters âTam Samsonâs dead!â Owre mony a weary hag he limpit, Anâ aye the tither shot he thumpit, Till coward Death behind him jumpit, Wiâ deadly feid; Now he proclaims wiâ tout oâ trumpet, âTam Samsonâs dead!â When at his heart he felt the dagger, He reelâd his wonted bottle-swagger, But yet he drew the mortal trigger, Wiâ weel-aimed heed; âLord, five!â he cryâd, anâ owre did staggerâ Tam Samsonâs dead! Ilk hoary hunter mournâd a brither; Ilk sportsman youth bemoanâd a father; Yon auld gray stane, amang the heather, Marks out his head; Whare Burns has wrote, in rhyming blether, âTam Samsonâs dead!â There, low he lies, in lasting rest; Perhaps upon his mouldâring breast Some spitefuâ muirfowl bigs her nest To hatch anâ breed: Alas! nae mair heâll them molest! Tam Samsonâs dead! When August winds the heather wave, And sportsmen wander by yon grave, Three volleys let his memory crave, Oâ pouther anâ lead, Till Echo answer frae her cave, âTam Samsonâs dead!â Heavân rest his saul whareâer he be! Is thâ wish oâ mony mae than me: He had twa fauts, or maybe three, Yet what remead? Ae social, honest man want we: Tam Samsonâs dead!





The Epitaph

Tam Samsonâs weel-worn clay here lies Ye canting zealots, spare him! If honest worth in Heaven rise, Yeâll mend or ye win near him.





Per Contra

Go, Fame, anâ canter like a filly Throâ aâ the streets anâ neuks oâ Killie;3 Tell evâry social honest billie To cease his grievinâ; For, yet unskaithed by Deathâs gleg gullie. Tam Samsonâs leevinâ!





Epistle To Major Logan

Hail, thairm-inspirinâ, rattlinâ Willie! Thoâ fortuneâs road be rough anâ hilly To every fiddling, rhyming billie, We never heed, But take it like the unbackâd filly, Proud oâ her speed. [Footnote 3: Kilmarnock.âR. B.] When, idly goavinâ, whiles we saunter, Yirr! fancy barks, awa we canter, Up hill, down brae, till some mischanter, Some black bog-hole, Arrests us; then the scathe anâ banter Weâre forced to thole. Hale be your heart! hale be your fiddle! Lang may your elbuck jink and diddle, To cheer you through the weary widdle Oâ this wild warlâ. Until you on a crummock driddle, A grey hairâd carl. Come wealth, come poortith, late or soon, Heaven send your heart-strings aye in tune, And screw your temper-pins aboon A fifth or mair The melancholious, lazy croon Oâ cankrie care. May still your life from day to day, Nae âlente largoâ in the play, But âallegretto forteâ gay, Harmonious flow, A sweeping, kindling, bauld strathspeyâ Encore! Bravo! A blessing on the cheery gang Wha dearly like a jig or sang, Anâ never think oâ right anâ wrang By square anâ rule, But, as the clegs oâ feeling stang, Are wise or fool. My hand-waled curse keep hard in chase The harpy, hoodock, purse-proud race, Wha count on poortith as disgrace; Their tuneless hearts, May fireside discords jar a base To aâ their parts. But come, your hand, my careless brither, Iâ thâ ither warlâ, if thereâs anither, Anâ that there is, Iâve little swither About the matter; We, cheek for chow, shall jog thegither, Iâse neâer bid better. Weâve faults and failingsâgranted clearly, Weâre frail backsliding mortals merely, Eveâs bonie squad, priests wyte them sheerly For our grand faâ; But still, but still, I like them dearlyâ God bless them aâ! Ochone for poor Castalian drinkers, When they faâ foul oâ earthly jinkers! The witching, cursâd, delicious blinkers Hae put me hyte, And gart me weet my waukrife winkers, Wiâ girninâspite. By by yon moon!âand thatâs high swearinâ Anâ every star within my hearin! Anâ by her een wha was a dear ane! Iâll neâer forget; I hope to gie the jads a clearin In fair play yet. My loss I mourn, but not repent it; Iâll seek my pursie whare I tint it; Ance to the Indies I were wonted, Some cantraip hour By some sweet elf Iâll yet be dinted; Then vive lâamour! Faites mes baissemains respectueuses, To sentimental sister Susie, And honest Lucky; no to roose you, Ye may be proud, That sic a couple Fate allows ye, To grace your blood. Nae mair at present can I measure, Anâ trowth my rhymin wareâs nae treasure; But when in Ayr, some half-hourâs leisure, Beât light, beât dark, Sir Bard will do himself the pleasure To call at Park. Robert Burns. Mossgiel, 30th October, 1786.





Fragment On Sensibility

Rusticityâs ungainly form May cloud the highest mind; But when the heart is nobly warm, The good excuse will find. Proprietyâs cold, cautious rules Warm fervour may oâerlook: But spare poor sensibility Thâ ungentle, harsh rebuke.





A Winter Night

Poor naked wretches, wheresoeâer you are, That bide the pelting of this pitiless storm! How shall your houseless heads, and unfed sides, Your loopâd and windowâd raggedness, defend you From seasons such as these?âShakespeare. When biting Boreas, fell and dour, Sharp shivers throâ the leafless bowâr; When Phoebus gies a short-livâd glowâr, Far south the lift, Dim-darkâning throâ the flaky showâr, Or whirling drift: Ae night the storm the steeples rocked, Poor Labour sweet in sleep was locked, While burns, wiâ snawy wreaths up-choked, Wild-eddying swirl; Or, throâ the mining outlet bocked, Down headlong hurl: Listâning the doors anâ winnocks rattle, I thought me on the ourie cattle, Or silly sheep, wha bide this brattle Oâ winter war, And throâ the drift, deep-lairing, sprattle Beneath a scar. Ilk happing bird,âwee, helpless thing! That, in the merry months oâ spring, Delighted me to hear thee sing, What comes oâ thee? Whare wilt thou cowâr thy chittering wing, Anâ close thy eâe? Evân you, on murdering errands toilâd, Lone from your savage homes exilâd, The blood-stainâd roost, and sheep-cote spoilâd My heart forgets, While pityless the tempest wild Sore on you beats! Now Phoebe in her midnight reign, Dark-muffâd, viewâd the dreary plain; Still crowding thoughts, a pensive train, Rose in my soul, When on my ear this plantive strain, Slow, solemn, stole:â âBlow, blow, ye winds, with heavier gust! And freeze, thou bitter-biting frost! Descend, ye chilly, smothering snows! Not all your rage, as now united, shows More hard unkindness unrelenting, Vengeful malice unrepenting. Than heaven-illuminâd Man on brother Man bestows! âSee stern Oppressionâs iron grip, Or mad Ambitionâs gory hand, Sending, like blood-hounds from the slip, Woe, Want, and Murder oâer a land! Evân in the peaceful rural vale, Truth, weeping, tells the mournful tale, How pamperâd Luxury, Flattâry by her side, The parasite empoisoning her ear, With all the servile wretches in the rear, Looks oâer proud Property, extended wide; And eyes the simple, rustic hind, Whose toil upholds the glittâring showâ A creature of another kind, Some coarser substance, unrefinâdâ Placâd for her lordly use thus far, thus vile, below! âWhere, where is Loveâs fond, tender throe, With lordly Honourâs lofty brow, The powârs you proudly own? Is there, beneath Loveâs noble name, Can harbour, dark, the selfish aim, To bless himself alone? Mark maiden-innocence a prey To love-pretending snares: This boasted Honour turns away, Shunning soft Pityâs rising sway, Regardless of the tears and unavailing prayârs! Perhaps this hour, in Miseryâs squalid nest, She strains your infant to her joyless breast, And with a motherâs fears shrinks at the rocking blast! âOh ye! who, sunk in beds of down, Feel not a want but what yourselves create, Think, for a moment, on his wretched fate, Whom friends and fortune quite disown! Ill-satisfyâd keen natureâs clamorous call, Stretchâd on his straw, he lays himself to sleep; While through the ragged roof and chinky wall, Chill, oâer his slumbers, piles the drifty heap! Think on the dungeonâs grim confine, Where Guilt and poor Misfortune pine! Guilt, erring man, relenting view, But shall thy legal rage pursue The wretch, already crushed low By cruel Fortuneâs undeserved blow? Afflictionâs sons are brothers in distress; A brother to relieve, how exquisite the bliss!â I heard nae mair, for Chanticleer Shook off the pouthery snaw, And hailâd the morning with a cheer, A cottage-rousing craw. But deep this truth impressâd my mindâ Throâ all His works abroad, The heart benevolent and kind The most resembles God.





SongâYon Wild Mossy Mountains

Yon wild mossy mountains sae lofty and wide, That nurse in their bosom the youth oâ the Clyde, Where the grouse lead their coveys throâ the heather to feed, And the shepherd tends his flock as he pipes on his reed. Not Gowrieâs rich valley, nor Forthâs sunny shores, To me hae the charms oâyon wild, mossy moors; For there, by a lanely, sequestered stream, Besides a sweet lassie, my thought and my dream. Amang thae wild mountains shall still be my path, Ilk stream foaming down its ain green, narrow strath; For there, wiâ my lassie, the day lang I rove, While oâer us unheeded flie the swift hours oâlove. She is not the fairest, althoâ she is fair; Oâ nice education but smaâ is her share; Her parentage humble as humble can be; But I loâe the dear lassie because she loâes me. To Beauty what man but maun yield him a prize, In her armour of glances, and blushes, and sighs? And when wit and refinement hae polishâd her darts, They dazzle our een, as they flie to our hearts. But kindness, sweet kindness, in the fond-sparkling eâe, Has lustre outshining the diamond to me; And the heart beating love as Iâm claspâd in her arms, O, these are my lassieâs all-conquering charms!





Address To Edinburgh

Edina! Scotiaâs darling seat! All hail thy palaces and towârs, Where once, beneath a Monarchâs feet, Sat Legislationâs sovâreign powârs: From marking wildly scattâred flowârs, As on the banks of Ayr I strayâd, And singing, lone, the lingering hours, I shelter in they honourâd shade. Here Wealth still swells the golden tide, As busy Trade his labours plies; There Architectureâs noble pride Bids elegance and splendour rise: Here Justice, from her native skies, High wields her balance and her rod; There Learning, with his eagle eyes, Seeks Science in her coy abode. Thy sons, Edina, social, kind, With open arms the stranger hail; Their views enlargâd, their liberal mind, Above the narrow, rural vale: Attentive still to Sorrowâs wail, Or modest Meritâs silent claim; And never may their sources fail! And never Envy blot their name! Thy daughters bright thy walks adorn, Gay as the gilded summer sky, Sweet as the dewy, milk-white thorn, Dear as the rapturâd thrill of joy! Fair Burnet strikes thâ adoring eye, Heavenâs beauties on my fancy shine; I see the Sire of Love on high, And own His work indeed divine! There, watching high the least alarms, Thy rough, rude fortress gleams afar; Like some bold veteran, grey in arms, And markâd with many a seamy scar: The pondârous wall and massy bar, Grimârising oâer the rugged rock, Have oft withstood assailing war, And oft repellâd thâ invaderâs shock. With awe-struck thought, and pitying tears, I view that noble, stately Dome, Where Scotiaâs kings of other years, Famâd heroes! had their royal home: Alas, how changâd the times to come! Their royal name low in the dust! Their hapless race wild-wandâring roam! Thoâ rigid Law cries out âtwas just! Wild beats my heart to trace your steps, Whose ancestors, in days of yore, Throâ hostile ranks and ruinâd gaps Old Scotiaâs bloody lion bore: Evân I who sing in rustic lore, Haply my sires have left their shed, And facâd grim Dangerâs loudest roar, Bold-following where your fathers led! Edina! Scotiaâs darling seat! All hail thy palaces and towârs; Where once, beneath a Monarchâs feet, Sat Legislationâs sovereign powârs: From marking wildly-scattâred flowârs, As on the banks of Ayr I strayâd, And singing, lone, the lingâring hours, I shelter in thy honourâd shade.





Address To A Haggis

Fair faâ your honest, sonsie face, Great chieftain oâ the pudding-race! Aboon them aâ yet tak your place, Painch, tripe, or thairm: Weel are ye wordy oâa grace As langâs my arm. The groaning trencher there ye fill, Your hurdies like a distant hill, Your pin was help to mend a mill In time oâneed, While throâ your pores the dews distil Like amber bead. His knife see rustic Labour dight, Anâ cut you up wiâ ready sleight, Trenching your gushing entrails bright, Like ony ditch; And then, O what a glorious sight, Warm-reekinâ, rich! Then, horn for horn, they stretch anâ strive: Deil tak the hindmost! on they drive, Till aâ their weel-swallâd kytes belyve Are bent like drums; Then auld Guidman, maist like to rive, Bethankit! hums. Is there that owre his French ragout Or olio that wad staw a sow, Or fricassee wad make her spew Wiâ perfect sconner, Looks down wiâ sneering, scornfuâ view On sic a dinner? Poor devil! see him owre his trash, As feckles as witherâd rash, His spindle shank, a guid whip-lash; His nieve a nit; Throâ blody flood or field to dash, O how unfit! But mark the Rustic, haggis-fed, The trembling earth resounds his tread. Clap in his walie nieve a blade, Heâll mak it whissle; Anâ legs anâ arms, anâ hands will sned, Like taps oâ trissle. Ye Powârs, wha mak mankind your care, And dish them out their bill oâ fare, Auld Scotland wants nae skinking ware That jaups in luggies; But, if ye wish her gratefuâ prayer Gie her a haggis!





1787





To Miss Logan, With Beattieâs Poems, For A New-Yearâs Gift, Jan. 1, 1787.

Again the silent wheels of time Their annual round have driven, And you, thoâ scarce in maiden prime, Are so much nearer Heaven. No gifts have I from Indian coasts The infant year to hail; I send you more than India boasts, In Edwinâs simple tale. Our sex with guile, and faithless love, Is chargâd, perhaps too true; But may, dear maid, each lover prove An Edwin still to you.





Mr. William SmellieâA Sketch

Rattlinâ, Roarinâ Willie1 As I cam by Crochallan, I cannilie keekit ben; Rattlinâ, roarinâ Willie Was sittin at yon boord-enâ; Sittin at yon boord-en, And amang gude companie; Rattlinâ, roarinâ Willie, Youâre welcome hame to me!

Inscription For The Headstone Of Fergusson The Poet1

No sculptured marble here, nor pompous lay, âNo storied urn nor animated bust;â This simple stone directs pale Scotiaâs way, To pour her sorrows oâer the Poetâs dust.
Additional Stanzas She mourns, sweet tuneful youth, thy hapless fate; Thoâ all the powers of song thy fancy fired, Yet Luxury and Wealth lay by in state, And, thankless, starvâd what they so much admired. This tribute, with a tear, now gives A brother Bardâhe can no more bestow: But dear to fame thy Song immortal lives, A nobler monument than Art can shew.
Inscribed Under Fergussonâs Portrait Curse on ungrateful man, that can be pleased, And yet can starve the author of the pleasure. O thou, my elder brother in misfortune, By far my elder brother in the Muses, With tears I pity thy unhappy fate! Why is the Bard unpitied by the world, Yet has so keen a relish of its pleasures?
