Epistle To Mrs. Scott

Gudewife of WauchopeâHouse, Roxburghshire.
Gudewife, I Mind it weel in early date, When I was bardless, young, and blate, Anâ first could thresh the barn, Or haud a yokinâ at the pleugh; An, thoâ forfoughten sair eneugh, Yet unco proud to learn: When first amang the yellow corn A man I reckonâd was, Anâ wiâ the lave ilk merry morn Could rank my rig and lass, Still shearing, and clearing The tither stooked raw, Wiâ claivers, anâ haivers, Wearing the day awa. Eâen then, a wish, (I mind its powâr), A wish that to my latest hour Shall strongly heave my breast, That I for poor auld Scotlandâs sake Some usefuâ plan or book could make, Or sing a sang at least. The rough burr-thistle, spreading wide Amang the bearded bear, I turnâd the weeder-clips aside, Anâ sparâd the symbol dear: No nation, no station, My envy eâer could raise; A Scot still, but blot still, I knew nae higher praise. But still the elements oâ sang, In formless jumble, right anâ wrang, Wild floated in my brain; âTill on that harâst I said before, May partner in the merry core, She rousâd the forming strain; I see her yet, the sonsie quean, That lighted up my jingle, Her witching smile, her pawky een That gart my heart-strings tingle; I fired, inspired, At every kindling keek, But bashing, and dashing, I feared aye to speak. Health to the sex! ilk guid chiel says: Wiâ merry dance in winter days, Anâ we to share in common; The gust oâ joy, the balm of woe, The saul oâ life, the heaven below, Is rapture-giving woman. Ye surly sumphs, who hate the name, Be mindfuâ oâ your mither; She, honest woman, may think shame That yeâre connected with her: Yeâre wae men, yeâre nae men That slight the lovely dears; To shame ye, disclaim ye, Ilk honest birkie swears. For you, no bred to barn and byre, Wha sweetly tune the Scottish lyre, Thanks to you for your line: The marled plaid ye kindly spare, By me should gratefully be ware; âTwad please me to the nine. Iâd be mair vauntie oâ my hap, Douce hingin owre my curple, Than ony ermine ever lap, Or proud imperial purple. Farewell then, lang hale then, Anâ plenty be your fa; May losses and crosses Neâer at your hallan caâ! R. Burns March, 1787

Prologue

Spoken by Mr. Woods on his benefit-night, Monday, 16th April, 1787. When, by a generous Publicâs kind acclaim, That dearest meed is grantedâhonest fame; Waen here your favour is the actorâs lot, Nor even the man in private life forgot; What breast so dead to heavenly Virtueâs glow, But heaves impassionâd with the grateful throe? Poor is the task to please a barbârous throng, It needs no Siddonsâ powers in Southernâs song; But here an ancient nation, famâd afar, For genius, learning high, as great in war. Hail, Caledonia, name for ever dear! Before whose sons Iâm honourâd to appear? [Footnote 1: The Nobleman is James, Fourteenth Earl of Glencairn.] Where every science, every nobler art, That can inform the mind or mend the heart, Is known; as grateful nations oft have found, Far as the rude barbarian marks the bound. Philosophy, no idle pedant dream, Here holds her search by heaven-taught Reasonâs beam; Here History paints with elegance and force The tide of Empireâs fluctuating course; Here Douglas forms wild Shakespeare into plan, And Harley rouses all the God in man. When well-formâd taste and sparkling wit unite With manly lore, or female beauty bright, (Beauty, where faultless symmetry and grace Can only charm us in the second place), Witness my heart, how oft with panting fear, As on this night, Iâve met these judges here! But still the hope Experience taught to live, Equal to judgeâyouâre candid to forgive. No hundredâheaded riot here we meet, With decency and law beneath his feet; Nor Insolence assumes fair Freedomâs name: Like Caledonians, you applaud or blame. O Thou, dread Power! whose empire-giving hand Has oft been stretchâd to shield the honourâd land! Strong may she glow with all her ancient fire; May every son be worthy of his sire; Firm may she rise, with generous disdain At Tyrannyâs, or direr Pleasureâs chain; Still Self-dependent in her native shore, Bold may she brave grim Dangerâs loudest roar, Till Fate the curtain drop on worlds to be no more.

Auld Phoebus himself, as he peepâd oâer the hill, In spite at her plumage he tried his skill; He levellâd his rays where she baskâd on the braeâ His rays were outshone, and but markâd where she lay. Address To Wm. Tytler, Esq., Of Woodhouselee

With an Impression of the Authorâs Portrait. Revered defender of beauteous Stuart, Of Stuart, a name once respected; A name, which to love was the mark of a true heart, But now âtis despisâd and neglected. Thoâ something like moisture conglobes in my eye, Let no one misdeem me disloyal; A poor friendless wandârer may well claim a sigh, Still more if that wandârer were royal. My fathers that name have reverâd on a throne: My fathers have fallen to right it; Those fathers would spurn their degenerate son, That name should he scoffingly slight it. Still in prayers for King George I most heartily join, The Queen, and the rest of the gentry: Be they wise, be they foolish, is nothing of mine; Their titleâs avowâd by my country. But why of that epocha make such a fuss, That gave us thâ Electoral stem? If bringing them over was lucky for us, Iâm sure âtwas as lucky for them. But, loyalty, truce! weâre on dangerous ground; Who knows how the fashions may alter? The doctrine, to-day, that is loyalty sound, To-morrow may bring us a halter! I send you a trifle, a head of a bard, A trifle scarce worthy your care; But accept it, good Sir, as a mark of regard, Sincere as a saintâs dying prayer. Now lifeâs chilly evening dim shades on your eye, And ushers the long dreary night: But you, like the star that athwart gilds the sky, Your course to the latest is bright.

Elegy On âStellaâ

The following poem is the work of some hapless son of the Muses who deserved a better fate. There is a great deal of âThe voice of Conaâ in his solitary, mournful notes; and had the sentiments been clothed in Shenstoneâs language, they would have been no discredit even to that elegant poet.âR.B.

Strait is the spot and green the sod From whence my sorrows flow; And soundly sleeps the ever dear Inhabitant below. Pardon my transport, gentle shade, While oâer the turf I bow; Thy earthy house is circumscribâd, And solitary now. Not one poor stone to tell thy name, Or make thy virtues known: But what avails to meâto thee, The sculpture of a stone? Iâll sit me down upon this turf, And wipe the rising tear: The chill blast passes swiftly by, And flits around thy bier. Dark is the dwelling of the Dead, And sad their house of rest: Low lies the head, by Deathâs cold arms In awful fold embracâd. I saw the grim Avenger stand Incessant by thy side; Unseen by thee, his deadly breath Thy lingering frame destroyâd. Pale grew the roses on thy cheek, And witherâd was thy bloom, Till the slow poison brought thy youth Untimely to the tomb. Thus wasted are the ranks of menâ Youth, Health, and Beauty fall; The ruthless ruin spreads around, And overwhelms us all. Behold where, round thy narrow house, The graves unnumberâd lie; The multitude that sleep below Existed but to die. Some, with the tottering steps of Age, Trod down the darksome way; And some, in youthâs lamented prime, Like thee were torn away: Yet these, however hard their fate, Their native earth receives; Amid their weeping friends they died, And fill their fathersâ graves. From thy lovâd friends, when first thy heart Was taught by Heavân to glow, Far, far removâd, the ruthless stroke Surprisâd and laid thee low. At the last limits of our isle, Washâd by the western wave, Touchâd by thy face, a thoughtful bard Sits lonely by thy grave. Pensive he eyes, before him spread The deep, outstretchâd and vast; His mourning notes are borne away Along the rapid blast. And while, amid the silent Dead Thy hapless fate he mourns, His own long sorrows freshly bleed, And all his grief returns: Like thee, cut off in early youth, And flower of beautyâs pride, His friend, his first and only joy, His much lovâd Stella, died. Him, too, the stern impulse of Fate Resistless bears along; And the same rapid tide shall whelm The Poet and the Song. The tear of pity which he sheds, He asks not to receive; Let but his poor remains be laid Obscurely in the grave. His grief-worn heart, with truest joy, Shall meet he welcome shock: His airy harp shall lie unstrung, And silent on the rock. O, my dear maid, my Stella, when Shall this sick period close, And lead the solitary bard To his belovâd repose?

Elegy On The Death Of Sir James Hunter Blair

The lamp of day, withâill presaging glare, Dim, cloudy, sank beneath the western wave; Thâ inconstant blast howlâd throâ the darkâning air, And hollow whistled in the rocky cave. Lone as I wanderâd by each cliff and dell, Once the lovâd haunts of Scotiaâs royal train;1 Or musâd where limpid streams, once hallowâd well,2 Or mouldâring ruins mark the sacred fane.3 Thâ increasing blast roarâd round the beetling rocks, The clouds swift-wingâd flew oâer the starry sky, The groaning trees untimely shed their locks, And shooting meteors caught the startled eye. [Footnote 1: The Kingâs Park at Holyrood House.âR. B.] [Footnote 2: St. Anthonyâs well.âR. B.] [Footnote 3: St. Anthonyâs Chapel.âR. B.] The paly moon rose in the livid east. And âmong the cliffs disclosâd a stately form In weeds of woe, that frantic beat her breast, And mixâd her wailings with the raving storm Wild to my heart the filial pulses glow, âTwas Caledoniaâs trophied shield I viewâd: Her form majestic droopâd in pensive woe, The lightning of her eye in tears imbued. Reversâd that spear, redoubtable in war, Reclined that banner, erst in fields unfurlâd, That like a deathful meteor gleamâd afar, And bravâd the mighty monarchs of the world. âMy patriot son fills an untimely grave!â With accents wild and lifted arms she cried; âLow lies the hand oft was stretchâd to save, Low lies the heart that swellâd with honest pride. âA weeping country joins a widowâs tear; The helpless poor mix with the orphanâs cry; The drooping arts surround their patronâs bier; And grateful science heaves the heartfelt sigh! âI saw my sons resume their ancient fire; I saw fair Freedomâs blossoms richly blow: But ah! how hope is born but to expire! Relentless fate has laid their guardian low. âMy patriot falls: but shall he lie unsung, While empty greatness saves a worthless name? No; every muse shall join her tuneful tongue, And future ages hear his growing fame. âAnd I will join a motherâs tender cares, Throâ future times to make his virtues last; That distant years may boast of other Blairs!ââ She said, and vanishâd with the sweeping blast.

The Humble Petition Of Bruar Water

To the noble Duke of Athole. My lord, I know your noble ear Woe neâer assails in vain; Emboldenâd thus, I beg youâll hear Your humble slave complain, How saucy Phoebusâ scorching beams, In flaming summer-pride, Dry-withering, waste my foamy streams, And drink my crystal tide.1 The lightly-jumping, glowrinâ trouts, That throâ my waters play, If, in their random, wanton spouts, They near the margin stray; [Footnote 1: Bruar Falls, in Athole, are exceedingly picturesque and beautiful; but their effect is much impaired by the want of trees and shrubs.âR.B.] If, hapless chance! they linger lang, Iâm scorching up so shallow, Theyâre left the whitening stanes amang, In gasping death to wallow. Last day I grat wiâ spite and teen, As poet Burns came by. That, to a bard, I should be seen Wiâ half my channel dry; A panegyric rhyme, I ween, Evân as I was, he shorâd me; But had I in my glory been, He, kneeling, wad adorâd me. Here, foaming down the skelvy rocks, In twisting strength I rin; There, high my boiling torrent smokes, Wild-roaring oâer a linn: Enjoying each large spring and well, As Nature gave them me, I am, althoâ I sayât myselâ, Worth gaun a mile to see. Would then my noble master please To grant my highest wishes, Heâll shade my banks wiâ towâring trees, And bonie spreading bushes. Delighted doubly then, my lord, Youâll wander on my banks, And listen mony a grateful bird Return you tuneful thanks. The sober lavârock, warbling wild, Shall to the skies aspire; The gowdspink, Musicâs gayest child, Shall sweetly join the choir; The blackbird strong, the lintwhite clear, The mavis mild and mellow; The robin pensive Autumn cheer, In all her locks of yellow. This, too, a covert shall ensure, To shield them from the storm; And coward maukin sleep secure, Low in her grassy form: Here shall the shepherd make his seat, To weave his crown of flowârs; Or find a sheltâring, safe retreat, From prone-descending showârs. And here, by sweet, endearing stealth, Shall meet the loving pair, Despising worlds, with all their wealth, As empty idle care; The flowârs shall vie in all their charms, The hour of heavân to grace; And birks extend their fragrant arms To screen the dear embrace. Here haply too, at vernal dawn, Some musing bard may stray, And eye the smoking, dewy lawn, And misty mountain grey; Or, by the reaperâs nightly beam, Mild-chequering throâ the trees, Rave to my darkly dashing stream, Hoarse-swelling on the breeze. Let lofty firs, and ashes cool, My lowly banks oâerspread, And view, deep-bending in the pool, Their shadowâs watâry bed: Let fragrant birks, in woodbines drest, My craggy cliffs adorn; And, for the little songsterâs nest, The close embowâring thorn. So may old Scotiaâs darling hope, Your little angel band Spring, like their fathers, up to prop Their honourâd native land! So may, throâ Albionâs farthest ken, To social-flowing glasses, The grace beââAtholeâs honest men, And Atholeâs bonie lasses!





Lines On The Fall Of Fyers Near Loch-Ness.

Written with a Pencil on the Spot.
Among the heathy hills and ragged woods The roaring Fyers pours his mossy floods; Till full he dashes on the rocky mounds, Where, throâ a shapeless breach, his stream resounds. As high in air the bursting torrents flow, As deep recoiling surges foam below, Prone down the rock the whitening sheet descends, And viewles Echoâs ear, astonished, rends. Dim-seen, through rising mists and ceaseless showârs, The hoary cavern, wide surrounding lours: Still throâ the gap the struggling river toils, And still, below, the horrid cauldron boilsâ

Castle Gordon

Streams that glide in orient plains, Never bound by Winterâs chains; Glowing here on golden sands, There immixâd with foulest stains From Tyrannyâs empurpled hands; These, their richly gleaming waves, I leave to tyrants and their slaves; Give me the stream that sweetly laves The banks by Castle Gordon. Spicy forests, ever gray, Shading from the burning ray Hapless wretches sold to toil; Or the ruthless nativeâs way, Bent on slaughter, blood, and spoil: Woods that ever verdant wave, I leave the tyrant and the slave; Give me the groves that lofty brave The storms by Castle Gordon. Wildly here, without control, Nature reigns and rules the whole; In that sober pensive mood, Dearest to the feeling soul, She plants the forest, pours the flood: Lifeâs poor day Iâll musing rave And find at night a sheltering cave, Where waters flow and wild woods wave, By bonie Castle Gordon.

On Scaring Some Water-Fowl In Loch-Turit

A wild scene among the Hills of Oughtertyre.

âThis was the production of a solitary forenoonâs walk from Oughtertyre House. I lived there, the guest of Sir William Murray, for two or three weeks, and was much flattered by my hospitable reception. What a pity that the mere emotions of gratitude are so impotent in this world. âTis lucky that, as we are told, they will be of some avail in the world to come.â âR.B., Glenriddell MSS.

Why, ye tenants of the lake, For me your watâry haunt forsake? Tell me, fellow-creatures, why At my presence thus you fly? Why disturb your social joys, Parent, filial, kindred ties?â Common friend to you and me, yatureâs gifts to all are free: Peaceful keep your dimpling wave, Busy feed, or wanton lave; Or, beneath the sheltering rock, Bide the surging billowâs shock. Conscious, blushing for our race, Soon, too soon, your fears I trace, Man, your proud, usurping foe, Would be lord of all below: Plumes himself in freedomâs pride, Tyrant stern to all beside. The eagle, from the cliffy brow, Marking you his prey below, In his breast no pity dwells, Strong necessity compels: But Man, to whom alone is givân A ray direct from pitying Heavân, Glories in his heart humaneâ And creatures for his pleasure slain! In these savage, liquid plains, Only known to wandâring swains, Where the mossy rivâlet strays, Far from human haunts and ways; All on Nature you depend, And lifeâs poor season peaceful spend. Or, if manâs superior might Dare invade your native right, On the lofty ether borne, Man with all his powârs you scorn; Swiftly seek, on clanging wings, Other lakes and other springs; And the foe you cannot brave, Scorn at least to be his slave.

A Rose-Bud By My Early Walk

A Rose-bud by my early walk, Adown a corn-enclosed bawk, Sae gently bent its thorny stalk, All on a dewy morning. Ere twice the shades oâ dawn are fled, In aâ its crimson glory spread, And drooping rich the dewy head, It scents the early morning. Within the bush her covert nest A little linnet fondly prest; The dew sat chilly on her breast, Sae early in the morning. She soon shall see her tender brood, The pride, the pleasure oâ the wood, Amang the fresh green leaves bedewâd, Awake the early morning. So thou, dear bird, young Jeany fair, On trembling string or vocal air, Shall sweetly pay the tender care That tents thy early morning. So thou, sweet Rose-bud, young and gay, Shalt beauteous blaze upon the day, And bless the parentâs evening ray That watchâd thy early morning.

Birthday Ode For 31st December, 17871

Afar the illustrious Exile roams, Whom kingdoms on this day should hail; An inmate in the casual shed, On transient pityâs bounty fed, Haunted by busy memoryâs bitter tale! Beasts of the forest have their savage homes, But He, who should imperial purple wear, Owns not the lap of earth where rests his royal head! His wretched refuge, dark despair, While ravening wrongs and woes pursue, And distant far the faithful few Who would his sorrows share. False flatterer, Hope, away! Nor think to lure us as in days of yore: We solemnize this sorrowing natal day, To prove our loyal truthâwe can no more, And owning Heavenâs mysterious sway, Submissive, low adore. Ye honored, mighty Dead, Who nobly perished in the glorious cause, Your King, your Country, and her laws, [Footnote 1: The last birthday of Prince Charles Edward.] From great Dundee, who smiling Victory led, And fell a Martyr in her arms, (What breast of northern ice but warms!) To bold Balmerinoâs undying name, Whose soul of fire, lighted at Heavenâs high flame, Deserves the proudest wreath departed heroes claim: Nor unrevenged your fate shall lie, It only lags, the fatal hour, Your blood shall, with incessant cry, Awake at last, thâ unsparing Power; As from the cliff, with thundering course, The snowy ruin smokes along With doubling speed and gathering force, Till deep it, crushing, whelms the cottage in the vale; So Vengeanceâ arm, ensanguinâd, strong, Shall with resistless might assail, Usurping Brunswickâs pride shall lay, And Stewartâs wrongs and yours, with tenfold weight repay. Perdition, baleful child of night! Rise and revenge the injured right Of Stewartâs royal race: Lead on the unmuzzled hounds of hell, Till all the frighted echoes tell The blood-notes of the chase! Full on the quarry point their view, Full on the base usurping crew, The tools of faction, and the nationâs curse! Hark how the cry grows on the wind; They leave the lagging gale behind, Their savage fury, pitiless, they pour; With murdering eyes already they devour; See Brunswick spent, a wretched prey, His life one poor despairing day, Where each avenging hour still ushers in a worse! Such havock, howling all abroad, Their utter ruin bring, The base apostates to their God, Or rebels to their King.





On The Death Of Robert Dundas, Esq., Of Arniston,

Late Lord President of the Court of Session.
Lone on the bleaky hills the straying flocks Shun the fierce storms among the sheltering rocks; Down from the rivulets, red with dashing rains, The gathering floods burst oâer the distant plains; Beneath the blast the leafless forests groan; The hollow caves return a hollow moan. Ye hills, ye plains, ye forests, and ye caves, Ye howling winds, and wintry swelling waves! Unheard, unseen, by human ear or eye, Sad to your sympathetic glooms I fly; Where, to the whistling blast and waterâs roar, Pale Scotiaâs recent wound I may deplore. O heavy loss, thy country ill could bear! A loss these evil days can neâer repair! Justice, the high vicegerent of her God, Her doubtful balance eyed, and swayâd her rod: Hearing the tidings of the fatal blow, She sank, abandonâd to the wildest woe. Wrongs, injuries, from many a darksome den, Now, gay in hope, explore the paths of men: See from his cavern grim Oppression rise, And throw on Poverty his cruel eyes; Keen on the helpless victim see him fly, And stifle, dark, the feebly-bursting cry: Mark Ruffian Violence, distained with crimes, Rousing elate in these degenerate times, View unsuspecting Innocence a prey, As guileful Fraud points out the erring way: While subtle Litigationâs pliant tongue The life-blood equal sucks of Right and Wrong: Hark, injurâd Want recounts thâ unlistenâd tale, And much-wrongâd Misâry pours the unpitied wail! Ye dark waste hills, ye brown unsightly plains, Congenial scenes, ye soothe my mournful strains: Ye tempests, rage! ye turbid torrents, roll! Ye suit the joyless tenor of my soul. Lifeâs social haunts and pleasures I resign; Be nameless wilds and lonely wanderings mine, To mourn the woes my country must endureâ That would degenerate ages cannot cure.





Sylvander To Clarinda1

Extempore Reply to Verses addressed to the Author by a Lady, under the signature of âClarindaâ and entitled, On Burns saying he âhad nothing else to do.â

When dear Clarinda, matchless fair, First struck Sylvanderâs rapturâd view, He gazâd, he listened to despair, Alas! âtwas all he dared to do. Love, from Clarindaâs heavenly eyes, Transfixed his bosom throâ and throâ; But still in Friendshipsâ guarded guise, For more the demon fearâd to do. That heart, already more than lost, The imp beleaguerâd all perdue; For frowning Honour kept his postâ To meet that frown, he shrunk to do. His pangs the Bard refused to own, Thoâ half he wishâd Clarinda knew; But Anguish wrung the unweeting groanâ Who blames what frantic Pain must do? That heart, where motley follies blend, Was sternly still to Honour true: To prove Clarindaâs fondest friend, Was what a lover sure might do. [Footnote 1: A grass-widow, Mrs. MâLehose.] The Muse his ready quill employed, No nearer bliss he could pursue; That bliss Clarinda cold denyâdâ âSend word by Charles how you do!â The chill behest disarmâd his muse, Till passion all impatient grew: He wrote, and hinted for excuse, âTwas, âcause âheâd nothing else to do.â But by those hopes I have above! And by those faults I dearly rue! The deed, the boldest mark of love, For thee that deed I dare uo do! O could the Fates but name the price Would bless me with your charms and you! With frantic joy Iâd pay it thrice, If human art and power could do! Then take, Clarinda, friendshipâs hand, (Friendship, at least, I may avow;) And lay no more your chill command,â Iâll write whatever Iâve to do.





1788





Love In The Guise Of Friendship

Your friendship much can make me blest, O why that bliss destroy! Why urge the only, one request You know I will deny! Your thought, if Love must harbour there, Conceal it in that thought; Nor cause me from my bosom tear The very friend I sought.





Go On, Sweet Bird, And Sooth My Care

For thee is laughing Nature gay, For thee she pours the vernal day; For me in vain is Nature drest, While Joyâs a stranger to my breast.





Clarinda, Mistress Of My Soul

Clarinda, mistres of my soul, The measurâd time is run! The wretch beneath the dreary pole So marks his latest sun. To what dark cave of frozen night Shall poor Sylvander hie; Deprivâd of thee, his life and light, The sun of all his joy? We partâbut by these precious drops, That fill thy lovely eyes, No other light shall guide my steps, Till thy bright beams arise! She, the fair sun of all her sex, Has blest my glorious day; And shall a glimmering planet fix My worship to its ray?

I composed these verses on Miss Isabella MâLeod of Raza, alluding to her feelings on the death of her sister, and the still more melancholy death of her sisterâs husband, the late Earl of Loudoun, who shot himself out of sheer heart-break at some mortifications he suffered, owing to the deranged state of his finances.âR.B., 1971.

Raving winds around her blowing, Yellow leaves the woodlands strowing, By a river hoarsely roaring, Isabella strayâd deploringâ âFarewell, hours that late did measure Sunshine days of joy and pleasure; Hail, thou gloomy night of sorrow, Cheerless night that knows no morrow! âOâer the past too fondly wandering, On the hopeless future pondering; Chilly grief my life-blood freezes, Fell despair my fancy seizes. âLife, thou soul of every blessing, Load to misery most distressing, Gladly how would I resign thee, And to dark oblivion join thee!â





Up In The Morning Early

Cauld blaws the wind frae east to west, The drift is driving sairly; Sae loud and shillâs I hear the blastâ Iâm sure itâs winter fairly. Chorus.âUp in the morningâs no for me, Up in the morning early; When aâ the hills are covered wiâ snaw, Iâm sure itâs winter fairly. The birds sit chittering in the thorn, Aâ day they fare but sparely; And langâs the night frae eâen to mornâ Iâm sure itâs winter fairly. Up in the morningâs, &c. How Long And Dreary Is The Night How long and dreary is the night, When I am frae my dearie! I sleepless lie frae eâen to morn, Thoâ I were neâer so weary: I sleepless lie frae eâen to morn, Thoâ I were neâer sae weary! When I think on the happy days I spent wiâ you my dearie: And now what lands between us lie, How can I be but eerie! And now what lands between us lie, How can I be but eerie! How slow ye move, ye heavy hours, As ye were wae and weary! It wasna sae ye glinted by, When I was wiâ my dearie! It wasna sae ye glinted by, When I was wiâ my dearie!





Hey, The Dusty Miller

Hey, the dusty Miller, And his dusty coat, He will win a shilling, Or he spend a groat: Dusty was the coat, Dusty was the colour, Dusty was the kiss That I gat frae the Miller. Hey, the dusty Miller, And his dusty sack; Leeze me on the calling Fills the dusty peck: Fills the dusty peck, Brings the dusty siller; I wad gie my coatie For the dusty Miller.





Duncan Davison

There was a lass, they caâd her Meg, And she held oâer the moors to spin; There was a lad that followâd her, They caâd him Duncan Davison. The moor was dreigh, and Meg was skeigh, Her favour Duncan could na win; For wiâ the rock she wad him knock, And aye she shook the temper-pin. As oâer the moor they lightly foor, A burn was clear, a glen was green, Upon the banks they easâd their shanks, And aye she set the wheel between: But Duncan swoor a haly aith, That Meg should be a bride the morn; Then Meg took up her spinning-graith, And flang them aâ out oâer the burn. We will big a wee, wee house, And we will live like king and queen; Sae blythe and merryâs we will be, When ye set by the wheel at eâen. A man may drink, and no be drunk; A man may fight, and no be slain; A man may kiss a bonie lass, And aye be welcome back again!

Her daddie forbad, her minnie forbad Forbidden she wadna be: She wadna trowât the browst she brewâd, Wad taste sae bitterlie. Chorus.âThe lang lad they caâJumpin John Beguilâd the bonie lassie, The lang lad they caâJumpin John Beguilâd the bonie lassie. A cow and a cauf, a yowe and a hauf, And thretty gude shillinâs and three; A vera gude tocher, a cotter-manâs dochter, The lass wiâ the bonie black eâe. The lang lad, &c.





Talk Of Him Thatâs Far Awa

Musing on the roaring ocean, Which divides my love and me; Wearying heavân in warm devotion, For his weal whereâer he be. Hope and Fearâs alternate billow Yielding late to Natureâs law, Whispering spirits round my pillow, Talk of him thatâs far awa. Ye whom sorrow never wounded, Ye who never shed a tear, Careâuntroubled, joyâsurrounded, Gaudy day to you is dear. Gentle night, do thou befriend me, Downy sleep, the curtain draw; Spirits kind, again attend me, Talk of him thatâs far awa!





To Daunton Me

The blude-red rose at Yule may blaw, The simmer lilies bloom in snaw, The frost may freeze the deepest sea; But an auld man shall never daunton me. Refrain.âTo daunton me, to daunton me, And auld man shall never daunton me. To daunton me, and me sae young, Wiâ his fause heart and flattâring tongue, That is the thing you shall never see, For an auld man shall never daunton me. To daunton me, &c. For aâ his meal and aâ his maut, For aâ his fresh beef and his saut, For aâ his gold and white monie, And auld men shall never daunton me. To daunton me, &c. His gear may buy him kye and yowes, His gear may buy him glens and knowes; But me he shall not buy nor fee, For an auld man shall never daunton me. To daunton me, &c. He hirples twa fauld as he dow, Wiâ his teethless gab and his auld beld pow, And the rain rains down frae his red blearâd eâe; That auld man shall never daunton me. To daunton me, &c.





The Winter It Is Past

The winter it is past, and the summer comes at last And the small birds, they sing on evâry tree; Now evâry thing is glad, while I am very sad, Since my true love is parted from me. The rose upon the breer, by the waters running clear, May have charms for the linnet or the bee; Their little loves are blest, and their little hearts at rest, But my true love is parted from me.





The Bonie Lad Thatâs Far Awa

O how can I be blythe and glad, Or how can I gang brisk and braw, When the bonie lad that I loâe best Is oâer the hills and far awa! Itâs no the frosty winter wind, Itâs no the driving drift and snaw; But aye the tear comes in my eâe, To think on him thatâs far awa. My father pat me frae his door, My friends they hae disownâd me aâ; But I hae ane will tak my part, The bonie lad thatâs far awa. A pair oâ glooves he bought to me, And silken snoods he gae me twa; And I will wear them for his sake, The bonie lad thatâs far awa. O weary Winter soon will pass, And Spring will cleed the birken shaw; And my young babie will be born, And heâll be hame thatâs far awa.





Verses To Clarinda

Sent with a Pair of Wine-Glasses.
Fair Empress of the Poetâs soul, And Queen of Poetesses; Clarinda, take this little boon, This humble pair of glasses: And fill them up with generous juice, As generous as your mind; And pledge them to the generous toast, âThe whole of human kind!â âTo those who love us!â second fill; But not to those whom we love; Lest we love those who love not usâ A thirdââTo thee and me, Love!â





The Chevalierâs Lament

AirââCaptain OâKean.â The small birds rejoice in the green leaves returning, The murmuring streamlet winds clear throâ the vale; The primroses blow in the dews of the morning, And wild scatterâd cowslips bedeck the green dale: But what can give pleasure, or what can seem fair, When the lingering moments are numbered by care? No birds sweetly singing, nor flowârs gaily springing, Can soothe the sad bosom of joyless despair. The deed that I dared, could it merit their malice? A king and a father to place on his throne! His right are these hills, and his right are these valleys, Where the wild beasts find shelter, thoâ I can find none! But âtis not my suffârings, thus wretched, forlorn, My brave gallant friends, âtis your ruin I mourn; Your faith proved so loyal in hot bloody trial,â Alas! I can make it no better return!





Epistle To Hugh Parker

In this strange land, this uncouth clime, A land unknown to prose or rhyme; Where words neâer crossât the Museâs heckles, Nor limpit in poetic shackles: A land that Prose did never view it, Except when drunk he stacherât throâ it; Here, ambushâd by the chimla cheek, Hid in an atmosphere of reek, I hear a wheel thrum iâ the neuk, I hear itâfor in vain I leuk. The red peat gleams, a fiery kernel, Enhusked by a fog infernal: Here, for my wonted rhyming raptures, I sit and count my sins by chapters; For life and spunk like ither Christians, Iâm dwindled down to mere existence, Wiâ nae converse but Gallowaâ bodies, Wiâ nae kennâd face but Jenny Geddes, Jenny, my Pegasean pride! Dowie she saunters down Nithside, And aye a westlin leuk she throws, While tears hap oâer her auld brown nose! Was it for this, wiâ cannie care, Thou bure the Bard through many a shire? At howes, or hillocks never stumbled, And late or early never grumbled?â O had I power like inclination, Iâd heeze thee up a constellation, To canter with the Sagitarre, Or loup the ecliptic like a bar; Or turn the pole like any arrow; Or, when auld Phoebus bids good-morrow, Down the zodiac urge the race, And cast dirt on his godshipâs face; For I could lay my bread and kail Heâd neâer cast saut upoâ thy tail.â Wiâ aâ this care and aâ this grief, And smaâ, smaâ prospect of relief, And nought but peat reek iâ my head, How can I write what ye can read?â Tarbolton, twenty-fourth oâ June, Yeâll find me in a better tune; But till we meet and weet our whistle, Tak this excuse for nae epistle. Robert Burns.





Of Aâ The Airts The Wind Can Blaw1

TuneââMiss Admiral Gordonâs Strathspey.â
Of aâ the airts the wind can blaw, I dearly like the west, For there the bonie lassie lives, The lassie I loâe best: [Footnote 1: Written during a separation from Mrs. Burns in their honeymoon. Burns was preparing a home at Ellisland; Mrs. Burns was at Mossgiel.âLang.] Thereâs wild-woods grow, and rivers row, And mony a hill between: But day and night my fancysâ flight Is ever wiâ my Jean. I see her in the dewy flowers, I see her sweet and fair: I hear her in the tunefuâ birds, I hear her charm the air: Thereâs not a bonie flower that springs, By fountain, shaw, or green; Thereâs not a bonie bird that sings, But minds me oâ my Jean.





SongâI Hae a Wife Oâ My Ain

I Hae a wife of my ain, Iâll partake wiâ naebody; Iâll take Cuckold frae nane, Iâll gie Cuckold to naebody. I hae a penny to spend, Thereâthanks to naebody! I hae naething to lend, Iâll borrow frae naebody. I am naebodyâs lord, Iâll be slave to naebody; I hae a gude braid sword, Iâll tak dunts frae naebody. Iâll be merry and free, Iâll be sad for naebody; Naebody cares for me, I care for naebody.





Lines Written In Friarsâ-Carse Hermitage

Glenriddel Hermitage, June 28th, 1788. Thou whom chance may hither lead, Be thou clad in russet weed, Be thou deckt in silken stole, Grave these maxims on thy soul. Life is but a day at most, Sprung from night, in darkness lost: Hope not sunshine every hour, Fear not clouds will always lour. Happiness is but a name, Make content and ease thy aim, Ambition is a meteor-gleam; Fame, an idle restless dream; Peace, the tendârest flowâr of spring; Pleasures, insects on the wing; Those that sip the dew aloneâ Make the butterflies thy own; Those that would the bloom devourâ Crush the locusts, save the flower. For the future be preparâd, Guard wherever thou canâst guard; But thy utmost duly done, Welcome what thou canâst not shun. Follies past, give thou to air, Make their consequence thy care: Keep the name of Man in mind, And dishonour not thy kind. Reverence with lowly heart Him, whose wondrous work thou art; Keep His Goodness still in view, Thy trust, and thy example, too. Stranger, go! Heaven be thy guide! Quod the Beadsman of Nidside.





To Alex. Cunningham, ESQ., Writer

Ellisland, Nithsdale, July 27th, 1788. My godlike friendânay, do not stare, You think the phrase is odd-like; But God is love, the saints declare, Then surely thou art god-like. And is thy ardour still the same? And kindled still at Anna? Others may boast a partial flame, But thou art a volcano! Evân Wedlock asks not love beyond Deathâs tie-dissolving portal; But thou, omnipotently fond, Mayâst promise love immortal! Thy wounds such healing powers defy, Such symptoms dire attend them, That last great antihectic tryâ Marriage perhaps may mend them. Sweet Anna has an airâa grace, Divine, magnetic, touching: She talks, she charmsâbut who can trace The process of bewitching?





Song.âAnna, Thy Charms

Anna, thy charms my bosom fire, And waste my soul with care; But ah! how bootless to admire, When fated to despair! Yet in thy presence, lovely Fair, To hope may be forgiven; For sure âtwere impious to despair So much in sight of heaven.





The Fete Champetre

TuneââKilliecrankie.â
O Wha will to Saint Stephenâs House, To do our errands there, man? O wha will to Saint Stephenâs House Oâ thâ merry lads of Ayr, man? Or will we send a man oâ law? Or will we send a sodger? Or him wha led oâer Scotland aâ The meikle Ursa-Major?1 Come, will ye court a noble lord, Or buy a score oâlairds, man? For worth and honour pawn their word, Their vote shall be Glencairdâs,2 man. Ane gies them coin, ane gies them wine, Anither gies them clatter: Annbank,3 wha guessed the ladiesâ taste, He gies a Fete Champetre. When Love and Beauty heard the news, The gay green woods amang, man; Where, gathering flowers, and busking bowers, They heard the blackbirdâs sang, man: A vow, they sealed it with a kiss, Sir Politics to fetter; As theirâs alone, the patent bliss, To hold a Fete Champetre. Then mounted Mirth, on gleesome wing Oâer hill and dale she flew, man; Ilk wimpling burn, ilk crystal spring, Ilk glen and shaw she knew, man: She summonâd every social sprite, That sports by wood or water, On thâ bonie banks of Ayr to meet, And keep this Fete Champetre. Cauld Boreas, wiâ his boisterous crew, Were bound to stakes like kye, man, And Cynthiaâs car, oâ silver fuâ, Clamb up the starry sky, man: Reflected beams dwell in the streams, Or down the current shatter; The western breeze steals throâthe trees, To view this Fete Champetre. [Footnote 1: James Boswell, the biographer of Dr. Johnson.] [Footnote 2: Sir John Whitefoord, then residing at Cloncaird or âGlencaird.â] [Footnote 3: William Cunninghame, Esq., of Annbank and Enterkin.] How many a robe sae gaily floats! What sparkling jewels glance, man! To Harmonyâs enchanting notes, As moves the mazy dance, man. The echoing wood, the winding flood, Like Paradise did glitter, When angels met, at Adamâs yett, To hold their Fete Champetre. When Politics came there, to mix And make his ether-stane, man! He circled round the magic ground, But entrance found he nane, man: He blushâd for shame, he quat his name, Forswore it, every letter, Wiâ humble prayer to join and share This festive Fete Champetre.





Epistle To Robert Graham, Esq., Of Fintry

Requesting a Favour When Nature her great master-piece designâd, And framâd her last, best work, the human mind, Her eye intent on all the mazy plan, She formâd of various parts the various Man. Then first she calls the useful many forth; Plain plodding Industry, and sober Worth: Thence peasants, farmers, native sons of earth, And merchandiseâ whole genus take their birth: Each prudent cit a warm existence finds, And all mechanicsâ many-apronâd kinds. Some other rarer sorts are wanted yet, The lead and buoy are needful to the net: The caput mortuum of grnss desires Makes a material for mere knights and squires; The martial phosphorus is taught to flow, She kneads the lumpish philosophic dough, Then marks thâ unyielding mass with grave designs, Law, physic, politics, and deep divines; Last, she sublimes thâ Aurora of the poles, The flashing elements of female souls. The orderâd system fair before her stood, Nature, well pleasâd, pronouncâd it very good; But ere she gave creating labour oâer, Half-jest, she tried one curious labour more. Some spumy, fiery, ignis fatuus matter, Such as the slightest breath of air might scatter; With arch-alacrity and conscious glee, (Nature may have her whim as well as we, Her Hogarth-art perhaps she meant to show it), She forms the thing and christens itâa Poet: Creature, thoâ oft the prey of care and sorrow, When blest to-day, unmindful of to-morrow; A being formâd tâ amuse his graver friends, Admirâd and praisâdâand there the homage ends; A mortal quite unfit for Fortuneâs strife, Yet oft the sport of all the ills of life; Prone to enjoy each pleasure riches give, Yet haply wanting wherewithal to live; Longing to wipe each tear, to heal each groan, Yet frequent all unheeded in his own. But honest Nature is not quite a Turk, She laughâd at first, then felt for her poor work: Pitying the propless climber of mankind, She cast about a standard tree to find; And, to support his helpless woodbine state, Attachâd him to the generous, truly great: A title, and the only one I claim, To lay strong hold for help on bounteous Graham. Pity the tuneful Musesâ hapless train, Weak, timid landsmen on lifeâs stormy main! Their hearts no selfish stern absorbent stuff, That never givesâthoâ humbly takes enough; The little fate allows, they share as soon, Unlike sage proverbâd Wisdomâs hard-wrung boon: The world were blest did bliss on them depend, Ah, that âthe friendly eâer should want a friend!â Let Prudence number oâer each sturdy son, Who life and wisdom at one race begun, Who feel by reason and who give by rule, (Instinctâs a brute, and sentiment a fool!) Who make poor âwill doâ wait upon âI shouldââ We own theyâre prudent, but who feels theyâre good? Ye wise ones hence! ye hurt the social eye! Godâs image rudely etchâd on base alloy! But come ye who the godlike pleasure know, Heavenâs attribute distinguishedâto bestow! Whose arms of love would grasp the human race: Come thou who givâst with all a courtierâs grace; Friend of my life, true patron of my rhymes! Prop of my dearest hopes for future times. Why shrinks my soul half blushing, half afraid, Backward, abashâd to ask thy friendly aid? I know my need, I know thy giving hand, I crave thy friendship at thy kind command; But there are such who court the tuneful Nineâ Heavens! should the branded character be mine! Whose verse in manhoodâs pride sublimely flows, Yet vilest reptiles in their begging prose. Mark, how their lofty independent spirit Soars on the spurning wing of injured merit! Seek not the proofs in private life to find Pity the best of words should be but wind! So, to heavenâs gates the larkâs shrill song ascends, But grovelling on the earth the carol ends. In all the clamârous cry of starving want, They dun Benevolence with shameless front; Oblige them, patronise their tinsel laysâ They persecute you all your future days! Ere my poor soul such deep damnation stain, My horny fist assume the plough again, The pie-bald jacket let me patch once more, On eighteenpence a week Iâve livâd before. Thoâ, thanks to Heaven, I dare even that last shift, I trust, meantime, my boon is in thy gift: That, placâd by thee upon the wishâd-for height, Where, man and nature fairer in her sight, My Muse may imp her wing for some sublimer flight.





Song.âThe Day Returns

TuneââSeventh of November.â
The day returns, my bosom burns, The blissful day we twa did meet: Thoâ winter wild in tempest toilâd, Neâer summer-sun was half sae sweet. Than aâ the pride that loads the tide, And crosses oâer the sultry line; Than kingly robes, than crowns and globes, Heavân gave me moreâit made thee mine! While day and night can bring delight, Or Nature aught of pleasure give; While joys above my mind can move, For thee, and thee alone, I live. When that grim foe of life below Comes in between to make us part, The iron hand that breaks our band, It breaks my blissâit breaks my heart!





Song.âO, Were I On Parnassus Hill

TuneââMy love is lost to me.â
O, were I on Parnassus hill, Or had oâ Helicon my fill, That I might catch poetic skill, To sing how dear I love thee! But Nith maun be my Museâs well, My Muse maun be thy bonie selâ, On Corsincon Iâll glowr and spell, And write how dear I love thee. Then come, sweet Muse, inspire my lay! For aâ the lee-lang simmerâs day I couldna sing, I couldna say, How much, how dear, I love thee, I see thee dancing oâer the green, Thy waist sae jimp, thy limbs sae clean, Thy tempting lips, thy roguish eenâ By Heaven and Earth I love thee! By night, by day, a-field, at hame, The thoughts oâ thee my breast inflame: And aye I muse and sing thy nameâ I only live to love thee. Thoâ I were doomâd to wander on, Beyond the sea, beyond the sun, Till my last weary sand was run; Till thenâand then I love thee!





A Motherâs Lament

For the Death of Her Son. Fate gave the word, the arrow sped, And piercâd my darlingâs heart; And with him all the joys are fled Life can to me impart. By cruel hands the sapling drops, In dust dishonourâd laid; So fell the pride of all my hopes, My ageâs future shade. The mother-linnet in the brake Bewails her ravishâd young; So I, for my lost darlingâs sake, Lament the live-day long. Death, oft Iâve feared thy fatal blow. Now, fond, I bare my breast; O, do thou kindly lay me low With him I love, at rest!





The Fall Of The Leaf

The lazy mist hangs from the brow of the hill, Concealing the course of the dark-winding rill; How languid the scenes, late so sprightly, appear! As Autumn to Winter resigns the pale year. The forests are leafless, the meadows are brown, And all the gay foppery of summer is flown: Apart let me wander, apart let me muse, How quick Time is flying, how keen Fate pursues! How long I have livâdâbut how much livâd in vain, How little of lifeâs scanty span may remain, What aspects old Time in his progress has worn, What ties cruel Fate, in my bosom has torn. How foolish, or worse, till our summit is gainâd! And downward, how weakenâd, how darkenâd, how painâd! Life is not worth having with all it can giveâ For something beyond it poor man sure must live.





I Reign In Jeanieâs Bosom

Louis, what reck I by thee, Or Geordie on his ocean? Dyvor, beggar louns to me, I reign in Jeanieâs bosom! Let her crown my love her law, And in her breast enthrone me, Kings and nationsâswith awaâ! Reif randies, I disown ye! It Is Na, Jean, Thy Bonie Face It is na, Jean, thy bonie face, Nor shape that I admire; Althoâ thy beauty and thy grace Might weel awauk desire. Something, in ilka part oâ thee, To praise, to love, I find, But dear as is thy form to me, Still dearer is thy mind. Nae mair ungenerous wish I hae, Nor stronger in my breast, Than, if I canna make thee sae, At least to see thee blest. Content am I, if heaven shall give But happiness, to thee; And as wiâ thee Iâd wish to live, For thee Iâd bear to die.

Should auld acquaintance be forgot, And never brought to mind? Should auld acquaintance be forgot, And auld lang syne! Chorus.âFor auld lang syne, my dear, For auld lang syne. Weâll tak a cup oâ kindness yet, For auld lang syne. And surely yeâll be your pint stowp! And surely Iâll be mine! And weâll tak a cup oâkindness yet, For auld lang syne. For auld, &c. We twa hae run about the braes, And pouâd the gowans fine; But weâve wanderâd mony a weary fit, Sinâ auld lang syne. For auld, &c. We twa hae paidlâd in the burn, Frae morning sun till dine; But seas between us braid hae roarâd Sinâ auld lang syne. For auld, &c. And thereâs a hand, my trusty fere! And gieâs a hand oâ thine! And weâll tak a right gude-willie waught, For auld lang syne. For auld, &c.





My Bonie Mary

Go, fetch to me a pint oâ wine, And fill it in a silver tassie; That I may drink before I go, A service to my bonie lassie. The boat rocks at the pier oâ Leith; Fuâ loud the wind blaws frae the Ferry; The ship rides by the Berwick-law, And I maun leave my bonie Mary. The trumpets sound, the banners fly, The glittering spears are ranked ready: The shouts oâ war are heard afar, The battle closes deep and bloody; Itâs not the roar oâ sea or shore, Wad mak me langer wish to tarry! Nor shouts oâ war thatâs heard afarâ Itâs leaving thee, my bonie Mary!





The Parting Kiss

Humid seal of soft affections, Tenderest pledge of future bliss, Dearest tie of young connections, Loveâs first snowdrop, virgin kiss! Speaking silence, dumb confession, Passionâs birth, and infantâs play, Dove-like fondness, chaste concession, Glowing dawn of future day! Sorrowing joy, Adieuâs last action, (Lingering lips must now disjoin), What words can ever speak affection So thrilling and sincere as thine!





Written In Friarâs-Carse Hermitage

On Nithside Thou whom chance may hither lead, Be thou clad in russet weed, Be thou deckt in silken stole, Grave these counsels on thy soul. Life is but a day at most, Sprung from night,âin darkness lost; Hope not sunshine evâry hour, Fear not clouds will always lour. As Youth and Love with sprightly dance, Beneath thy morning star advance, Pleasure with her siren air May delude the thoughtless pair; Let Prudence bless Enjoymentâs cup, Then rapturâd sip, and sip it up. As thy day grows warm and high, Lifeâs meridian flaming nigh, Dost thou spurn the humble vale? Lifeâs proud summits wouldst thou scale? Check thy climbing step, elate, Evils lurk in felon wait: Dangers, eagle-pinioned, bold, Soar around each cliffy hold! While cheerful Peace, with linnet song, Chants the lowly dells among. As the shades of evâning close, Beckâning thee to long repose; As life itself becomes disease, Seek the chimney-nook of ease; There ruminate with sober thought, On all thouâst seen, and heard, and wrought, And teach the sportive younkers round, Saws of experience, sage and sound: Say, manâs true, genuine estimate, The grand criterion of his fate, Is not,âArth thou high or low? Did thy fortune ebb or flow? Did many talents gild thy span? Or frugal Nature grudge thee one? Tell them, and press it on their mind, As thou thyself must shortly find, The smile or frown of awful Heavân, To virtue or to Vice is givân, Say, to be just, and kind, and wiseâ There solid self-enjoyment lies; That foolish, selfish, faithless ways Lead to be wretched, vile, and base. Thus resignâd and quiet, creep To the bed of lasting sleep,â Sleep, whence thou shalt neâer awake, Night, where dawn shall never break, Till future life, future no more, To light and joy the good restore, To light and joy unknown before. Stranger, go! Heavân be thy guide! Quod the Beadsman of Nithside.





The Poetâs Progress

A Poem In Embryo Thou, Nature, partial Nature, I arraign; Of thy caprice maternal I complain. The peopled fold thy kindly care have found, The horned bull, tremendous, spurns the ground; The lordly lion has enough and more, The forest trembles at his very roar; Thou givâst the ass his hide, the snail his shell, The puny wasp, victorious, guards his cell. Thy minions, kings defend, controul devour, In all thâ omnipotence of rule and power: Foxes and statesmen subtle wiles ensure; The cit and polecat stink, and are secure: Toads with their poison, doctors with their drug, The priest and hedgehog, in their robes, are snug: Eâen silly women have defensive arts, Their eyes, their tonguesâand nameless other parts. But O thou cruel stepmother and hard, To thy poor fenceless, naked child, the Bard! A thing unteachable in worldly skill, And half an idiot too, more helpless still: No heels to bear him from the opâning dun, No claws to dig, his hated sight to shun: No horns, but those by luckless Hymen worn, And those, alas! not Amaltheaâs horn: No nerves olfactâry, true to Mammonâs foot, Or grunting, grub sagacious, evilâs root: The silly sheep that wanders wild astray, Is not more friendless, is not more a prey; Vampyreâbooksellers drain him to the heart, And viperâcritics cureless venom dart. Critics! appllâd I venture on the name, Those cut-throat bandits in the paths of fame, Bloody dissectors, worse than ten Monroes, He hacks to teach, they mangle to expose: By blockheadâs daring into madness stung, His heart by wanton, causeless malice wrung, His well-won waysâthan life itself more dearâ By miscreants torn who neâer one sprig must wear; Foilâd, bleeding, torturâd in thâ unequal strife, The hapless Poet flounces on through life, Till, fled each hope that once his bosom fired, And fled each Muse that glorious once inspirâd, Low-sunk in squalid, unprotected age, Dead even resentment for his injurâd page, He heeds no more the ruthless criticsâ rage. So by some hedge the generous steed deceasâd, For half-starvâd, snarling curs a dainty feast; By toil and famine worn to skin and bone, Lies, senseless of each tugging bitchâs son. A little upright, pert, tart, tripping wight, And still his precious self his dear delight; Who loves his own smart shadow in the streets, Better than eâer the fairest she he meets; Much specious lore, but little understood, (Veneering oft outshines the solid wood), His solid sense, by inches you must tell, But mete his cunning by the Scottish ell! A man of fashion too, he made his tour, Learnâd âvive la bagatelle et vive lâamour;â So travellâd monkeys their grimace improve, Polish their grinânay, sigh for ladiesâ love! His meddling vanity, a busy fiend, Still making work his selfish craft must mend. * * * Crochallan came, The old cockâd hat, the brown surtoutâthe same; His grisly beard just bristling in its mightâ âTwas four long nights and days from shaving-night; His uncombâd, hoary locks, wild-staring, thatchâd A head, for thought profound and clear, unmatchâd; Yet, thoâ his caustic wit was biting-rude, His heart was warm, benevolent and good. O Dulness, portion of the truly blest! Calm, shelterâd haven of eternal rest! Thy sons neâer madden in the fierce extremes Of Fortuneâs polar frost, or torrid beams; If mantling high she fills the golden cup, With sober, selfish ease they sip it up; Conscious the bounteous meed they well deserve, They only wonder âsome folksâ do not starve! The grave, sage hern thus easy picks his frog, And thinks the mallard a sad worthless dog. When disappointment snaps the thread of Hope, When, throâ disastrous night, they darkling grope, With deaf endurance sluggishly they bear, And just conclude that âfools are Fortuneâs care:â So, heavy, passive to the tempestâs shocks, Strong on the sign-post stands the stupid ox. Not so the idle Musesâ mad-cap train, Not such the workings of their moon-struck brain; In equanimity they never dwell, By turns in soaring heaven, or vaulted hell!





Elegy On The Year 1788

For lords or kings I dinna mourn, Eâen let them dieâfor that theyâre born: But oh! prodigious to reflecâ! A Towmont, sirs, is gane to wreck! O Eighty-eight, in thy smaâ space, What dire events hae taken place! Of what enjoyments thou hast reft us! In what a pickle thou has left us! The Spanish empireâs tint a head, And my auld teethless, Bawtieâs dead: The tulyieâs teugh âtween Pitt and Fox, And âtween our Maggieâs twa wee cocks; The tane is game, a bluidy devil, But to the hen-birds unco civil; The titherâs something dour oâ treadin, But better stuff neâer clawâd a middin. Ye ministers, come mount the poupit, Anâ cry till ye be hearse anâ roupit, For Eighty-eight, he wished you weel, Anâ gied ye aâ baith gear anâ meal; Eâen monc a plack, and mony a peck, Ye ken yoursels, for little feck! Ye bonie lasses, dight your eâen, For some oâ you hae tint a frienâ; In Eighty-eight, ye ken, was taen, What yeâll neâer hae to gie again. Observe the very nowt anâ sheep, How dowff anâ daviely they creep; Nay, even the yirth itselâ does cry, For Eânburgh wells are grutten dry. O Eighty-nine, thouâs but a bairn, Anâ no owre auld, I hope, to learn! Thou beardless boy, I pray tak care, Thou now hast got thy Daddyâs chair; Nae handcuffâd, mizlâd, hap-shacklâd Regent, But, like himsel, a full free agent, Be sure ye follow out the plan Nae waur than he did, honest man! As muckle better as you can. January, 1, 1789.





The Henpecked Husband

Cursâd be the man, the poorest wretch in life, The crouching vassal to a tyrant wife! Who has no will but by her high permission, Who has not sixpence but in her possession; Who must to he, his dear friendâs secrets tell, Who dreads a curtain lecture worse than hell. Were such the wife had fallen to my part, Iâd break her spirit or Iâd break her heart; Iâd charm her with the magic of a switch, Iâd kiss her maids, and kick the perverse bitch.

His face with smile eternal drest, Just like the Landlordâs to his Guestâs, High as they hang with creaking din, To index out the Country Inn. He looked just as your sign-post Lions do, With aspect fierce, and quite as harmless too. A head, pure, sinless quite of brain and soul, The very image of a barberâs Poll; It shews a human face, and wears a wig, And looks, when well preservâd, amazing big.

Ode, Sacred To The Memory Of Mrs. Oswald Of Auchencruive

Dweller in yon dungeon dark, Hangman of creation! mark, Who in widow-weeds appears, Laden with unhonourâd years, Noosing with care a bursting purse, Baited with many a deadly curse?
Strophe View the witherâd Beldamâs face; Can thy keen inspection trace Aught of Humanityâs sweet, melting grace? Note that eye, âtis rheum oâerflows; Pityâs flood there never rose, See these hands neâer stretched to save, Hands that took, but never gave: Keeper of Mammonâs iron chest, Lo, there she goes, unpitied and unblest, She goes, but not to realms of everlasting rest!
Antistrophe Plunderer of Armies! lift thine eyes, (A while forbear, ye torturing fiends;) Seest thou whose step, unwilling, hither bends? No fallen angel, hurlâd from upper skies; âTis thy trusty quondam Mate, Doomâd to share thy fiery fate; She, tardy, hell-ward plies.
Epode And are they of no more avail, Ten thousand glittering pounds a-year? In other worlds can Mammon fail, Omnipotent as he is here! O, bitter mockery of the pompous bier, While down the wretched Vital Part is driven! The cave-lodged Beggar,with a conscience clear, Expires in rags, unknown, and goes to Heaven.





Pegasus At Wanlockhead

With Pegasus upon a day, Apollo, weary flying, Through frosty hills the journey lay, On foot the way was plying. Poor slipshod giddy Pegasus Was but a sorry walker; To Vulcan then Apollo goes, To get a frosty caulker. Obliging Vulcan fell to work, Threw by his coat and bonnet, And did Solâs business in a crack; Sol paid him with a sonnet. Ye Vulcanâs sons of Wanlockhead, Pity my sad disaster; My Pegasus is poorly shod, Iâll pay you like my master.





Sappho RedivivusâA Fragment

By all I lovâd, neglected and forgot, No friendly face eâer lights my squalid cot; Shunnâd, hated, wrongâd, unpitied, unredrest, The mockâd quotation of the scornerâs jest! Evân the poor support of my wretched life, Snatched by the violence of legal strife. Oft grateful for my very daily bread To those my familyâs once large bounty fed; A welcome inmate at their homely fare, My griefs, my woes, my sighs, my tears they share: (Their vulgar souls unlike the souls refinâd, The fashioned marble of the polished mind). In vain would Prudence, with decorous sneer, Point out a censuring world, and bid me fear; Above the world, on wings of Love, I riseâ I know its worst, and can that worst despise; Let Prudenceâ direst bodements on me fall, M[ontgomer]y, rich reward, oâerpays them all! Mild zephyrs waft thee to lifeâs farthest shore, Nor think of me and my distress more,â Falsehood accurst! No! still I beg a place, Still near thy heart some little, little trace: For that dear trace the world I would resign: O let me live, and die, and think it mine! âI burn, I burn, as when throâ ripenâd corn By driving winds the crackling flames are borne;â Now raving-wild, I curse that fatal night, Then bless the hour that charmâd my guilty sight: In vain the laws their feeble force oppose, Chainâd at Loveâs feet, they groan, his vanquishâd foes. In vain Religion meets my shrinking eye, I dare not combat, but I turn and fly: Conscience in vain upbraids thâ unhallowâd fire, Love grasps her scorpionsâstifled they expire! Reason drops headlong from his sacred throne, Your dear idea reigns, and reigns alone; Each thought intoxicated homage yields, And riots wanton in forbidden fields. By all on high adoring mortals know! By all the conscious villain fears below! By your dear self!âthe last great oath I swear, Not life, nor soul, were ever half so dear!

Sheâs fair and fause that causes my smart, I loâed her meikle and lang; Sheâs broken her vow, sheâs broken my heart, And I may eâen gae hang. Impromptu Lines To Captain Riddell

On Returning a Newspaper. Your News and Review, sir. Iâve read through and through, sir, With little admiring or blaming; The Papers are barren Of home-news or foreign, No murders or rapes worth the naming. Our friends, the Reviewers, Those chippers and hewers, Are judges of mortar and stone, sir; But of meet or unmeet, In a fabric complete, Iâll boldly pronounce they are none, sir; My goose-quill too rude is To tell all your goodness Bestowâd on your servant, the Poet; Would to God I had one Like a beam of the sun, And then all the world, sir, should know it!

CaledoniaâA Ballad

TuneââCaledonian Huntsâ Delightâ of Mr. Gow.
There was once a day, but old Time wasythen young, That brave Caledonia, the chief of her line, From some of your northern deities sprung, (Who knows not that brave Caledoniaâs divine?) From Tweed to the Orcades was her domain, To hunt, or to pasture, or do what she would: Her heavânly relations there fixed her reign, And pledgâd her their godheads to warrant it good. A lambkin in peace, but a lion in war, The pride of her kindred, the heroine grew: Her grandsire, old Odin, triumphantly swore,â âWhoeâer shall provoke thee, thâ encounter shall rue!â With tillage or pasture at times she would sport, To feed her fair flocks by her green rustling corn; But chiefly the woods were her favârite resort, Her darling amusement, the hounds and the horn. Long quiet she reigned; till thitherward steers A flight of bold eagles from Adriaâs strand: Repeated, successive, for many long years, They darkenâd the air, and they plunderâd the land: Their pounces were murder, and terror their cry, Theyâd conquerâd and ruinâd a world beside; She took to her hills, and her arrows let fly, The daring invaders they fled or they died. The Cameleon-Savage disturbâd her repose, With tumult, disquiet, rebellion, and strife; Provokâd beyond bearing, at last she arose, And robbâd him at once of his hopes and his life: The Anglian lion, the terror of France, Oft prowling, ensanguinâd the Tweedâs silver flood; But, taught by the bright Caledonian lance, He learned to fear in his own native wood. The fell Harpy-raven took wing from the north, The scourge of the seas, and the dread of the shore; The wild Scandinavian boar issued forth To wanton in carnage and wallow in gore: Oâer countries and kingdoms their fury prevailâd, No arts could appease them, no arms could repel; But brave Caledonia in vain they assailâd, As Largs well can witness, and Loncartie tell. Thus bold, independent, unconquerâd, and free, Her bright course of glory for ever shall run: For brave Caledonia immortal must be; Iâll prove it from Euclid as clear as the sun: Rectangleâtriangle, the figure weâll chuse: The upright is Chance, and old Time is the base; But brave Caledoniaâs the hypothenuse; Then, ergo, sheâll match them, and match them always.





To Miss Cruickshank

A very Young Lady

Written on the Blank Leaf of a Book, presented to her by the Author.

Beauteous Rosebud, young and gay, Blooming in thy early May, Never mayâst thou, lovely flower, Chilly shrink in sleety shower! Never Boreasâ hoary path, Never Eurusâ poisânous breath, Never baleful stellar lights, Taint thee with untimely blights! Never, never reptile thief Riot on thy virgin leaf! Nor even Sol too fiercely view Thy bosom blushing still with dew! Mayâst thou long, sweet crimson gem, Richly deck thy native stem; Till some evâning, sober, calm, Dropping dews, and breathing balm, While all around the woodland rings, And evâry bird thy requiem sings; Thou, amid the dirgeful sound, Shed thy dying honours round, And resign to parent Earth The loveliest form she eâer gave birth.





Beware Oâ Bonie Ann

Ye gallants bright, I rede you right, Beware oâ bonie Ann; Her comely face sae fuâ oâ grace, Your heart she will trepan: Her een sae bright, like stars by night, Her skin sae like the swan; Sae jimply lacâd her genty waist, That sweetly ye might span. Youth, Grace, and Love attendant move, And pleasure leads the van: In aâ their charms, and conquering arms, They wait on bonie Ann. The captive bands may chain the hands, But love enslaves the man: Ye gallants braw, I rede you aâ, Beware oâ bonie Ann!





Ode On The Departed Regency Bill

(March, 1789) Daughter of Chaosâ doting years, Nurse of ten thousand hopes and fears, Whether thy airy, insubstantial shade (The rights of sepulture now duly paid) Spread abroad its hideous form On the roaring civil storm, Deafening din and warring rage Factions wild with factions wage; Or under-ground, deep-sunk, profound, Among the demons of the earth, With groans that make the mountains shake, Thou mourn thy ill-starrâd, blighted birth; Or in the uncreated Void, Where seeds of future being fight, With lessenâd step thou wander wide, To greet thy MotherâAncient Night. And as each jarring, monster-mass is past, Fond recollect what once thou wast: In manner due, beneath this sacred oak, Hear, Spirit, hear! thy presence I invoke! By a Monarchâs heaven-struck fate, By a disunited State, By a generous Princeâs wrongs. By a Senateâs strife of tongues, By a Premierâs sullen pride, Louring on the changing tide; By dread Thurlowâs powers to awe Rhetoric, blasphemy and law; By the turbulent oceanâ A Nationâs commotion, By the harlot-caresses Of borough addresses, By days few and evil, (Thy portion, poor devil!) By Power, Wealth, and Show, (The Gods by men adored,) By nameless Poverty, (Their hell abhorred,) By all they hope, by all they fear, Hear! and appear! Stare not on me, thou ghastly Power! Nor, grim with chained defiance, lour: No Babel-structure would I build Where, order exilâd from his native sway, Confusion may the regent-sceptre wield, While all would rule and none obey: Go, to the world of man relate The story of thy sad, eventful fate; And call presumptuous Hope to hear And bid him check his blind career; And tell the sore-prest sons of Care, Never, never to despair! Paint Charlesâ speed on wings of fire, The object of his fond desire, Beyond his boldest hopes, at hand: Paint all the triumph of the Portland Band; Hark how they lift the joy-elated voice! And who are these that equally rejoice? Jews, Gentiles, what a motley crew! The iron tears their flinty cheeks bedew; See how unfurled the parchment ensigns fly, And Principal and Interest all the cry! And how their numârous creditors rejoice; But just as hopes to warm enjoyment rise, Cry Convalescence! and the vision flies. Then next pourtray a darkâning twilight gloom, Eclipsing sad a gay, rejoicing morn, While proud Ambition to thâ untimely tomb By gnashing, grim, despairing fiends is borne: Paint ruin, in the shape of high D[undas] Gaping with giddy terror oâer the brow; In vain he struggles, the fates behind him press, And clamârous hell yawns for her prey below: How fallen That, whose pride late scaled the skies! And This, like Lucifer, no more to rise! Again pronounce the powerful word; See Day, triumphant from the night, restored. Then know this truth, ye Sons of Men! (Thus ends thy moral tale,) Your darkest terrors may be vain, Your brightest hopes may fail.





Epistle To James Tennant Of Glenconner

Auld comrade dear, and brither sinner, Howâs aâ the folk about Glenconner? How do you this blae eastlin wind, Thatâs like to blaw a body blind? For me, my faculties are frozen, My dearest member nearly dozenâd. Iâve sent you here, by Johnie Simson, Twa sage philosophers to glimpse on; Smith, wiâ his sympathetic feeling, Anâ Reid, to common sense appealing. Philosophers have fought and wrangled, Anâ meikle Greek anâ Latin mangled, Till wiâ their logic-jargon tirâd, And in the depth of science mirâd, To common sense they now appeal, What wives and wabsters see and feel. But, hark ye, friend! I charge you strictly, Peruse them, anâ return them quickly: For now Iâm grown sae cursed douce I pray and ponder butt the house; My shins, my lane, I there sit roastinâ, Perusing Bunyan, Brown, anâ Boston, Till by anâ by, if I haud on, Iâll grunt a real gospel-groan: Already I begin to try it, To cast my eâen up like a pyet, When by the gun she tumbles oâer Fluttâring anâ gasping in her gore: Sae shortly you shall see me bright, A burning anâ a shining light. My heart-warm love to guid auld Glen, The ace anâ wale of honest men: When bending down wiâ auld grey hairs Beneath the load of years and cares, May He who made him still support him, Anâ views beyond the grave comfort him; His worthy famâly far and near, God bless them aâ wiâ grace and gear! My auld schoolfellow, Preacher Willie, The manly tar, my mason-billie, And Auchenbay, I wish him joy, If heâs a parent, lass or boy, May he be dad, and Meg the mither, Just five-and-forty years thegither! And no forgetting wabster Charlie, Iâm tauld he offers very fairly. Anâ Lord, remember singing Sannock, Wiâ hale breeks, saxpence, anâ a bannock! And next, my auld acquaintance, Nancy, Since she is fitted to her fancy, Anâ her kind stars hae airted till her gA guid chiel wiâ a pickle siller. My kindest, best respects, I senâ it, To cousin Kate, anâ sister Janet: Tell them, frae me, wiâ chiels be cautious, For, faith, theyâll aiblins finâ them fashious; To grant a heart is fairly civil, But to grant a maidenheadâs the devil. Anâ lastly, Jamie, for yoursel, May guardian angels tak a spell, Anâ steer you seven miles south oâ hell: But first, before you see heavenâs glory, May ye get mony a merry story, Mony a laugh, and mony a drink, And aye eneugh oâ needfuâ clink. Now fare ye weel, anâ joy be wiâ you: For my sake, this I beg it oâ you, Assist poor Simson aâ ye can, Yeâll fin; him just an honest man; Sae I conclude, and quat my chanter, Yourâs, saint or sinner, Rob the Ranter.





A New Psalm For The Chapel Of Kilmarnock

On the Thanksgiving-Day for His Majestyâs Recovery.

O sing a new song to the Lord, Make, all and every one, A joyful noise, even for the King His restoration. The sons of Belial in the land Did set their heads together; Come, let us sweep them off, said they, Like an oâerflowing river. They set their heads together, I say, They set their heads together; On right, on left, on every hand, We saw none to deliver. Thou madest strong two chosen ones To quell the Wickedâs pride; That Young Man, great in Issachar, The burden-bearing tribe. And him, among the Princes chief In our Jerusalem, The judge thatâs mighty in thy law, The man that fears thy name. Yet they, even they, with all their strength, Began to faint and fail: Even as two howling, ravenous wolves To dogs do turn their tail. Thâ ungodly oâer the just prevailâd, For so thou hadst appointed; That thou mightâst greater glory give Unto thine own anointed. And now thou hast restored our State, Pity our Kirk also; For she by tribulations Is now brought very low. Consume that high-place, Patronage, From off thy holy hill; And in thy fury burn the bookâ Even of that man MâGill.1 Now hear our prayer, accept our song, And fight thy chosenâs battle: We seek but little, Lord, from thee, Thou kens we get as little. [Footnote 1: Dr. William MâGill of Ayr, whose âPractical Essay on the Death of Jesus Christâ led to a charge of heresy against him. Burns took up his cause in âThe Kirk of Scotlandâs Alarmâ (p. 351).âLang.]





Sketch In Verse

Inscribed to the Right Hon. C. J. Fox. How wisdom and Folly meet, mix, and unite, How Virtue and Vice blend their black and their white, How Genius, thâ illustrious father of fiction, Confounds rule and law, reconciles contradiction, I sing: If these mortals, the critics, should bustle, I care not, not Iâlet the Critics go whistle! But now for a Patron whose name and whose glory, At once may illustrate and honour my story. Thou first of our orators, first of our wits; Yet whose parts and acquirements seem just lucky hits; With knowledge so vast, and with judgment so strong, No man with the half of âem eâer could go wrong; With passions so potent, and fancies so bright, No man with the half of âem eâer could go right; A sorry, poor, misbegot son of the Muses, For using thy name, offers fifty excuses. Good Lord, what is Man! for as simple he looks, Do but try to develop his hooks and his crooks; With his depths and his shallows, his good and his evil, All in all heâs a problem must puzzle the devil. On his one ruling passion Sir Pope hugely labours, That, like thâ old Hebrew walking-switch, eats up its neighbours: Mankind are his show-boxâa friend, would you know him? Pull the string, Ruling Passion the picture will show him, What pity, in rearing so beauteous a system, One trifling particular, Truth, should have missâd him; For, spite of his fine theoretic positions, Mankind is a science defies definitions. Some sort all our qualities each to its tribe, And think human nature they truly describe; Have you found this, or tâother? Thereâs more in the wind; As by one drunken fellow his comrades youâll find. But such is the flaw, or the depth of the plan, In the make of that wonderful creature called Man, No two virtues, whatever relation they claim. Nor even two different shades of the same, Though like as was ever twin brother to brother, Possessing the one shall imply youâve the other. But truce with abstraction, and truce with a Muse Whose rhymes youâll perhaps, Sir, neâer deign to peruse: Will you leave your justings, your jars, and your quarrels, Contending with Billy for proud-nodding laurels? My much-honourâd Patron, believe your poor poet, Your courage, much more than your prudence, you show it: In vain with Squire Billy for laurels you struggle: Heâll have them by fair trade, if not, he will smuggle: Not cabinets even of kings would conceal âem, Heâd up the back stairs, and by God, he would steal âem, Then feats like Squire Billyâs you neâer can achieve âem; It is not, out-do himâthe task is, out-thieve him!





The Wounded Hare

Inhuman man! curse on thy barbârous art, And blasted be thy murder-aiming eye; May never pity soothe thee with a sigh, Nor ever pleasure glad thy cruel heart! Go live, poor wandârer of the wood and field! The bitter little that of life remains: No more the thickening brakes and verdant plains To thee a home, or food, or pastime yield. Seek, mangled wretch, some place of wonted rest, No more of rest, but now thy dying bed! The sheltering rushes whistling oâer thy head, The cold earth with thy bloody bosom prest. Perhaps a motherâs anguish adds its woe; The playful pair crowd fondly by thy side; Ah! helpless nurslings, who will now provide That life a mother only can bestow! Oft as by winding Nith I, musing, wait The sober eve, or hail the cheerful dawn, Iâll miss thee sporting oâer the dewy lawn, And curse the ruffianâs aim, and mourn thy hapless fate.

Her closed eyes, like weapons sheathâd, Were sealâd in soft repose; Her lip, still as she fragrant breathâd, It richer dyed the rose; The springing lilies, sweetly prest, Wild-wanton kissed her rival breast; He gazâd, he wishâd, He mearâd, he blushâd, His bosom ill at rest. Her robes, light-waving in the breeze, Her tender limbs embrace; Her lovely form, her native ease, All harmony and grace; Tumultuous tides his pulses roll, A faltering, ardent kiss he stole; He gazâd, he wishâd, He fearâd, he blushâd, And sighâd his very soul. 10 Aug., 1979. Addressed to Robert Graham, Esq. of Fintry. I call no Goddess to inspire my strains, A fabled Muse may suit a bard that feigns: Friend of my life! my ardent spirit burns, And all the tribute of my heart returns, For boons accorded, goodness ever new, The gifts still dearer, as the giver you. Thou orb of day! thou other paler light! And all ye many sparkling stars of night! If aught that giver from my mind efface, If I that giverâs bounty eâer disgrace, Then roll to me along your wandârig spheres, Only to number out a villainâs years! I lay my hand upon my swelling breast, And grateful would, but cannot speak the rest.

I Gaed A Waefuâ Gate Yestreen

I gaed a waefuâ gate yestreen, A gate, I fear, Iâll dearly rue; I gat my death frae twa sweet een, Twa lovely een oâbonie blue. âTwas not her golden ringlets bright, Her lips like roses wat wiâ dew, Her heaving bosom, lily-whiteâ It was her een sae bonie blue. She talkâd, she smilâd, my heart she wylâd; She charmâd my soul I wist na how; And aye the stound, the deadly wound, Cam frae her een so bonie blue. But âspare to speak, and spare to speed;â Sheâll aiblins listen to my vow: Should she refuse, Iâll lay my dead To her twa een sae bonie blue.
