The Battle Of Sherramuir

TuneââThe Cameronian Rant.â
âO cam ye here the fight to shun, Or herd the sheep wiâ me, man? Or were ye at the Sherra-moor, Or did the battle see, man?â I saw the battle, sair and teugh, And reekin-red ran mony a sheugh; My heart, for fear, gaed sough for sough, To hear the thuds, and see the cluds Oâ clans frae woods, in tartan duds, Wha glaumâd at kingdoms three, man. La, la, la, la, &c. The red-coat lads, wiâ black cockauds, To meet them were na slaw, man; They rushâd and pushâd, and blude outgushâd And mony a bouk did faâ, man: The great Argyle led on his files, I wat they glanced twenty miles; They houghâd the clans like nine-pin kyles, They hackâd and hashâd, while braid-swords, clashâd, And throâ they dashâd, and hewâd and smashâd, Till fey men died awa, man. La, la, la, la, &c. But had ye seen the philibegs, And skyrin tartan trews, man; When in the teeth they darâd our Whigs, And covenant True-blues, man: In lines extended lang and large, When baiginets oâerpowerâd the targe, And thousands hastenâd to the charge; Wiâ Highland wrath they frae the sheath Drew blades oâ death, till, out oâ breath, They fled like frighted dows, man! La, la, la, la, &c. âO how deil, Tam, can that be true? The chase gaed frae the north, man; I saw mysel, they did pursue, The horsemen back to Forth, man; And at Dunblane, in my ain sight, They took the brig wiâ aâ their might, And straught to Stirling wingâd their flight; But, cursed lot! the gates were shut; And mony a huntit poor red-coat, For fear amaist did swarf, man!â La, la, la, la, &c. My sister Kate cam up the gate Wiâ crowdie unto me, man; She swoor she saw some rebels run To Perth unto Dundee, man; Their left-hand general had nae skill; The Angus lads had nae gude will That day their neiborsâ blude to spill; For fear, for foes, that they should lose Their cogs oâ brose; they scarâd at blows, And hameward fast did flee, man. La, la, la, la, &c. Theyâve lost some gallant gentlemen, Amang the Highland clans, man! I fear my Lord Panmure is slain, Or fallen in Whiggish hands, man, Now wad ye sing this double fight, Some fell for wrang, and some for right; But mony bade the world gude-night; Then ye may tell, how pell and mell, By red claymores, and muskets knell, Wiâ dying yell, the Tories fell, And Whigs to hell did flee, man. La, la, la, la, &c.

A Waukrife Minnie

Whare are you gaun, my bonie lass, Whare are you gaun, my hinnie? She answered me right saucilie, âAn errand for my minnie.â O whare live ye, my bonie lass, O whare live ye, my hinnie? âBy yon burnside, gin ye maun ken, In a wee house wiâ my minnie.â But I foor up the glen at eâen. To see my bonie lassie; And lang before the grey morn cam, She was na hauf sae saucie. O weary faâ the waukrife cock, And the foumart lay his crawin! He waukenâd the auld wife frae her sleep, A wee blink or the dawin. An angry wife I wat she raise, And oâer the bed she brocht her; And wiâ a meikle hazel rung She made her a weel-payâd dochter. O fare thee weel, my bonie lass, O fare thee well, my hinnie! The WhistleâA Ballad

I sing of a Whistle, a Whistle of worth, I sing of a Whistle, the pride of the North. Was brought to the court of our good Scottish King, And long with this Whistle all Scotland shall ring. Old Loda, still rueing the arm of Fingal, The god of the bottle sends down from his hallâ âThe Whistleâs your challenge, to Scotland get oâer, And drink them to hell, Sir! or neâer see me more!â Old poets have sung, and old chronicles tell, What champions venturâd, what champions fell: The son of great Loda was conqueror still, And blew on the Whistle their requiem shrill. Till Robert, the lord of the Cairn and the Scaur, Unmatchâd at the bottle, unconquerâd in war, He drank his poor god-ship as deep as the sea; No tide of the Baltic eâer drunker than he. Thus Robert, victorious, the trophy has gainâd; Which now in his house has for ages remainâd; Till three noble chieftains, and all of his blood, The jovial contest again have renewâd. Three joyous good fellows, with hearts clear of flaw Craigdarroch, so famous for with, worth, and law; And trusty Glenriddel, so skillâd in old coins; And gallant Sir Robert, deep-read in old wines. Craigdarroch began, with a tongue smooth as oil, Desiring Downrightly to yield up the spoil; Or else he would muster the heads of the clan, And once more, in claret, try which was the man. âBy the gods of the ancients!â Downrightly replies, âBefore I surrender so glorious a prize, Iâll conjure the ghost of the great Rorie More, And bumper his horn with him twenty times oâer.â Sir Robert, a soldier, no speech would pretend, But he neâer turnâd his back on his foe, or his friend; Said, âToss down the Whistle, the prize of the field,â And, knee-deep in claret, heâd die ere heâd yield. To the board of Glenriddel our heroes repair, So noted for drowning of sorrow and care; But, for wine and for welcome, not more known to fame, Than the sense, wit, and taste, of a sweet lovely dame. A bard was selected to witness the fray, And tell future ages the feats of the day; A Bard who detested all sadness and spleen, And wishâd that Parnassus a vineyard had been. The dinner being over, the claret they ply, And evâry new cork is a new spring of joy; In the bands of old friendship and kindred so set, And the bands grew the tighter the more they were wet. Gay Pleasure ran riot as bumpers ran oâer: Bright Phoebus neâer witnessâd so joyous a core, And vowâd that to leave them he was quite forlorn, Till Cynthia hinted heâd see them next morn. Six bottles a-piece had well wore out the night, When gallant Sir Robert, to finish the fight, Turnâd oâer in one bumper a bottle of red, And swore âtwas the way that their ancestor did. Then worthy Glenriddel, so cautious and sage, No longer the warfare ungodly would wage; A high Ruling Elder to wallow in wine; He left the foul business to folks less divine. The gallant Sir Robert fought hard to the end; But who can with Fate and quart bumpers contend! Though Fate said, a hero should perish in light; So uprose bright Phoebusâand down fell the knight. Next uprose our Bard, like a prophet in drink:â âCraigdarroch, thouâlt soar when creation shall sink! But if thou would flourish immortal in rhyme, Comeâone bottle moreâand have at the sublime! âThy line, that have struggled for freedom with Bruce, Shall heroes and patriots ever produce: So thine be the laurel, and mine be the bay; The field thou hast won, by yon bright god of day!â





To Mary In Heaven

Thou lingâring star, with lessening ray, That lovâst to greet the early morn, Again thou usherâst in the day My Mary from my soul was torn. O Mary! dear departed shade! Where is thy place of blissful rest? Seeâst thou thy lover lowly laid? Hearâst thou the groans that rend his breast? That sacred hour can I forget, Can I forget the hallowâd grove, Where, by the winding Ayr, we met, To live one day of parting love! Eternity will not efface Those records dear of transports past, Thy image at our last embrace, Ah! little thought we âtwas our last! Ayr, gurgling, kissâd his pebbled shore, Oâerhung with wild-woods, thickening green; The fragrant birch and hawthorn hoar, âTwinâd amorous round the rapturâd scene: The flowers sprang wanton to be prest, The birds sang love on every spray; Till too, too soon, the glowing west, Proclaimâd the speed of winged day. Still oâer these scenes my memâry wakes, And fondly broods with miser-care; Time but thâ impression stronger makes, As streams their channels deeper wear, My Mary! dear departed shade! Where is thy blissful place of rest? Seeâst thou thy lover lowly laid? Hearâst thou the groans that rend his breast?





Epistle To Dr. Blacklock

Ellisland, 21st Oct., 1789. Wow, but your letter made me vauntie! And are ye hale, and weel and cantie? I kenâd it still, your wee bit jauntie Wad bring ye to: Lord send you aye as weelâs I want ye! And then yeâll do. The ill-thief blaw the Heron south! And never drink be near his drouth! He tauld myself by word oâ mouth, Heâd tak my letter; I lippenâd to the chiel in trouth, And bade nae better. But aiblins, honest Master Heron Had, at the time, some dainty fair one To ware this theologic care on, And holy study; And tired oâ sauls to waste his lear on, Eâen tried the body. But what dâye think, my trusty fere, Iâm turned a gaugerâPeace be here! Parnassian queans, I fear, I fear, Yeâll now disdain me! And then my fifty pounds a year Will little gain me. Ye glaikit, gleesome, dainty damies, Wha, by Castaliaâs wimplin streamies, Lowp, sing, and lave your pretty limbies, Ye ken, ye ken, That strang necessity supreme is âMang sons oâ men. I hae a wife and twa wee laddies; They maun hae brose and brats oâ duddies; Ye ken yoursels my heart right proud isâ I need na vaunt But Iâll sned besoms, thraw saugh woodies, Before they want. Lord help me throâ this warld oâ care! Iâm weary sick oât late and air! Not but I hae a richer share Than mony ithers; But why should ae man better fare, And aâ men brithers? Come, Firm Resolve, take thou the van, Thou stalk oâ carl-hemp in man! And let us mind, faint heart neâer wan A lady fair: Wha does the utmost that he can, Will whiles do mair. But to conclude my silly rhyme (Iâm scant oâ verse and scant oâ time), To make a happy fireside clime To weans and wife, Thatâs the true pathos and sublime Of human life. My compliments to sister Beckie, And eke the same to honest Lucky; I wat she is a daintie chuckie, As eâer tread clay; And gratefully, my gude auld cockie, Iâm yours for aye. Robert Burns.





The Five Carlins

An Election Ballad. TuneââChevy Chase.â
There was five Carlins in the South, They fell upon a scheme, To send a lad to London town, To bring them tidings hame. Nor only bring them tidings hame, But do their errands there, And aiblins gowd and honor baith Might be that laddieâs share. There was Maggy by the banks oâ Nith, A dame wiâ pride eneugh; And Marjory oâ the mony Lochs, A Carlin auld and teugh. And blinkin Bess of Annandale, That dwelt near Solway-side; And whisky Jean, that took her gill, In Galloway sae wide. And auld black Joan frae Crichton Peel,1 Oâ gipsy kith anâ kin; Five wighter Carlins were na found The South countrie within. To send a lad to London town, They met upon a day; And mony a knight, and mony a laird, This errand fain wad gae. O mony a knight, and mony a laird, This errand fain wad gae; But nae ane could their fancy please, O neâer a ane but twae. The first ane was a belted Knight, Bred of a Border band;2 And he wad gae to London town, Might nae man him withstand. And he wad do their errands weel, And meikle he wad say; And ilka ane about the court Wad bid to him gude-day. [Footnote 1: Sanquhar.] [Footnote 2: Sir James Johnston of Westerhall.] The neist cam in a Soger youth,3 Who spak wiâ modest grace, And he wad gae to London town, If sae their pleasure was. He wad na hecht them courtly gifts, Nor meikle speech pretend; But he wad hecht an honest heart, Wad neâer desert his friend. Now, wham to chuse, and wham refuse, At strife thir Carlins fell; For some had Gentlefolks to please, And some wad please themselâ. Then out spak mim-mouâd Meg oâ Nith, And she spak up wiâ pride, And she wad send the Soger youth, Whatever might betide. For the auld Gudeman oâ London court4 She didna care a pin; But she wad send the Soger youth, To greet his eldest son.5 Then up sprang Bess oâ Annandale, And a deadly aith sheâs taâen, That she wad vote the Border Knight, Though she should vote her lane. âFor far-off fowls hae feathers fair, And fools oâ change are fain; But I hae tried the Border Knight, And Iâll try him yet again.â Says black Joan frae Crichton Peel, A Carlin stoor and grim. âThe auld Gudeman or young Gudeman, For me may sink or swim; [Footnote 3: Captain Patrick Millar of Dalswinton.] [Footnote 4: The King.] [Footnote 5: The Prince of Wales.] For fools will prate oâ right or wrang, While knaves laugh them to scorn; But the Sogerâs friends hae blawn the best, So he shall bear the horn.â Then whisky Jean spak owre her drink, âYe weel ken, kimmers aâ, The auld gudeman oâ London court, His backâs been at the waâ; âAnd mony a friend that kissâd his caup Is now a fremit wight; But itâs neâer be said oâ whisky Jeanâ Weâll send the Border Knight.â Then slow raise Marjory oâ the Lochs, And wrinkled was her brow, Her ancient weed was russet gray, Her auld Scots bluid was true; âThereâs some great folk set light by me, I set as light by them; But I will send to London town Wham I like best at hame.â Sae how this mighty plea may end, Nae mortal wight can tell; God grant the King and ilka man May look weel to himsel.

Prologue Spoken At The Theatre Of Dumfries

On New Yearâs Day Evening, 1790. No song nor dance I bring from yon great city, That queens it oâer our tasteâthe moreâs the pity: Thoâ by the bye, abroad why will you roam? Good sense and taste are natives here at home: But not for panegyric I appear, I come to wish you all a good New Year! Old Father Time deputes me here before ye, Not for to preach, but tell his simple story: The sage, grave Ancient coughâd, and bade me say, âYouâre one year older this important day,â If wiser tooâhe hinted some suggestion, But âtwould be rude, you know, to ask the question; And with a would-be roguish leer and wink, SaidââSutherland, in one word, bid them Think!â Ye sprightly youths, quite flush with hope and spirit, Who think to storm the world by dint of merit, To you the dotard has a deal to say, In his sly, dry, sententious, proverb way! He bids you mind, amid your thoughtless rattle, That the first blow is ever half the battle; That thoâ some by the skirt may try to snatch him, Yet by the foreclock is the hold to catch him; That whether doing, suffering, or forbearing, You may do miracles by persevering. Last, thoâ not least in love, ye youthful fair, Angelic forms, high Heavenâs peculiar care! To you old Bald-pate smoothes his wrinkled brow, And humbly begs youâll mind the importantâNow! To crown your happiness he asks your leave, And offers, bliss to give and to receive. For our sincere, thoâ haply weak endeavours, With grateful pride we own your many favours; And howsoeâer our tongues may ill reveal it, Believe our glowing bosoms truly feel it.





1790





SketchâNew Yearâs Day, 1790

To Mrs. Dunlop.
This day, Time winds thâ exhausted chain; To run the twelvemonthâs length again: I see, the old bald-pated fellow, With ardent eyes, complexion sallow, Adjust the unimpairâd machine, To wheel the equal, dull routine. The absent lover, minor heir, In vain assail him with their prayer; Deaf as my friend, he sees them press, Nor makes the hour one moment less, Will you (the Majorâs with the hounds, The happy tenants share his rounds; Coilaâs fair Rachelâs care to-day, And blooming Keithâs engaged with Gray) From housewife cares a minute borrow, (That grandchildâs cap will do to-morrow,) And join with me a-moralizing; This dayâs propitious to be wise in. First, what did yesternight deliver? âAnother year has gone for ever.â And what is this dayâs strong suggestion? âThe passing momentâs all we rest on!â Rest onâfor what? what do we here? Or why regard the passing year? Will Time, amusâd with proverbâd lore, Add to our date one minute more? A few days mayâa few years mustâ Repose us in the silent dust. Then, is it wise to damp our bliss? Yesâall such reasonings are amiss! The voice of Nature loudly cries, And many a message from the skies, That something in us never dies: That on his frail, uncertain state, Hang matters of eternal weight: That future life in worlds unknown Must take its hue from this alone; Whether as heavenly glory bright, Or dark as Miseryâs woeful night. Since then, my honourâd first of friends, On this poor being all depends, Let us thâ important now employ, And live as those who never die. Thoâ you, with days and honours crownâd, Witness that filial circle round, (A sight lifeâs sorrows to repulse, A sight pale Envy to convulse), Others now claim your chief regard; Yourself, you wait your bright reward.





Scotsâ Prologue For Mr. Sutherland

On his Benefit-Night, at the Theatre, Dumfries.
What needs this din about the town oâ Lonâon, How this new play anâ that new sang is comin? Why is outlandish stuff sae meikle courted? Does nonsense mend, like brandy, when imported? Is there nae poet, burning keen for fame, Will try to gie us sangs and plays at hame? For Comedy abroad he need to toil, A fool and knave are plants of every soil; Nor need he hunt as far as Rome or Greece, To gather matter for a serious piece; Thereâs themes enow in Caledonian story, Would shew the Tragic Muse in aâ her glory.â Is there no daring Bard will rise and tell How glorious Wallace stood, how hapless fell? Where are the Muses fled that could produce A drama worthy oâ the name oâ Bruce? How here, even here, he first unsheathâd the sword âGainst mighty England and her guilty Lord; And after mony a bloody, deathless doing, Wrenchâd his dear country from the jaws of Ruin! O for a Shakespeare, or an Otway scene, To draw the lovely, hapless Scottish Queen! Vain all thâ omnipotence of female charms âGainst headlong, ruthless, mad Rebellionâs arms: She fell, but fell with spirit truly Roman, To glut that direst foeâa vengeful woman; A woman, (thoâ the phrase may seem uncivil,) As able and as wicked as the Devil! One Douglas lives in Homeâs immortal page, But Douglasses were heroes every age: And thoâ your fathers, prodigal of life, A Douglas followed to the martial strife, Perhaps, if bowls row right, and Right succeeds, Ye yet may follow where a Douglas leads! As ye hae generous done, if aâ the land Would take the Musesâ servants by the hand; Not only hear, but patronize, befriend them, And where he justly can commend, commend them; And aiblins when they winna stand the test, Wink hard, and say The folks hae done their best! Would aâ the land do this, then Iâll be caition, Yeâll soon hae Poets oâ the Scottish nation Will gar Fame blaw until her trumpet crack, And warsle Time, anâ lay him on his back! For us and for our Stage, should ony spier, âWhase aught thae chiels maks aâ this bustle here?â My best leg foremost, Iâll set up my browâ We have the honour to belong to you! Weâre your ain bairns, eâen guide us as ye like, But like good mithers shore before ye strike; And gratefuâ still, I trust yeâll ever find us, For genârous patronage, and meikle kindness Weâve got frae aâ professions, sets and ranks: God help us! weâre but poorâyeâse get but thanks.





Lines To A Gentleman,

Who had sent the Poet a Newspaper, and offered to continue it free of Expense. Kind Sir, Iâve read your paper through, And faith, to me, âtwas really new! How guessed ye, Sir, what maist I wanted? This mony a day Iâve grainâd and gaunted, To ken what French mischief was brewin; Or what the drumlie Dutch were doin; That vile doup-skelper, Emperor Joseph, If Venus yet had got his nose off; Or how the collieshangie works Atween the Russians and the Turks, Or if the Swede, before he halt, Would play anither Charles the twalt; If Denmark, any body spak oât; Or Poland, wha had now the tack oât: How cut-throat Prussian blades were hingin; How libbet Italy was singin; If Spaniard, Portuguese, or Swiss, Were sayinâ or takinâ aught amiss; Or how our merry lads at hame, In Britainâs court kept up the game; How royal George, the Lord leuk oâer him! Was managing St. Stephenâs quorum; If sleekit Chatham Will was livin, Or glaikit Charlie got his nieve in; How daddie Burke the plea was cookin, If Warren Hastingâs neck was yeukin; How cesses, stents, and fees were raxâd. Or if bare arses yet were taxâd; The news oâ princes, dukes, and earls, Pimps, sharpers, bawds, and opera-girls; If that daft buckie, Geordie Wales, Was threshing still at hizziesâ tails; Or if he was grown oughtlins douser, And no a perfect kintra cooser: Aâ this and mair I never heard of; And, but for you, I might despairâd of. So, gratefuâ, back your news I send you, And pray aâ gude things may attend you. Ellisland, Monday Morning, 1790.





Elegy On Willie Nicolâs Mare

Peg Nicholson was a good bay mare, As ever trod on airn; But now sheâs floating down the Nith, And past the mouth oâ Cairn. Peg Nicholson was a good bay mare, Anâ rode throâ thick and thin; But now sheâs floating down the Nith, And wanting even the skin. Peg Nicholson was a good bay mare, And ance she bore a priest; But now sheâs floating down the Nith, For Solway fish a feast. Peg Nicholson was a good bay mare, Anâ the priest he rode her sair; And much oppressâd and bruisâd she was, As priest-rid cattle are,â&c. &c.





The Gowden Locks Of Anna

Yestreen I had a pint oâ wine, A place where body saw na; Yestreen lay on this breast oâ mine The gowden locks of Anna. The hungry Jew in wilderness, Rejoicing oâer his manna, Was naething to my hinny bliss Upon the lips of Anna. Ye monarchs, take the East and West Frae Indus to Savannah; Gie me, within my straining grasp, The melting form of Anna: There Iâll despise Imperial charms, An Empress or Sultana, While dying raptures in her arms I give and take wiâ Anna! Awa, thou flaunting God of Day! Awa, thou pale Diana! Ilk Star, gae hide thy twinkling ray, When Iâm to meet my Anna! Come, in thy raven plumage, Night, (Sun, Moon, and Stars, withdrawn aâ;) And bring an angel-pen to write My transports with my Anna!





Postscript

The Kirk anâ State may join anâ tell, To do sic things I maunna: The Kirk anâ State may gae to hell, And Iâll gae to my Anna. She is the sunshine oâ my eâe, To live but her I canna; Had I on earth but wishes three, The first should be my Anna.





SongâI Murder Hate

I murder hate by flood or field, Thoâ gloryâs name may screen us; In wars at home Iâll spend my bloodâ Life-giving wars of Venus. The deities that I adore Are social Peace and Plenty; Iâm better pleasâd to make one more, Than be the death of twenty. I would not die like Socrates, For all the fuss of Plato; Nor would I with Leonidas, Nor yet would I with Cato: The zealots of the Church and State Shall neâer my mortal foes be; But let me have bold Zimriâs fate, Within the arms of Cozbi!





Gudewife, Count The Lawin

Gane is the day, and mirkâs the night, But weâll neâer stray for faut oâ light; Gude ale and bratdyâs stars and moon, And blue-red wineâs the risinâ sun. Chorus.âThen gudewife, count the lawin, The lawin, the lawin, Then gudewife, count the lawin, And bring a coggie mair. Thereâs wealth and ease for gentlemen, And simple folk maun fecht and fenâ; But here weâre aâ in ae accord, For ilka man thatâs drunkâs a lord. Then gudewife, &c. My coggie is a haly pool That heals the wounds oâ care and dool; And Pleasure is a wanton trout, An ye drink it aâ, yeâll find him out. Then gudewife, &c.





Election Ballad

At the close of the contest for representing the Dumfries Burghs, 1790.
Addressed to R. Graham, Esq. of Fintry. Fintry, my stay in wordly strife, Friend oâ my muse, friend oâ my life, Are ye as idleâs I am? Come then, wiâ uncouth kintra fleg, Oâer Pegasus Iâll fling my leg, And ye shall see me try him. But where shall I go rin a ride, That I may splatter nane beside? I wad na be uncivil: In manhoodâs various paths and ways Thereâs aye some doytinâ body strays, And I ride like the devil. Thus I break aff wiâ aâ my birr, And down yon dark, deep alley spur, Where Theologics daunder: Alas! curst wiâ eternal fogs, And damnâd in everlasting bogs, As sureâs the creed Iâll blunder! Iâll stain a band, or jaup a gown, Or rin my reckless, guilty crown Against the haly door: Sair do I rue my luckless fate, When, as the Muse anâ Deil wad haeât, I rade that road before. Suppose I take a spurt, and mix Amang the wilds oâ Politicsâ Electors and elected, Where dogs at Court (sad sons of bitches!) Septennially a madness touches, Till all the landâs infected. All hail! Drumlanrigâs haughty Grace, Discarded remnant of a race Once godlikeâgreat in story; Thy forbearsâ virtues all contrasted, The very name of Douglas blasted, Thine that inverted glory! Hate, envy, oft the Douglas bore, But thou hast superadded more, And sunk them in contempt; Follies and crimes have stainâd the name, But, Queensberry, thine the virgin claim, From aught thatâs good exempt! Iâll sing the zeal Drumlanrig bears, Who left the all-important cares Of princes, and their darlings: And, bent on winning borough touns, Came shaking hands wiâ wabster-loons, And kissing barefit carlins. Combustion throâ our boroughs rode, Whistling his roaring pack abroad Of mad unmuzzled lions; As Queensberry blue and buff unfurlâd, And Westerhaâ and Hopetoun hurled To every Whig defiance. But cautious Queensberry left the war, Thâ unmannerâd dust might soil his star, Besides, he hated bleeding: But left behind him heroes bright, Heroes in Caesarean fight, Or Ciceronian pleading. O for a throat like huge Mons-Meg, To muster oâer each ardent Whig Beneath Drumlanrigâs banners; Heroes and heroines commix, All in the field of politics, To win immortal honours. MâMurdo and his lovely spouse, (Thâ enamourâd laurels kiss her brows!) Led on the Loves and Graces: She won each gaping burgessâ heart, While he, sub rosa, played his part Amang their wives and lasses. Craigdarroch led a light-armâd core, Tropes, metaphors, and figures pour, Like Hecla streaming thunder: Glenriddel, skillâd in rusty coins, Blew up each Toryâs dark designs, And bared the treason under. In either wing two champions fought; Redoubted Staig, who set at nought The wildest savage Tory; And Welsh who neâer yet flinchâd his ground, High-wavâd his magnum-bonum round With Cyclopeian fury. Miller brought up thâ artillery ranks, The many-pounders of the Banks, Resistless desolation! While Maxwelton, that baron bold, âMid Lawsonâs port entrenchâd his hold, And threatenâd worse damnation. To these what Tory hosts opposâd With these what Tory warriors closâd Surpasses my descriving; Squadrons, extended long and large, With furious speed rush to the charge, Like furious devils driving. What verse can sing, what prose narrate, The butcher deeds of bloody Fate, Amid this mighty tulyie! Grim Horror girnâd, pale Terror roarâd, As Murder at his thrapple shorâd, And Hell mixâd in the brulyie. As Highland craigs by thunder cleft, When lightnings fire the stormy lift, Hurl down with crashing rattle; As flames among a hundred woods, As headlong foam from a hundred floods, Such is the rage of Battle. The stubborn Tories dare to die; As soon the rooted oaks would fly Before thâ approaching fellers: The Whigs come on like Oceanâs roar, When all his wintry billows pour Against the Buchan Bullers. Lo, from the shades of Deathâs deep night, Departed Whigs enjoy the fight, And think on former daring: The muffled murtherer of Charles The Magna Charter flag unfurls, All deadly gules its bearing. Nor wanting ghosts of Tory fame; Bold Scrimgeour follows gallant Graham; Auld Covenanters shiverâ Forgive! forgive! much-wrongâd Montrose! Now Death and Hell engulph thy foes, Thou livâst on high for ever. Still oâer the field the combat burns, The Tories, Whigs, give way by turns; But Fate the word has spoken: For womanâs wit and strength oâman, Alas! can do but what they can; The Tory ranks are broken. O that my een were flowing burns! My voice, a lioness that mourns Her darling cubsâ undoing! That I might greet, that I might cry, While Tories fall, while Tories fly, And furious Whigs pursuing! What Whig but melts for good Sir James, Dear to his country, by the names, Friend, Patron, Benefactor! Not Pulteneyâs wealth can Pulteney save; And Hopetoun falls, the generous, brave; And Stewart, bold as Hector. Thou, Pitt, shalt rue this overthrow, And Thurlow growl a curse of woe, And Melville melt in wailing: Now Fox and Sheridan rejoice, And Burke shall sing, âO Prince, arise! Thy power is all-prevailing!â For your poor friend, the Bard, afar He only hears and sees the war, A cool spectator purely! So, when the storm the forest rends, The robin in the hedge descends, And sober chirps securely. Now, for my friendsâ and brethrenâs sakes, And for my dear-lovâd Land oâ Cakes, I pray with holy fire: Lord, send a rough-shod troop oâ Hell Oâer aâ wad Scotland buy or sell, To grind them in the mire!





Elegy On Captain Matthew Henderson

A Gentleman who held the Patent for his Honours immediately from Almighty God.

Should the poor be flattered?âShakespeare.
O Death! thou tyrant fell and bloody! The meikle devil wiâ a woodie Haurl thee hame to his black smiddie, Oâer hurcheon hides, And like stock-fish come oâer his studdie Wiâ thy auld sides! Heâs gane, heâs gane! heâs frae us torn, The ae best fellow eâer was born! Thee, Matthew, Natureâs selâ shall mourn, By wood and wild, Where haply, Pity strays forlorn, Frae man exilâd. Ye hills, near neighbours oâ the starns, That proudly cock your cresting cairns! Ye cliffs, the haunts of sailing earns, Where Echo slumbers! Come join, ye Natureâs sturdiest bairns, My wailing numbers! Mourn, ilka grove the cushat kens! Ye hazâly shaws and briery dens! Ye burnies, wimplinâ down your glens, Wiâ toddlin din, Or foaming, strang, wiâ hasty stens, Frae lin to lin. Mourn, little harebells oâer the lea; Ye stately foxgloves, fair to see; Ye woodbines hanging bonilie, In scented bowârs; Ye roses on your thorny tree, The first oâ flowârs. At dawn, when evâry grassy blade Droops with a diamond at his head, At evân, when beans their fragrance shed, Iâ thâ rustling gale, Ye maukins, whiddin throâ the glade, Come join my wail. Mourn, ye wee songsters oâ the wood; Ye grouse that crap the heather bud; Ye curlews, calling throâ a clud; Ye whistling plover; And mourn, we whirring paitrick brood; Heâs gane for ever! Mourn, sooty coots, and speckled teals; Ye fisher herons, watching eels; Ye duck and drake, wiâ airy wheels Circling the lake; Ye bitterns, till the quagmire reels, Rair for his sake. Mourn, clamâring craiks at close oâ day, âMang fields oâ flowâring clover gay; And when ye wing your annual way Frae our claud shore, Tell thae far warlds wha lies in clay, Wham we deplore. Ye houlets, frae your ivy bowâr In some auld tree, or eldritch towâr, What time the moon, wiâ silent glowâr, Sets up her horn, Wail throâ the dreary midnight hour, Till waukrife morn! O rivers, forests, hills, and plains! Oft have ye heard my canty strains; But now, what else for me remains But tales of woe; And frae my een the drapping rains Maun ever flow. Mourn, Spring, thou darling of the year! Ilk cowslip cup shall kep a tear: Thou, Simmer, while each corny spear Shoots up its head, Thy gay, green, flowâry tresses shear, For him thatâs dead! Thou, Autumn, wiâ thy yellow hair, In grief thy sallow mantle tear! Thou, Winter, hurling throâ the air The roaring blast, Wide oâer the naked world declare The worth weâve lost! Mourn him, thou Sun, great source of light! Mourn, Empress of the silent night! And you, ye twinkling starnies bright, My Matthew mourn! For through your orbs heâs taâen his flight, Neâer to return. O Henderson! the man! the brother! And art thou gone, and gone for ever! And hast thou crost that unknown river, Lifeâs dreary bound! Like thee, where shall I find another, The world around! Go to your sculpturâd tombs, ye Great, In aâ the tinsel trash oâ state! But by thy honest turf Iâll wait, Thou man of worth! And weep the ae best fellowâs fate Eâer lay in earth.





The Epitaph

Stop, passenger! my storyâs brief, And truth I shall relate, man; I tell nae common tale oâ grief, For Matthew was a great man. If thou uncommon merit hast, Yet spurnâd at Fortuneâs door, man; A look of pity hither cast, For Matthew was a poor man. If thou a noble sodger art, That passest by this grave, man; There moulders here a gallant heart, For Matthew was a brave man. If thou on men, their works and ways, Canst throw uncommon light, man; Here lies wha weel had won thy praise, For Matthew was a bright man. If thou, at Friendshipâs sacred caâ, Wad life itself resign, man: Thy sympathetic tear maun faâ, For Matthew was a kind man. If thou art staunch, without a stain, Like the unchanging blue, man; This was a kinsman oâ thy ain, For Matthew was a true man. If thou hast wit, and fun, and fire, And neâer guid wine did fear, man; This was thy billie, dam, and sire, For Matthew was a queer man. If ony whiggish, whinginâ sot, To blame poor Matthew dare, man; May dool and sorrow be his lot, For Matthew was a rare man. But now, his radiant course is run, For Matthewâs was a bright one! His soul was like the glorious sun, A matchless, Heavenly light, man.





Verses On Captain Grose

Written on an Envelope, enclosing a Letter to Him.
Ken ye aught oâ Captain Grose?âIgo, and ago, If heâs amang his friends or foes?âIram, coram, dago. Is he to Abraâmâs bosom gane?âIgo, and ago, Or haudin Sarah by the wame?âIram, coram dago. Is he south or is he north?âIgo, and ago, Or drowned in the river Forth?âIram, coram dago. Is he slain by Hielanâ bodies?âIgo, and ago, And eaten like a wether haggis?âIram, coram, dago. But please transmit thâ enclosed letter,âIgo, and ago, Which will oblige your humble debtor.âIram, coram, dago. So may ye hae auld stanes in store,âIgo, and ago, The very stanes that Adam bore.âIram, coram, dago, So may ye get in glad possession,âIgo, and ago, The coins oâ Satanâs coronation!âIram coram dago.





Tam Oâ Shanter

A Tale. âOf Brownyis and of Bogillis full is this Buke.â Gawin Douglas.
When chapman billies leave the street, And drouthy neibors, neibors, meet; As market days are wearing late, And folk begin to tak the gate, While we sit bousing at the nappy, Anâ getting fou and unco happy, We think na on the lang Scots miles, The mosses, waters, slaps and stiles, That lie between us and our hame, Where sits our sulky, sullen dame, Gathering her brows like gathering storm, Nursing her wrath to keep it warm. This truth fand honest Tam oâ Shanter, As he frae Ayr ae night did canter: (Auld Ayr, wham neâer a town surpasses, For honest men and bonie lasses). O Tam! hadâst thou but been sae wise, As taen thy ain wife Kateâs advice! She tauld thee weel thou was a skellum, A blethering, blustering, drunken blellum; That frae November till October, Ae market-day thou was na sober; That ilka melder wiâ the Miller, Thou sat as lang as thou had siller; That evâry naig was caâd a shoe on The Smith and thee gat roarinâ fou on; That at the Lordâs house, evân on Sunday, Thou drank wiâ Kirkton Jean till Monday, She prophesied that late or soon, Thou wad be found, deep drownâd in Doon, Or catchâd wiâ warlocks in the mirk, By Allowayâs auld, haunted kirk. Ah, gentle dames! it gars me greet, To think how mony counsels sweet, How mony lengthenâd, sage advices, The husband frae the wife despises! But to our tale: Ae market night, Tam had got planted unco right, Fast by an ingle, bleezing finely, Wi reaming saats, that drank divinely; And at his elbow, Souter Johnie, His ancient, trusty, drougthy crony: Tam loâed him like a very brither; They had been fou for weeks thegither. The night drave on wiâ sangs anâ clatter; And aye the ale was growing better: The Landlady and Tam grew gracious, Wiâ favours secret, sweet, and precious: The Souter tauld his queerest stories; The Landlordâs laugh was ready chorus: The storm without might rair and rustle, Tam did na mind the storm a whistle. Care, mad to see a man sae happy, Eâen drownâd himsel amang the nappy. As bees flee hame wiâ lades oâ treasure, The minutes wingâd their way wiâ pleasure: Kings may be blest, but Tam was glorious, Oâer aâ the ills oâ life victorious! But pleasures are like poppies spread, You seize the flowâr, its bloom is shed; Or like the snow falls in the river, A moment whiteâthen melts for ever; Or like the Borealis race, That flit ere you can point their place; Or like the Rainbowâs lovely form Evanishing amid the storm.â Nae man can tether Time nor Tide, The hour approaches Tam maun ride; That hour, oâ nightâs black arch the key-stane, That dreary hour he mounts his beast in; And sic a night he taks the road in, As neâer poor sinner was abroad in. The wind blew as âtwad blawn its last; The rattling showers rose on the blast; The speedy gleams the darkness swallowâd; Loud, deep, and lang, the thunder bellowâd: That night, a child might understand, The deil had business on his hand. Weel-mounted on his grey mare, Meg, A better never lifted leg, Tam skelpit on throâ dub and mire, Despising wind, and rain, and fire; Whiles holding fast his gude blue bonnet, Whiles crooning oâer some auld Scots sonnet, Whiles glowârin round wiâ prudent cares, Lest bogles catch him unawares; Kirk-Alloway was drawing nigh, Where ghaists and houlets nightly cry. By this time he was cross the ford, Where in the snaw the chapman smoorâd; And past the birks and meikle stane, Where drunken Charlie brakâs neck-bane; And throâ the whins, and by the cairn, Where hunters fand the murderâd bairn; And near the thorn, aboon the well, Where Mungoâs mither hangâd herselâ. Before him Doon pours all his floods, The doubling storm roars throâ the woods, The lightnings flash from pole to pole, Near and more near the thunders roll, When, glimmering throâ the groaning trees, Kirk-Alloway seemâd in a bleeze, Throâ ilka bore the beams were glancing, And loud resounded mirth and dancing. Inspiring bold John Barleycorn! What dangers thou canst make us scorn! Wiâ tippenny, we fear nae evil; Wiâ usquabae, weâll face the devil! The swats sae reamâd in Tammieâs noddle, Fair play, he carâd na deils a boddle, But Maggie stood, right sair astonishâd, Till, by the heel and hand admonishâd, She venturâd forward on the light; And, wow! Tam saw an unco sight! Warlocks and witches in a dance: Nae cotillon, brent new frae France, But hornpipes, jigs, strathspeys, and reels, Put life and mettle in their heels. A winnock-bunker in the east, There sat auld Nick, in shape oâ beast; A towzie tyke, black, grim, and large, To gie them music was his charge: He screwâd the pipes and gart them skirl, Till roof and rafters aâ did dirl.â Coffins stood round, like open presses, That shawâd the Dead in their last dresses; And (by some devilish cantraip sleight) Each in its cauld hand held a light. By which heroic Tam was able To note upon the haly table, A murdererâs banes, in gibbet-airns; Twa span-lang, wee, unchristened bairns; A thief, new-cutted frae a rape, Wiâ his last gasp his gabudid gape; Five tomahawks, wiâ blude red-rusted: Five scimitars, wiâ murder crusted; A garter which a babe had strangled: A knife, a fatherâs throat had mangled. Whom his ain son of life bereft, The grey-hairs yet stack to the heft; Wiâ mair of horrible and awfuâ, Which even to name wad be unlawfuâ. As Tammie glowrâd, amazâd, and curious, The mirth and fun grew fast and furious; The Piper loud and louder blew, The dancers quick and quicker flew, The reelâd, they set, they crossâd, they cleekit, Till ilka carlin swat and reekit, And coost her duddies to the wark, And linkit at it in her sark! Now Tam, O Tam! had they been queans, Aâ plump and strapping in their teens! Their sarks, instead oâ creeshie flainen, Been snaw-white seventeen hunder linen!â Thir breeks oâ mine, my only pair, That ance were plush oâ guid blue hair, I wad hae gien them off my hurdies, For ae blink oâ the bonie burdies! But witherâd beldams, auld and droll, Rigwoodie hags wad spean a foal, Louping anâ flinging on a crummock. I wonder did na turn thy stomach. But Tam kent what was what fuâ brawlie: There was ae winsome wench and waulie That night enlisted in the core, Lang after kenâd on Carrick shore; (For mony a beast to dead she shot, And perishâd mony a bonie boat, And shook baith meikle corn and bear, And kept the country-side in fear); Her cutty sark, oâ Paisley harn, That while a lassie she had worn, In longitude thoâ sorely scanty, It was her best, and she was vauntie. Ah! little kenâd thy reverend grannie, That sark she coft for her wee Nannie, Wi twa pund Scots (âtwas aâ her riches), Wad ever gracâd a dance of witches! But here my Muse her wing maun cour, Sic flights are far beyond her power; To sing how Nannie lap and flang, (A souple jade she was and strang), And how Tam stood, like ane bewithcâd, And thought his very een enrichâd: Even Satan glowrâd, and fidgâd fuâ fain, And hotchâd and blew wiâ might and main: Till first ae caper, syne anither, Tam tint his reason a thegither, And roars out, âWeel done, Cutty-sark!â And in an instant all was dark: And scarcely had he Maggie rallied. When out the hellish legion sallied. As bees bizz out wiâ angry fyke, When plundering herds assail their byke; As open pussieâs mortal foes, When, pop! she starts before their nose; As eager runs the market-crowd, When âCatch the thief!â resounds aloud; So Maggie runs, the witches follow, Wiâ mony an eldritch skreich and hollow. Ah, Tam! Ah, Tam! thouâll get thy fairin! In hell, theyâll roast thee like a herrin! In vain thy Kate awaits thy comin! Kate soon will be a woefuâ woman! Now, do thy speedy-utmost, Meg, And win the key-stone oâ the brig;1 There, at them thou thy tail may toss, A running stream they dare na cross. But ere the keystane she could make, The fient a tail she had to shake! For Nannie, far before the rest, Hard upon noble Maggie prest, And flew at Tam wiâ furious ettle; But little wist she Maggieâs mettle! Ae spring brought off her master hale, But left behind her ain grey tail: The carlin claught her by the rump, And left poor Maggie scarce a stump. Now, wha this tale oâ truth shall read, Ilk man and motherâs son, take heed: Wheneâer to Drink you are inclinâd, Or Cutty-sarks rin in your mind, Think ye may buy the joys oâer dear; Remember Tam oâ Shanterâs mare.





On The Birth Of A Posthumous Child

Born in peculiar circumstances of family distress.

November hirples oâer the lea, Chil, on thy lovely form: And gane, alas! the sheltâring tree, Should shield thee frae the storm. It may be proper likewise to mention to the benighted traveller, that when he falls in with bogles, whatever danger may be in his going forward, there is much more hazard in turning back.âR.B.] May He who gives the rain to pour, And wings the blast to blaw, Protect thee frae the driving showâr, The bitter frost and snaw. May He, the friend oâ Woe and Want, Who heals lifeâs various stounds, Protect and guard the mother plant, And heal her cruel wounds. But late she flourishâd, rooted fast, Fair in the summer morn, Now feebly bends she in the blast, Unshelterâd and forlorn. Blest be thy bloom, thou lovely gem, Unscathâd by ruffian hand! And from thee many a parent stem Arise to deck our land!





Elegy On The Late Miss Burnet Of Monboddo

Life neâer exulted in so rich a prize, As Burnet, lovely from her native skies; Nor envious death so triumphâd in a blow, As that which laid thâ accomplishâd Burnet low. Thy form and mind, sweet maid, can I forget? In richest ore the brightest jewel set! In thee, high Heaven above was truest shown, As by His noblest work the Godhead best is known. In vain ye flaunt in summerâs pride, ye groves; Thou crystal streamlet with thy flowery shore, Ye woodland choir that chaunt your idle loves, Ye cease to charm; Eliza is no more. Ye healthy wastes, immixâd with reedy fens; Ye mossy streams, with sedge and rushes storâd: Ye rugged cliffs, oâerhanging dreary glens, To you I flyâye with my soul accord. Princes, whose cumbârous pride was all their worth, Shall venal lays their pompous exit hail, And thou, sweet Excellence! forsake our earth, And not a Muse with honest grief bewail? We saw thee shine in youth and beautyâs pride, And Virtueâs light, that beams beyond the spheres; But, like the sun eclipsâd at morning tide, Thou left us darkling in a world of tears. The parentâs heart that nestled fond in thee, That heart how sunk, a prey to grief and care; So deckt the woodbine sweet yon aged tree; So, from it ravishâd, leaves it bleak and bare.

Lament Of Mary, Queen Of Scots, On The Approach Of Spring

Now Nature hangs her mantle green On every blooming tree, And spreads her sheets oâ daisies white Out oâer the grassy lea; Now Phoebus cheers the crystal streams, And glads the azure skies; But nought can glad the weary wight That fast in durance lies. Now laverocks wake the merry morn Aloft on dewy wing; The merle, in his noontide bowâr, Makes woodland echoes ring; The mavis wild wiâ mony a note, Sings drowsy day to rest: In love and freedom they rejoice, Wiâ care nor thrall opprest. Now blooms the lily by the bank, The primrose down the brae; The hawthornâs budding in the glen, And milk-white is the slae: The meanest hind in fair Scotland May rove their sweets amang; But I, the Queen of aâ Scotland, Maun lie in prison strang. I was the Queen oâ bonie France, Where happy I hae been; Fuâ lightly raise I in the morn, As blythe lay down at eâen: And Iâm the sovâreign of Scotland, And mony a traitor there; Yet here I lie in foreign bands, And never-ending care. But as for thee, thou false woman, My sister and my fae, Grim Vengeance yet shall whet a sword That throâ thy soul shall gae; The weeping blood in womanâs breast Was never known to thee; Nor thâ balm that draps on wounds of woe Frae womanâs pitying eâe. My son! my son! may kinder stars Upon thy fortune shine; And may those pleasures gild thy reign, That neâer wad blink on mine! God keep thee frae thy motherâs faes, Or turn their hearts to thee: And where thou meetâst thy motherâs friend, Remember him for me! O! soon, to me, may Summer suns Nae mair light up the morn! Nae mair to me the Autumn winds Wave oâer the yellow corn? And, in the narrow house of death, Let Winter round me rave; And the next flowârs that deck the Spring, Bloom on my peaceful grave!

SongâOut Over The Forth

Out over the Forth, I look to the North; But what is the north and its Highlands to me? The south nor the east gie ease to my breast, The far foreign land, or the wide rolling sea. Lament For James, Earl Of Glencairn

The wind blew hollow frae the hills, By fits the sunâs departing beam Lookâd on the fading yellow woods, That wavâd oâer Lugarâs winding stream: Beneath a craigy steep, a Bard, Laden with years and meikle pain, In loud lament bewailâd his lord, Whom Death had all untimely taâen. He leanâd him to an ancient aik, Whose trunk was mouldâring down with years; His locks were bleached white with time, His hoary cheek was wet wiâ tears! And as he touchâd his trembling harp, And as he tunâd his doleful sang, The winds, lamenting throâ their caves, To Echo bore the notes alang. âYe scatterâd birds that faintly sing, The reliques oâ the vernal queir! Ye woods that shed on aâ the winds The honours of the aged year! A few short months, and glad and gay, Again yeâll charm the ear and eâe; But nocht in all-revolving time Can gladness bring again to me. âI am a bending aged tree, That long has stood the wind and rain; But now has come a cruel blast, And my last hald of earth is gane; Nae leaf oâ mine shall greet the spring, Nae simmer sun exalt my bloom; But I maun lie before the storm, And ithers plant them in my room. âIâve seen sae mony changefuâ years, On earth I am a stranger grown: I wander in the ways of men, Alike unknowing, and unknown: Unheard, unpitied, unrelievâd, I bear alane my lade oâ care, For silent, low, on beds of dust, Lie aâ hat would my sorrows share. âAnd last, (the sum of aâ my griefs!) My noble master lies in clay; The flowâr amang our barons bold, His countryâs pride, his countryâs stay: In weary being now I pine, For aâ the life of life is dead, And hope has left may aged ken, On forward wing for ever fled. âAwake thy last sad voice, my harp! The voice of woe and wild despair! Awake, resound thy latest lay, Then sleep in silence evermair! And thou, my last, best, only, friend, That fillest an untimely tomb, Accept this tribute from the Bard Thou brought from Fortuneâs mirkest gloom. âIn Povertyâs low barren vale, Thick mists obscure involvâd me round; Though oft I turnâd the wistful eye, Nae ray of fame was to be found: Thou foundâst me, like the morning sun That melts the fogs in limpid air, The friendless bard and rustic song Became alike thy fostering care. âO! why has worth so short a date, While villains ripen grey with time? Must thou, the noble, genârous, great, Fall in bold manhoodâs hardy prim Why did I live to see that dayâ A day to me so full of woe? O! had I met the mortal shaft That laid my benefactor low! âThe bridegroom may forget the bride Was made his wedded wife yestreen; The monarch may forget the crown That on his head an hour has been; The mother may forget the child That smiles sae sweetly on her knee; But Iâll remember thee, Glencairn, And aâ that thou hast done for me!â

With The Lament On The Death Of the Earl Of Glencairn

Each eye it cheers when she appears, Like Phoebus in the morning, When past the shower, and every flower The garden is adorning: As the wretch looks oâer Siberiaâs shore, When winter-bound the wave is; Sae droops our heart, when we maun part Frae charming, lovely Davies. The Posie

O luve will venture in where it daur na weel be seen, O luve will venture in where wisdom ance has been; But I will doun yon river rove, amang the wood sae green, And aâ to puâ a Posie to my ain dear May. The primrose I will puâ, the firstling oâ the year, And I will puâ the pink, the emblem oâ my dear; For sheâs the pink oâ womankind, and blooms without a peer, And aâ to be a Posie to my ain dear May. Iâll puâ the budding rose, when Phoebus peeps in view, For itâs like a baumy kiss oâ her sweet, bonie mou; The hyacinthâs for constancy wiâ its unchanging blue, And aâ to be a Posie to my ain dear May. The lily it is pure, and the lily it is fair, And in her lovely bosom Iâll place the lily there; The daisyâs for simplicity and unaffected air, And aâ to be a Posie to my ain dear May. The hawthorn I will puâ, wiâ its locks oâ siller gray, Where, like an aged man, it stands at break oâ day; But the songsterâs nest within the bush I winna tak away And aâ to be a Posie to my ain dear May. The woodbine I will puâ, when the eâening star is near, And the diamond draps oâ dew shall be her een sae clear; The violetâs for modesty, which weel she faâs to wear, And aâ to be a Posie to my ain dear May. Iâll tie the Posie round wiâ the silken band oâ luve, And Iâll place it in her breast, and Iâll swear by aâ above, That to my latest draught oâ life the band shall neâer remove, And this will be a Posie to my ain dear May.





On Glenriddellâs Fox Breaking His Chain

A Fragment, 1791.
Thou, Liberty, thou art my theme; Not such as idle poets dream, Who trick thee up a heathen goddess That a fantastic cap and rod has; Such stale conceits are poor and silly; I paint thee out, a Highland filly, A sturdy, stubborn, handsome dapple, As sleekâs a mouse, as roundâs an apple, That when thou pleasest canst do wonders; But when thy luckless rider blunders, Or if thy fancy should demur there, Wilt break thy neck ere thou go further. These things premised, I sing a Fox, Was caught among his native rocks, And to a dirty kennel chained, How he his liberty regained. Glenriddell! Whig without a stain, A Whig in principle and grain, Couldâst thou enslave a free-born creature, A native denizen of Nature? How couldâst thou, with a heart so good, (A better neâer was sluiced with blood!) Nail a poor devil to a tree, That neâer did harm to thine or thee? The staunchest Whig Glenriddell was, Quite frantic in his countryâs cause; And oft was Reynardâs prison passing, And with his brother-Whigs canvassing The Rights of Men, the Powers of Women, With all the dignity of Freemen. Sir Reynard daily heard debates Of Princesâ, Kingsâ, and Nationsâ fates, With many rueful, bloody stories Of Tyrants, Jacobites, and Tories: From liberty how angels fell, That now are galley-slaves in hell; How Nimrod first the trade began Of binding Slaveryâs chains on Man; How fell SemiramisâGod damn her! Did first, with sacrilegious hammer, (All ills till then were trivial matters) For Man dethronâd forge hen-peck fetters; How Xerxes, that abandoned Tory, Thought cutting throats was reaping glory, Until the stubborn Whigs of Sparta Taught him great Natureâs Magna Charta; How mighty Rome her fiat hurlâd Resistless oâer a bowing world, And, kinder than they did desire, Polishâd mankind with sword and fire; With much, too tedious to relate, Of ancient and of modern date, But ending still, how Billy Pitt (Unlucky boy!) with wicked wit, Has gaggâd old Britain, drainâd her coffer, As butchers bind and bleed a heifer, Thus wily Reynard by degrees, In kennel listening at his ease, Suckâd in a mighty stock of knowledge, As much as some folks at a College; Knew Britainâs rights and constitution, Her aggrandisement, diminution, How fortune wrought us good from evil; Let no man, then, despise the Devil, As who should say, âI never can need him,â Since we to scoundrels owe our freedom.





Poem On Pastoral Poetry

Hail, Poesie! thou Nymph reservâd! In chase oâ thee, what crowds hae swervâd Frae common sense, or sunk enervâd âMang heaps oâ clavers: And och! oâer aft thy joes hae starvâd, âMid aâ thy favours! Say, Lassie, why, thy train amang, While loud the trumpâs heroic clang, And sock or buskin skelp alang To death or marriage; Scarce ane has tried the shepherdâsang But wiâ miscarriage? In Homerâs craft Jock Milton thrives; Eschylusâ pen Will Shakespeare drives; Wee Pope, the knurlinâ, till him rives Horatian fame; In thy sweet sang, Barbauld, survives Even Sapphoâs flame. But thee, Theocritus, wha matches? Theyâre no herdâs ballats, Maroâs catches; Squire Pope but busks his skinklinâ patches Oâ heathen tatters: I pass by hunders, nameless wretches, That ape their betters. In this braw age oâ wit and lear, Will nane the Shepherdâs whistle mair Blaw sweetly in its native air, And rural grace; And, wiâ the far-famâd Grecian, share A rival place? Yes! there is aneâa Scottish callan! Thereâs ane; come forrit, honest Allan! Thou need na jouk behint the hallan, A chiel sae clever; The teeth oâ time may gnaw Tantallan, But thouâs for ever. Thou paints auld Nature to the nines, In thy sweet Caledonian lines; Nae gowden stream throâ myrtle twines, Where Philomel, While nightly breezes sweep the vines, Her griefs will tell! In gowany glens thy burnie strays, Where bonie lasses bleach their claes, Or trots by hazelly shaws and braes, Wiâ hawthorns gray, Where blackbirds join the shepherdâs lays, At close oâ day. Thy rural loves are Natureâs selâ; Nae bombast spates oâ nonsense swell; Nae snap conceits, but that sweet spell Oâ witchin love, That charm that can the strongest quell, The sternest move.





Verses On The Destruction Of The Woods Near Drumlanrig

As on the banks oâ wandering Nith, Ae smiling simmer morn I strayâd, And traced its bonie howes and haughs, Where linties sang and lammies playâd, I sat me down upon a craig, And drank my fill oâ fancyâs dream, When from the eddying deep below, Up rose the genius of the stream. Dark, like the frowning rock, his brow, And troubled, like his wintry wave, And deep, as sughs the boding wind Amang his caves, the sigh he gaveâ âAnd come ye here, my son,â he cried, âTo wander in my birken shade? To muse some favourite Scottish theme, Or sing some favourite Scottish maid? âThere was a time, itâs nae lang syne, Ye might hae seen me in my pride, When aâ my banks sae bravely saw Their woody pictures in my tide; When hanging beech and spreading elm Shaded my stream sae clear and cool: And stately oaks their twisted arms Threw broad and dark across the pool; âWhen, glinting throâ the trees, appearâd The wee white cot aboon the mill, And peacefuâ rose its ingle reek, That, slowly curling, clamb the hill. But now the cot is bare and cauld, Its leafy bield for ever gane, And scarce a stinted birk is left To shiver in the blast its lane.â âAlas!â quoth I, âwhat ruefuâ chance Has twinâd ye oâ your stately trees? Has laid your rocky bosom bareâ Has stripped the cleeding oâ your braes? Was it the bitter eastern blast, That scatters blight in early spring? Or wasât the wilâfire scorchâd their boughs, Or canker-worm wiâ secret sting?â âNae eastlin blast,â the sprite replied; âIt blaws na here sae fierce and fell, And on my dry and halesome banks Nae canker-worms get leave to dwell: Man! cruel man!â the genius sighedâ As through the cliffs he sank him downâ âThe worm that gnawâd my bonie trees, That reptile wears a ducal crown.â1





The Gallant Weaver

Where Cart rins rowinâ to the sea, By mony a flower and spreading tree, There lives a lad, the lad for me, He is a gallant Weaver. O, I had wooers aught or nine, They gied me rings and ribbons fine; And I was fearâd my heart wad tine, And I gied it to the Weaver. My daddie signâd my tocher-band, To gie the lad that has the land, But to my heart Iâll add my hand, And give it to the Weaver. While birds rejoice in leafy bowers, While bees delight in opening flowers, While corn grows green in summer showers, I love my gallant Weaver. [Footnote 1: The Duke of Queensberry.]

If to love thy heart denies, Oh, in pity hide the sentence Under friendshipâs kind disguise! Thee, sweet maid, hae I offended? My Bonie Bell

The smiling Spring comes in rejoicing, And surly Winter grimly flies; Now crystal clear are the falling waters, And bonie blue are the sunny skies. Fresh oâer the mountains breaks forth the morning, The evâning gilds the oceanâs swell; All creatures joy in the sunâs returning, And I rejoice in my bonie Bell. The flowery Spring leads sunny Summer, The yellow Autumn presses near; Then in his turn comes gloomy Winter, Till smiling Spring again appear: Thus seasons dancing, life advancing, Old Time and Nature their changes tell; But never ranging, still unchanging, I adore my bonie Bell.

Flow gently, sweet Afton! amang thy green braes, Flow gently, Iâll sing thee a song in thy praise; My Maryâs asleep by thy murmuring stream, Flow gently, sweet Afton, disturb not her dream. Thou stockdove whose echo resounds throâ the glen, Ye wild whistling blackbirds in yon thorny den, Thou green-crested lapwing thy screaming forbear, I charge you, disturb not my slumbering Fair. How lofty, sweet Afton, thy neighbouring hills, Far markâd with the courses of clear, winding rills; There daily I wander as noon rises high, My flocks and my Maryâs sweet cot in my eye. How pleasant thy banks and green valleys below, Where, wild in the woodlands, the primroses blow; There oft, as mild Evâning weeps over the lea, The sweet-scented birk shades my Mary and me. Thy crystal stream, Afton, how lovely it glides, And winds by the cot where my Mary resides; How wanton thy waters her snowy feet lave, As, gathering sweet flowerets, she stems thy clear wave. Flow gently, sweet Afton, amang thy green braes, Flow gently, sweet river, the theme of my lays; My Maryâs asleep by thy murmuring stream, Flow gently, sweet Afton, disturb not her dream.





Address To The Shade Of Thomson

On Crowning His Bust at Ednam, Roxburghshire, with a Wreath of Bays.
While virgin Spring by Edenâs flood, Unfolds her tender mantle green, Or pranks the sod in frolic mood, Or tunes Eolian strains between. While Summer, with a matron grace, Retreats to Dryburghâs cooling shade, Yet oft, delighted, stops to trace The progress of the spiky blade. While Autumn, benefactor kind, By Tweed erects his aged head, And sees, with self-approving mind, Each creature on his bounty fed. While maniac Winter rages oâer The hills whence classic Yarrow flows, Rousing the turbid torrentâs roar, Or sweeping, wild, a waste of snows. So long, sweet Poet of the year! Shall bloom that wreath thou well hast won; While Scotia, with exulting tear, Proclaims that Thomson was her son.

Epistle To John Maxwell, ESQ., Of Terraughty

On His Birthday.
Health to the Maxwellâs veteran Chief! Health, aye unsourâd by care or grief: Inspirâd, I turnâd Fateâs sibyl leaf, This natal morn, I see thy life is stuff oâ prief, Scarce quite half-worn. This day thou metes threescore eleven, And I can tell that bounteous Heaven (The second-sight, ye ken, is given To ilka Poet) On thee a tack oâ seven times seven Will yet bestow it. If envious buckies view wiâ sorrow Thy lengthenâd days on this blest morrow, May Desolationâs lang-teethâd harrow, Nine miles an hour, Rake them, like Sodom and Gomorrah, In brunstane stour. But for thy friends, and they are mony, Baith honest men, and lassies bonie, May couthie Fortune, kind and cannie, In social glee, Wiâ mornings blythe, and eâenings funny, Bless them and thee! Fareweel, auld birkie! Lord be near ye, And then the deil, he daurna steer ye: Your friends aye love, your faes aye fear ye; For me, shame faâ me, If neist my heart I dinna wear ye, While Burns they caâ me.





Second Epistle To Robert Graham, ESQ., Of Fintry

5th October 1791.
Late cripplâd of an arm, and now a leg, About to beg a pass for leave to beg; Dull, listless, teasâd, dejected, and deprest (Nature is adverse to a crippleâs rest); Will generous Graham list to his Poetâs wail? (It soothes poor Misery, hearkening to her tale) And hear him curse the light he first surveyâd, And doubly curse the luckless rhyming trade? Thou, Nature! partial Nature, I arraign; Of thy caprice maternal I complain; The lion and the bull thy care have found, One shakes the forests, and one spurns the ground; Thou givâst the ass his hide, the snail his shell; Thâ envenomâd wasp, victorious, guards his cell; Thy minions kings defend, control, devour, In all thâ omnipotence of rule and power; Foxes and statesmen subtile wiles ensure; The cit and polecat stink, and are secure; Toads with their poison, doctors with their drug, The priest and hedgehog in their robes, are snug; Evân silly woman has her warlike arts, Her tongue and eyesâher dreaded spear and darts. But Oh! thou bitter step-mother and hard, To thy poor, fenceless, naked childâthe Bard! A thing unteachable in worldâs skill, And half an idiot too, more helpless still: No heels to bear him from the opâning dun; No claws to dig, his hated sight to shun; No horns, but those by luckless Hymen worn, And those, alas! not, Amaltheaâs horn: No nerves olfactâry, Mammonâs trusty cur, Clad in rich Dulnessâ comfortable fur; In naked feeling, and in aching pride, He bears thâ unbroken blast from evâry side: Vampyre booksellers drain him to the heart, And scorpion critics cureless venom dart. Criticsâappallâd, I venture on the name; Those cut-throat bandits in the paths of fame: Bloody dissectors, worse than ten Monroes; He hacks to teach, they mangle to expose: His heart by causeless wanton malice wrung, By blockheadsâ daring into madness stung; His well-won bays, than life itself more dear, By miscreants torn, who neâer one sprig must wear; Foilâd, bleeding, torturâd in thâ unequal strife, The hapless Poet flounders on throâ life: Till, fled each hope that once his bosom firâd, And fled each muse that glorious once inspirâd, Low sunk in squalid, unprotected age, Dead even resentment for his injurâd page, He heeds or feels no more the ruthless criticâs rage! So, by some hedge, the genârous steed deceasâd, For half-starvâd snarling curs a dainty feast; By toil and famine wore to skin and bone, Lies, senseless of each tugging bitchâs son. O Dulness! portion of the truly blest! Calm shelterâd haven of eternal rest! Thy sons neâer madden in the fierce extremes Of Fortuneâs polar frost, or torrid beams. If mantling high she fills the golden cup, With sober selfish ease they sip it up; Conscious the bounteous meed they well deserve, They only wonder âsome folksâ do not starve. The grave sage hern thus easy picks his frog, And thinks the mallard a sad worthless dog. When disappointments snaps the clue of hope, And throâ disastrous night they darkling grope, With deaf endurance sluggishly they bear, And just conclude that âfools are fortuneâs care.â So, heavy, passive to the tempestâs shocks, Strong on the sign-post stands the stupid ox. Not so the idle Musesâ mad-cap train, Not such the workings of their moon-struck brain; In equanimity they never dwell, By turns in soaring heavân, or vaulted hell. I dread thee, Fate, relentless and severe, With all a poetâs, husbandâs, fatherâs fear! Already one strong hold of hope is lostâ Glencairn, the truly noble, lies in dust (Fled, like the sun eclipsâd as noon appears, And left us darkling in a world of tears); O! hear my ardent, grateful, selfish prayâr! Fintry, my other stay, long bless and spare! Throâ a long life his hopes and wishes crown, And bright in cloudless skies his sun go down! May bliss domestic smooth his private path; Give energy to life; and soothe his latest breath, With many a filial tear circling the bed of death!

Farewell, thou fair day, thou green earth, and ye skies, Now gay with the broad setting sun; Farewell, loves and friendships, ye dear tender ties, Our race of existence is run! Thou grim King of Terrors; thou Lifeâs gloomy foe! Go, frighten the coward and slave; Go, teach them to tremble, fell tyrant! but know No terrors hast thou to the brave! Thou strikâst the dull peasantâhe sinks in the dark, Nor saves eâen the wreck of a name; Thou strikâst the young heroâa glorious mark; He falls in the blaze of his fame! In the field of proud honourâour swords in our hands, Our King and our country to save; While victory shines on Lifeâs last ebbing sands,â O! who would not die with the brave!

Sensibility, how charming, Dearest Nancy, thou canst tell; But distress, with horrors arming, Thou alas! hast known too well! Fairest flower, behold the lily Blooming in the sunny ray: Let the blast sweep oâer the valley, See it prostrate in the clay. Hear the wood lark charm the forest, Telling oâer his little joys; But alas! a prey the surest To each pirate of the skies. Dearly bought the hidden treasure Finer feelings can bestow: Chords that vibrate sweetest pleasure Thrill the deepest notes of woe.

Thou Gloomy December

Ance mair I hail thee, thou gloomy December! Ance mair I hail thee wiâ sorrow and care; Sad was the parting thou makes me rememberâ Parting wiâ Nancy, oh, neâer to meet mair! Fond loversâ parting is sweet, painful pleasure, Hope beaming mild on the soft parting hour; But the dire feeling, O farewell for ever! Is anguish unmingled, and agony pure! Wild as the winter now tearing the forest, Till the last leaf oâ the summer is flown; Such is the tempest has shaken my bosom, Till my last hope and last comfort is gone. Still as I hail thee, thou gloomy December, Still shall I hail thee wiâ sorrow and care; For sad was the parting thou makes me remember, Parting wiâ Nancy, oh, neâer to meet mair.

O sad and heavy, should I part, But for her sake, sae far awa; Unknowing what my way may thwart, My native land sae far awa. The Rights Of Woman

An Occasional Address. Spoken by Miss Fontenelle on her benefit night, November 26, 1792.
While Europeâs eye is fixâd on mighty things, The fate of Empires and the fall of Kings; While quacks of State must each produce his plan, And even children lisp the Rights of Man; Amid this mighty fuss just let me mention, The Rights of Woman merit some attention. First, in the Sexesâ intermixâd connection, One sacred Right of Woman is, protection.â The tender flower that lifts its head, elate, Helpless, must fall before the blasts of Fate, Sunk on the earth, defacâd its lovely form, Unless your shelter ward thâ impending storm. Our second Rightâbut needless here is caution, To keep that right inviolateâs the fashion; Each man of sense has it so full before him, Heâd die before heâd wrong itââtis decorum.â There was, indeed, in far less polishâd days, A time, when rough rude man had naughty ways, Would swagger, swear, get drunk, kick up a riot, Nay even thus invade a Ladyâs quiet. Now, thank our stars! those Gothic times are fled; Now, well-bred menâand you are all well-bredâ Most justly think (and we are much the gainers) Such conduct neither spirit, wit, nor manners. For Right the third, our last, our best, our dearest, That right to fluttering female hearts the nearest; Which even the Rights of Kings, in low prostration, Most humbly ownââtis dear, dear admiration! In that blest sphere alone we live and move; There taste that life of lifeâimmortal love. Smiles, glances, sighs, tears, fits, flirtations, airs; âGainst such an host what flinty savage dares, When awful Beauty joins with all her charmsâ Who is so rash as rise in rebel arms? But truce with kings, and truce with constitutions, With bloody armaments and revolutions; Let Majesty your first attention summon, Ah! ca ira! The Majesty Of Woman!

There was a lass, and she was fair, At kirk or market to be seen; When aâ our fairest maids were met, The fairest maid was bonie Jean. From those drear solitudes and frowsy cells, Where Infamy with sad Repentance dwells; Where turnkeys make the jealous portal fast, And deal from iron hands the spare repast; Where truant âprentices, yet young in sin, Blush at the curious stranger peeping in; Where strumpets, relics of the drunken roar, Resolve to drink, nay, half, to whore, no more; Where tiny thieves not destinâd yet to swing, Beat hemp for others, riper for the string: From these dire scenes my wretched lines I date, To tell Maria her Esopusâ fate. âAlas! I feel I am no actor here!â âTis real hangmen real scourges bear! Prepare Maria, for a horrid tale Will turn thy very rouge to deadly pale; Will make thy hair, thoâ erst from gipsy pollâd, By barber woven, and by barber sold, Though twisted smooth with Harryâs nicest care, Like hoary bristles to erect and stare. The hero of the mimic scene, no more I start in Hamlet, in Othello roar; Or, haughty Chieftain, âmid the din of arms In Highland Bonnet, woo Malvinaâs charms; While sans-culottes stoop up the mountain high, And steal from me Mariaâs prying eye. Blest Highland bonnet! once my proudest dress, Now prouder still, Mariaâs temples press; I see her wave thy towering plumes afar, And call each coxcomb to the wordy war: I see her face the first of Irelandâs sons, And even out-Irish his Hibernian bronze; The crafty Colonel leaves the tartanâd lines, For other wars, where he a hero shines: The hopeful youth, in Scottish senate bred, Who owns a Bushbyâs heart without the head, Comes âmid a string of coxcombs, to display That veni, vidi, vici, is his way: The shrinking Bard adown the alley skulks, And dreads a meeting worse than Woolwich hulks: Though there, his heresies in Church and State Might well award him Muir and Palmerâs fate: Still she undaunted reels and rattles on, And dares the public like a noontide sun. What scandal called Mariaâs jaunty stagger The ricket reeling of a crooked swagger? Whose spleen (eâen worse than Burnsâ venom, when He dips in gall unmixâd his eager pen, And pours his vengeance in the burning line,)â Who christenâd thus Mariaâs lyre-divine The idiot strum of Vanity bemusâd, And even the abuse of Poesy abusâd?â Who called her verse a Parish Workhouse, made For motley foundling Fancies, stolen or strayed? A Workhouse! ah, that sound awakes my woes, And pillows on the thorn my rackâd repose! In durance vile here must I wake and weep, And all my frowsy couch in sorrow steep; That straw where many a rogue has lain of yore, And verminâd gipsies litterâd heretofore. Why, Lonsdale, thus thy wrath on vagrants pour? Must earth no rascal save thyself endure? Must thou alone in guilt immortal swell, And make a vast monopoly of hell? Thou knowâst the Virtues cannot hate thee worse; The Vices also, must they club their curse? Or must no tiny sin to others fall, Because thy guiltâs supreme enough for all? Maria, send me too thy griefs and cares; In all of thee sure thy Esopus shares. As thou at all mankind the flag unfurls, Who on my fair one Satireâs vengeance hurlsâ Who calls thee, pert, affected, vain coquette, A wit in folly, and a fool in wit! Who says that fool alone is not thy due, And quotes thy treacheries to prove it true! Our force united on thy foes weâll turn, And dare the war with all of woman born: For who can write and speak as thou and I? My periods that deciphering defy, And thy still matchless tongue that conquers all reply!

A tyrantâs proudest insults bravâd, They shoutâa People freed! They hail an Empire saved. Where is manâs god-like form? Immingled with the mighty dead, Beneath that hallowâd turf where Wallace lies Hear it not, Wallace! in thy bed of death. Inscription

Written on the blank leaf of a copy of the last edition of my poems, presented to the Lady whom, in so many fictitious reveries of passion, but with the most ardent sentiments of real friendship, I have so often sung under the name ofââChloris.â1

âTis Friendshipâs pledge, my young, fair Friend, Nor thou the gift refuse, Nor with unwilling ear attend The moralising Muse. Since thou, in all thy youth and charms, Must bid the world adieu, (A world âgainst Peace in constant arms) To join the Friendly Few. Since, thy gay morn of life oâercast, Chill came the tempestâs lour; (And neâer Misfortuneâs eastern blast Did nip a fairer flower.) Since lifeâs gay scenes must charm no more, Still much is left behind, Still nobler wealth hast thou in storeâ The comforts of the mind! Thine is the self-approving glow, Of conscious Honourâs part; And (dearest gift of Heaven below) Thine Friendshipâs truest heart. The joys refinâd of Sense and Taste, With every Muse to rove: And doubly were the Poet blest, These joys could he improve. R.B. [Footnote 1: Miss Lorimer.]

This Hal for genius, wit and lore, Among the first was numberâd; But pious Bob, âmid learningâs store, Commandment the tenth rememberâd: Yet simple Bob the victory got, And wan his heartâs desire, Which shews that heaven can boil the pot, Thoâ the devil piss in the fire. O what a canty world were it, Would pain and care and sickness spare it; And Fortune favour worth and merit As they deserve; And aye rowth oâ roast-beef and claret, Syne, wha wad starve? Then that curst carmagnole, auld Satan, Watches like baudrons by a ratton Our sinfuâ saul to get a claut on, Wiâfelon ire; Syne, whip! his tail yeâll neâer cast saut on, Heâs aff like fire. Ah Nick! ah Nick! it is na fair, First showing us the tempting ware, Bright wines, and bonie lasses rare, To put us daft Syne weave, unseen, thy spider snare O hellâs damned waft. Poor Man, the flie, aft bizzes by, And aft, as chance he comes thee nigh, Thy damnâd auld elbow yeuks wiâjoy And hellish pleasure! Already in thy fancyâs eye, Thy sicker treasure. Soon, heels oâer gowdie, in he gangs, And, like a sheep-head on a tangs, Thy girning laugh enjoys his pangs, And murdering wrestle, As, dangling in the wind, he hangs, A gibbetâs tassel. But lest you think I am uncivil To plague you with this draunting drivel, Abjuring aâ intentions evil, I quat my pen, The Lord preserve us frae the devil! Amen! Amen!

Complimentary Versicles To Jessie Lewars

The Toast Fill me with the rosy wine, Call a toast, a toast divine: Giveth me Poetâs darling flame, Lovely Jessie be her name; Then thou mayest freely boast, Thou hast given a peerless toast.
The Menagerie Talk not to me of savages, From Africâs burning sun; No savage eâer could rend my heart, As Jessie, thou hast done: But Jessieâs lovely hand in mine, A mutual faith to plight, Not even to view the heavenly choir, Would be so blest a sight.
Jessieâs illness Say, sages, whatâs the charm on earth Can turn Deathâs dart aside! It is not purity and worth, Else Jessie had not died.
On Her Recovery But rarely seen since Natureâs birth, The natives of the sky; Yet still one seraphâs left on earth, For Jessie did not die.

ChorusâO lay thy loof in mine, lass, In mine, lass, in mine, lass; And swear on thy white hand, lass, That thou wilt be my ain. Thereâs mony a lass has broke my rest, That for a blink I hae loâed best; But thou art Queen within my breast, For ever to remain. O lay thy loof, &c.

ChorusâHereâs a health to ane I loe dear, Hereâs a health to ane I loe dear; Thou art sweet as the smile when fond lovers meet, And soft as their parting tearâJessy. I guess by the dear angel smile, I guess by the love-rolling eâe; But why urge the tender confession, âGainst Fortuneâs fell, cruel decree?âJessy. Hereâs a health, &c.





O Wert Thou In The Cauld Blast

O wert thou in the cauld blast, On yonder lea, on yonder lea, My plaidie to the angry airt, Iâd shelter thee, Iâd shelter thee; Or did Misfortuneâs bitter storms Around thee blaw, around thee blaw, Thy bield should be my bosom, To share it aâ, to share it aâ. Or were I in the wildest waste, Sae black and bare, sae black and bare, The desert were a Paradise, If thou wert there, if thou wert there; Or were I Monarch oâ the globe, Wiâ thee to reign, wiâ thee to reign, The brightest jewel in my Crown Wad be my Queen, wad be my Queen.





Inscription To Miss Jessy Lewars

On a copy of the Scots Musical Museum, in four volumes, presented to her by Burns. 1

Thine be the volumes, Jessy fair, And with them take the Poetâs prayer, That Fate may, in her fairest page, With evâry kindliest, best presage Of future bliss, enroll thy name: With native worth and spotless fame, And wakeful caution, still aware Of illâbut chief, Manâs felon snare; All blameless joys on earth we find, And all the treasures of the mindâ These be thy guardian and reward; So prays thy faithful friend, the Bard. Dumfries, June 26, 1769. [Footnote 1: Written for music played by Miss Lewars, who nursed him in his last illness.]
